12414-the-inferno:
Henri Barbusse, author of Under Fire, wrote The Inferno, translated from the hundredth French edition in 1918 with an introduction by Edward J. O Brien. Barbusse novel is a study of voyeurism, desire, and solitude, not the Dante hell of its title.

The narrator takes a room in Madame Lemercier boarding house, grey and dusty smelling, with two chairs and his valise. Through a peephole in the wall he watches other lodgers love, quarrel, pray, and die, and the scenes become a mirror of his own longing. A mid-book memory recalls a father in a shaggy cloak and felt cap, on a lawn strewn with flowers in summer and leaves in winter. The novel is intense, erotic, and philosophical.
12527-kimono:
John Paris's 1922 novel, Kimono, follows an Anglo-Japanese marriage, honeymoon and journey eastward to Nagasaki and across Japan. Chapters run from the embassy and a half-caste girl to Ito San, Yoshiwara women, a geisha dinner and fallen cherry blossoms. The family altar, dwarf trees, Eurasia, the great Buddha, the rainy season and Nikko mountains follow.

Yaé Smith, the kimono itself, Fujinami Asako, real Shinto, an autumn festival, Japanese courtship, alone in Tokyo and Lady Brandan complete the tale. Paris, writing after years in Japan, mixes romance with observation of custom. The novel offers a period view of East meeting West, lyrical in places, dated in others, and vivid on Japan itself.
13218-don-orsino:
F. Marion Crawford's Don Orsino, first published in 1891 and reprinted to a fifty-sixth thousand, follows a young Roman of the Saracinesca house. Orsino lives in the younger Rome with his parents in a vast old palace that has sheltered his family in peace and war, rarely holding three generations at once for twenty-one years. Crawford sets old rank against new Rome.

Orsino reads the daily chronicle of Roman life and watches who dines with whom, noting Madame d'Aranjuez in olive-green brocade at the Del Ferice party. He writes to Maria Consuelo at a Paris address she left two years before, and she asks who gave it him. The novel is a rich society tale, full of rank, gossip, and love in a changing city.
13489-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, volume one for 1895, offers plates and short essays for architects and students, published in Boston by Bates and Guild. Venetian palaces lead the list: the Ducal Palace, Palazzo Contarini Fasan, Palazzo Cavalli, and the Ca d'Oro, with window tracery drawn in detail.

Byzantine-Romanesque doorways of Apulia follow, from Trani and Conversano to Altamura and Loreto. Notes explain why Venice, secure behind natural defences, built palaces open to the water while neighbours walled themselves in. The Ca d'Oro, next to the Ducal Palace, is praised as the most beautiful Gothic palace in Venice, much changed by restoration.
14291-the-story-of-geographical-discover:
Joseph Jacobs told how the world became known in this illustrated history with twenty-four maps. Chapters run from the world as ancients knew it through conquest, dark ages, and medieval travels with Marco Polo and Ibn Batuta. Roads and commerce explain how knowledge moved, before Portuguese, Spanish, and northern routes split the Indies quest three ways.

Explorers fill the later chapters. Prince Henry and Vasco da Gama sail east, Columbus and Magellan west, while English, French, Dutch, and Russian sailors probe north. Tasman and Cook open Australia and the South Seas, and Park, Livingstone, and Stanley map Africa's interior. Jacobs notes how steam and American expansion finally revealed lands between Mississippi and Rockies, ceded by Napoleon in 1803. A clear, map-minded history for readers who love voyages.
14987-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration for October 1895, volume one number ten, presents French farmhouses, with a plate of Ferme de Turpe in Normandy. Its editors explain that the series aims to cover a wide field while giving subscribers only what will be useful.

Italian work has formed most plates so far, but domestic architecture of France and England has served as a model for much American work, especially in the present generation. French chateaux stand behind more pretentious American residences, as recent productions show. The number suits architects and students who want clear plates of farmhouses that shaped American domestic design.
15020-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration for November 1895, volume one number eleven, presents country houses of Normandy, with a plate of Ferme la Vallauine. Houses chosen differ in type, date, station of their builders and materials, yet all lie in Normandy in northern France and outside towns.

Beyond that, the editors warn, classification is unwise, for variety is the point. Like the French farmhouses of the previous issue, these country houses offer models for American domestic work. The number suits architects, students and lovers of old houses who want clear plates and short notes on buildings shaped by land, climate and local craft.
15091-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
This February 1895 number of an architectural picture series shows Byzantine-Romanesque doorways in southern Italy, with the cathedral at Trani on its cover plate. The text explains Apulia, the heel of Italy's boot, where Roman traditions met trade with the Levant through Venice and Pisa. Styles blend there in ways that defy neat labels.

Plates let readers study carved doorways stone by stone, while short notes point out Roman and Byzantine traits side by side. The issue served architects and students who learned by looking. Even today it works as a clear, visual guide to a rich corner of medieval building.
15270-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
This July 1895 number of the Brochure Series shows Italian wrought iron, from medieval work through the Renaissance to the last century. The text argues that limits of hand work gave even crude iron pieces the virtues of true decorative art. Lack of machinery, it says, forced honest design and execution.

Plates display gates, grilles, and fittings from Italy, France, and Germany, with notes on craft and form. The issue served architects who learned by looking at good work. Modern readers interested in ironwork will find the number a clear, visual primer on a noble craft.
15467-the-first-soprano:
Mary Hitchcock published this religious novel in Cleveland in 1912, through the Union Gospel Press. It opens on a Sunday morning in a church at New Laodicea, where the organ prelude fills a stately building and the choir takes its place in the rear gallery. Worshipers file down carpeted aisles as stained windows tint the light in blue, violet, and crimson.

Chapters follow a first soprano through choir rehearsals, a confession, a church social, a missionary meeting, and hard questions about faith. Titles such as Is God Demonstrable, Two of Me, and God, My Exceeding Joy mark the spiritual path. The novel blends church life with inward struggle, asking how music, pride, and belief fit together in one woman's walk of faith.
15872-the-memories-of-fifty-years-contai:
A memoir by W. H. Sparks, issued in Philadelphia by Claxton, Remsen and Haffelfinger, and in Macon by J. W. Burke and Company, in 1870. Sparks dedicates the volume to his brother Ovid Garten Sparks and his nephew Colonel Thomas Hardeman of Macon. Fifty years of observation, chiefly spent in the Southwest, fill its pages. Brief lives of distinguished Americans join anecdotes of remarkable men.

Scenes and incidents from a long life break the biographies: courts, camps, and frontier towns. Sparks writes as an aged relative, affectionate and plain. His memories give the Southwest a human face, before railroads changed it. The book still serves historians: a witness to American life, told in stories rather than in dates.
1629-i-say-no:
Wilkie Collins's I Say No opens at school, where a smuggled supper in a black and still bedroom sets a girl's story in motion. From schoolroom secrets the novel moves to a woman's refusal, a title that echoes through love, money, and a mystery of identity, with Collins's usual blend of domestic detail and sensation.

Through bedrooms, gardens, and watchdogs asleep in the calm, the plot builds toward a heroine who will not be moved. The novel is long and winding. It is a late Collins work for readers who enjoy his full, leisurely manner and his determined heroines.
1643-meno:
Plato's Meno, translated by Benjamin Jowett, opens abruptly with Meno asking whether virtue can be taught. Socrates replies that he does not yet know what virtue is, and has never met anyone who did, though he has met Gorgias at Athens and remembers him badly.

From this puzzle the dialogue moves to learning as recollection, shown when a slave boy, questioned by Socrates, works out a geometry problem he was never taught. The talk ends without a settled answer. The Meno is a central Platonic text on knowledge, teaching, and the soul.
17160-modern-prose-and-poetry-for-second:
Margaret Ashmun edited this 1914 school reader with notes, study helps, and reading lists for secondary pupils. Selections run from F. Hopkinson Smith's day at Laguerre's and Aldrich's Quite So to Whitman's lilac-time warble, his learned astronomer, and a strange vigil on the field. Mary Johnston, Mary Antin, Howells, and Stedman add prose and verse beside them.

Each piece comes by special permission, with helps for teachers and pupils alike. The set aims to build taste and skill in reading modern American work. Teachers and students of period school books will find a rich, well-chosen anthology, still useful as a sampler of early-1900s American letters.
18852-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, volume one, number three, dated March 1895, presents the cloister at Monreale near Palermo in Sicily. Its essay first sketches Sicily itself, a near-triangle facing Italy, Greece, and Africa, overrun in turn by Greeks, Carthaginians, Romans, Byzantines, Moors, and Normans.

Most surviving monuments, it explains, belong to Byzantine, Saracenic, and Romanesque work, mixed because each new master added forms to those already in use. Palermo, on the northern coast, felt Norman rule strongly, and its Romanesque buildings carry Byzantine and Saracenic detail in rich color. The issue's plates show that blend at work, in a series made for architects and students of building.
19262-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
This April 1895 number of The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration treats Byzantine-Romanesque windows in southern Italy. Photographs made under Signor Boni, an Italian official for historic monuments, show Apulia, a poor, barren region where inland towns are seldom visited and rich medieval work hides. Bari and Brindisi are the known ports.

Later pages report the Rotch Travelling Scholarship, won by William S. Aldrich, late of McKim, Mead and White and Peabody and Stearns, after work on Tremont Temple and World's Fair buildings. Readers get a scholarly architectural journal on southern Italian windows and American practice.
19364-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
This May 1895 number of The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration treats two Florentine pavements. San Miniato al Monte, outside Florence, and the Baptistery of San Giovanni Battista are praised as fine Tuscan Romanesque works of the early twelfth century, alike yet different in plan. The interior of San Miniato earns special praise.

Later pages turn to modern floors, from Johnson parquetry to mosaic work for corridors and entrances, warning that bad mosaic work proves the need for a firm of repute. Readers get a handsome architectural journal on historic pavements and modern floor craft.
19444-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
This number of the Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, from June of eighteen ninety-five, studies Renaissance panels from Perugia. Carved walnut panels from the choir stalls of San Pietro, designed in the fifteen hundreds, show the later Italian Renaissance style at its best.

The text traces the ornament from flat painted pilasters, after Raphael's Vatican work, to carving on many kinds of objects. A note on art theory closes the number, praising clear writing on beauty for readers without training in philosophy. It is a small, rich lesson in design.
19769-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration gave architects plates of classic buildings. This number treats Greek art at its height. It covers the Parthenon era, just after the middle of the fifth century BC. The Erechtheion and Propylaea followed a few years later, the text notes. Exact dates for all three remain in doubt. The series aimed at working designers, not just scholars.

Architects once learned the classical orders from plates like these. Good measured images were hard to get before cheap photography. A brochure series put Athens on the drafting table. American classic revival buildings owe much to such pages. Students of the Greek Revival will value the selection. It shows what the profession admired and copied.
20223-two-boys-in-wyoming-a-tale-of-adve:
Two Boys in Wyoming is a tale of adventure in the Northwest Series. Jack Dudley, at seventeen, is the bright son of a rich merchant. His father means him for the legal profession in due time. Jack leads his class at the Orphion Academy in study and sport alike.

He is also a fine athlete who loves outdoor life deeply. Wyoming offers space where such a boy can test himself fully. Ranch life, wild country, and risk pull him far from law books. Readers get a classic boys' western of grit, friendship, and wide skies.
24776-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration shows American houses of its day in this issue, mostly in Massachusetts and Rhode Island. Full-page pictures present shingle-style homes at Monument Beach, Woburn, Brookline, Bar Harbor, and Newport, naming each architect and the stain used on its shingles. Later pages turn to design contests and prize drawings.

Judges' notes praise or fault lettering, drawing, and placing, and honorable mentions list young designers by name and address. The issue thus mixes a picture book of fine houses with a working journal for architects. Readers interested in early American domestic design will find real homes, real firms, and the taste of the period on every page.
25735-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, volume one, number nine for September 1895, treats pulpits of southern Italy. Pulpits and ambos chosen for pictures stand out for wonderful mosaic work among the finest ever executed.

Cosmati work, the Roman mosaic or inlay named for that family, appears in plate seventy-one. Its design and method match other plates. One difference marks southern work. Bands and borders of geometrical patterns in Sicily and southern Italy use glass or composition largely. Cosmati confined themselves to coloured marbles, with gold rich in the south.
2576-alps-and-sanctuaries-of-piedmont-an:
Samuel Butler, author of Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh, wrote this travel book on the Alps and shrines of Piedmont and the canton of Ticino. The 1913 edition adds his own revisions, an index, and an introduction by R. A. Streatfeild, with etchings of chapels and mountain scenes.

Butler walks from village to sanctuary, noting frescoes, local saints, and the odd humors of guides and priests. His eye is that of a painter and a skeptic, fond of out of the way art. The book charms as a ramble through Italian Switzerland, where faith, landscape, and village life meet on steep paths.
281-father-damien-an-open-letter-to-the-:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote from Sydney on February 25, 1890, to defend Father Damien of Molokai. His open letter to the Reverend Dr. Hyde of Honolulu answers Hyde's attack on the priest who served lepers. Stevenson grants Hyde's past courtesies, then sets duty above gratitude.

Stevenson argues that Hyde's letter to Reverend Gage would absolve any debt of thanks. He invokes the devil's advocate who must speak against a saint a century after death. The letter's scorn and eloquence made it famous. It stands as a classic defense of a maligned good man.
29112-the-bow-its-history-manufacture-an:
Henry Saint-George wrote The Bow: Its History, Manufacture and Use, number three in The Strad Library, in a third edition published in London and New York in 1922, illustrated by the author. Saint-George opens by wondering that the bow, which the fiddle needs in order to sound at all, has received so scant attention from fiddlers and writers alike. Of twenty violinists who know Cremonese fiddles, barely three care for the bow beyond finding one that suits them.

Players know the names of Dodd and Tourte, but seldom more, and few fiddle experts claim real authority on bows as works of art. Saint-George wrote to bring the bow into general notice, and to stir interest in its making and use. Readers get a specialist's loving study, useful to violinists and to anyone curious about craft.
29340-the-story-of-the-great-war-volume-:
Francis J. Reynolds edited this fourth volume of The Story of the Great War, a history of the European war from official sources, covering Champagne, Artois, and Grodno among its campaigns. Like its companions, it is illustrated with drawings, maps, and photographs, and gathers complete historical records of events to date. The volume is the fourth of eight.

Parts cover war in Syria and Egypt, war in the air, the western front, the war at sea, and the eastern front. Later parts treat the Balkans, the Dardanelles and the Russo-Turkish campaign, Italy in the war, Mesopotamia, and the United States and the belligerents. Readers get a contemporary illustrated history of the war's campaigns, written from official sources while the war continued.
30180-perugino:
Selwyn Brinton presents Pietro Perugino, 1446 to 1524, in the Masterpieces in Colour series edited by T. Leman Hare. Eight reproductions in colour anchor the short life and study, from the Virgin and Child with Adoring Angels in the National Gallery, London, to St. Sebastian in the Louvre and the Deposition in the Pitti Palace, Florence. Other plates show St. Mary Magdalen, the Virgin with little St. John, Francesco delle Opere, the Dead Christ, and a second Virgin and Child.

Brinton notes the centre panel of the great altarpiece made for the Certosa of Pavia. Completed in 1499 for Duke Lodovico of Milan, its lower panels now hang as copies in the church. The book suits readers who want a brief, picture-led guide to a master of calm religious art, with each plate tied to its gallery and its place in Perugino's best period.
33085-the-admirable-bashville-or-constan:
Bernard Shaw's Admirable Bashville, or Constancy Unrewarded, turns his novel Cashel Byron's Profession into a stage play in three acts and in blank verse. It adds a note on modern prize fighting. It was published by Brentano's in 1913 at forty cents net. Shaw, already known for plays pleasant and unpleasant, Man and Superman. Major Barbara, takes a boxer hero and a society lady and lets their romance play out in verse, where fists and feelings meet on equal terms.

The play's joke is serious: a prizefighter's constancy, admired in the ring, earns little reward in drawing rooms that prize polish over loyalty. Shaw uses blank verse to lift a sporting story into comedy of manners, and his note on prize fighting argues the case for the sport he dramatizes. It is a witty, unusual Shaw piece, short, sharp, and fond of its fighting hero.
37969-the-marquis-of-pen-alta-marta-y-ma:
Armando Palacio Valdes wrote a realistic social novel Englished from the Spanish by Nathan Haskell Dole and printed at New York in 1886. In the street opens the tale, then the soiree at the Elorza mansion and the nine days' festival of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. How the Marquis of Penalta was converted into Duke of Thuringen follows.

The road to perfection, in search of Menino, and husband or soul fill the middle. As you like it, an excursion to El Moral and the island, and a strange circumstance lead to gathered threads. The labors of a Christian virgin, Pallida Mors, and the marquis's dream close the book. Though Marta y Maria may not be a beautiful novel, it is a realistic one, the author holds in his prologue. Faith and fashion fight for two sisters.
38045-marvels-of-scientific-invention-an:
Marvels of Scientific Invention is a plain-language account by Thomas Corbin. Lippincott of Philadelphia and Seeley, Service of London shared the book in 1917. Thirty-two illustrations and diagrams back the non-technical telling of it. Corbin had writ Engineering of To-Day and Mechanical Inventions of To-Day. A huge lighthouse lamp for Chilang in China fronts the volume.

Digging with dynamite opens the chapters of modern wonders told here. Measuring electricity, the fuel of the future, and machine-made cold follow. Inventions at sea and the gyro-compass fill the middle of the book. Torpedoes and submarine mines get a chapter of their own in wartime. Gold recovery and intense heat stand among the later marvels told. Folk fear the word explosion and shudder at dynamite, he opens. Yet farmers may one day count it among their trusty tools.
39799-bobby-blake-at-rockledge-school-or:
Warner's school story sends Bobby Blake to Rockledge to win the medal of honor. Whitman published it at Racine, Wisconsin, under a 1915 copyright, in the Bobby Blake series that began at Bass Cove. The first chapter, The Overland Limited, is a game: Bobby comes down the stairs of the Blake house in Clinton whistling like a steam engine. His red-haired friend comes to the porch to find him, and Meena, the Swedish girl, guards her clean kitchen against boys.

The contents promise the schoolboy round. There are apples and Applethwaite Plunkit, Fred in trouble, a fish fry, and a startling announcement. At Rockledge come new surroundings, the dormitory, and the Poguey fight. The honor medal is explained, lost boys are found at sea, and red hair stands for more than temper. The winner of the medal closes the book, as the title requires.
41537-the-divine-comedy-of-dante-alighie:
James Romanes Sibbald translated The Divine Comedy of Dante Alighieri, here the Inferno, with notes and an introductory essay, published at Edinburgh by David Douglas in MDCCCLXXXIV. A preface speaks for the translator. Sibbald strove to be faithful to the words as well as to the sense of his author, he says. The translation is not offered as always closely literal, he grants.

The kind of verse used best fits the measured strength of Dante terza rima, Sibbald holds. Yet its constant demand for rhymes makes the translator in some degree its servant, he adds. Students who wish to follow the poet word by word will find what they need in Dr J A Carlyle prose version, he notes. His own debts to that version are many, he grants. The notes draw largely on existing commentaries. Poetry readers get a Victorian verse Inferno, canto by canto.
4228-giordano-bruno:
Walter Horatio Pater imagined this portrait of Giordano Bruno in Paris in 1586. The scene is the afternoon of Pentecost. Curious Parisians gather to hear a Dominican brother speak of the Spirit and of freedom. The city is full of Italian fashions, courtiers, and suspicion of newcomers.

The piece is less a straight biography than a study of a mind. It follows Bruno's talk of the Spirit and his independence. It captures the charged religious air of Paris under a king surrounded by Italians. Pater uses one afternoon to suggest why Bruno unsettled churchmen and scholars alike.
43957-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appletons Popular Science Monthly for November 1898 opens volume fifty four. Youmans edited the New York magazine founded by his father Edward. Morse asks if Middle America was peopled from Asia first. Dodge treats possible fibre industries of the United States with plates.

Herbert Spencer asks what social evolution is in the third piece. Torrents of Switzerland, colony evolution, and forms in nature follow. The mongoose in Jamaica, cause of rain, and dream and reality appear. A sketch of chemist Frank Clarke closes the number contents. Yellow ant herds and a practical Dutch charity fill two more pieces of the number.
44092-plays-of-old-japan-the-no:
Plays of Old Japan, on the Nō drama, by Marie Stopes, brings the classic theatre of Japan to English readers. The title page is ringed with notices of kindred books on Japanese art. Those notices list works on colour prints, on Japanese plays, and on the literature of Japan. The Nō is the stately masked drama of old Japan.

Stopes was among the first to set the Nō plays before a wide English public. The plays are short, grave, and full of ghosts and memory. A warrior, a god, or a wandering spirit stands at the heart of each. Dance, chant, and flute carry what little action there is. The book gives texts and accounts of this spare art. It opened a window on a theatre most western readers had never seen.
44097-appletons-popular-science-monthly-:
Appletons' Popular Science Monthly for January 1899 is number three of volume 54 of that magazine. The volume ran from November 1898 to April 1899. The magazine was set up by Edward L. Youmans and edited by William Jay Youmans. It came out in New York from D. Appleton and Company. The contents set out the range of the number.

The Evolution of Colonies, on industrial evolution, by James Collier stands first. The Mind's Eye, by Professor Joseph Jastrow, stands next, with pictures. Nature Study in the Philadelphia Normal School and a piece on the diffusion of taxes by David A. Wells stand in the list. Our Florida Alligator, by I. W. Blake, stands there too. The number is a sample of the science writing sold to the broad public of its day.
46326-brick-and-marble-in-the-middle-age:
The hosted copy is the second edition, printed at London by John Murray in 1874. Street also wrote on the Gothic architecture of Spain. The book is filled with illustrations. Its frontispiece shows the north porch of Santa Maria Maggiore at Bergamo.

Street was an architect, a member of the Royal Academy, who travelled to look at buildings with his own eyes. The tours recorded here take in the churches and town halls of northern Italy. The volume was first dedicated in 1855 to Samuel Wilberforce, bishop of Winchester. After the bishop's death the author inscribed it again to his memory, in gratitude for many kindnesses. Books of this kind taught Victorian readers to see medieval building as a living art. Street writes as a working architect, noting how walls were raised, arches turned and ornament cut, town by town.
46524-the-pleasant-historie-of-the-conqu:
The Pleasant Historie of the Conquest of the West India, now called New Spain, was translated out of the Spanish tongue by T N. It was imprinted at London by Henry Bynneman in fifteen seventy eight. Hernando Cortes is its hero. The translator dedicated it to Sir Francis Walsingham, the Queen principal secretary.

He had abode in the Isle of Palma on merchandise affairs, he says. There he had conference with ancient gentlemen who had served in the conquest under Cortes, he writes. They told him the history is a most true and just report of matter past, he says. He calls it a mirror and excellent precedent for all who govern new discoveries. Glory and renown are not gotten but with great pains, travail, peril, and danger of life, he promises. Historians get the first English telling of the conquest of Mexico.
46682-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Number 680 of Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art came out on Saturday, January 6, 1877. William and Robert Chambers ran the weekly, and the price was three halfpence. The first piece is a serial tale called The Last of the Haddons. Its author, Newman, had written a book called Too Late.

The tale opens at a large, gloomy house in a dull street in Westminster. The teller has an address in hand and a card for Wentworth, who lives there. A tall, grim woman opens the door a crack and tries to turn the guest away. She claims the call is late and that Wentworth can see no one. The guest holds firm and wins a way into the hall. The scene sets a mood of pride, want, and secrets behind a once grand door.
46739-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 681 of the fourth series, was dated Saturday, January 13, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly. The lead essay, A Wasted Existence, attacks a new life of Camille Desmoulins by the French writer Jules Claretie, in English dress.

The essay fears that books now gloss over the worst men of the French Revolution and hold them up for pity. Robespierre, Marat, Danton, and others, it argues, were too set in evil to earn soft words. Claretie's book, near five hundred pages from fresh papers, is treated as a handsome start to a bad trend. The piece shows Victorian taste for stern moral judgment.
46780-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
William and Robert Chambers ran this weekly journal of tales, science, and art for a wide public. Number 682, fourth series, came out on Saturday, January 20, 1877. The price was a penny and a half, and a scheme for a town of health leads the number.

Hygeia: A Model City of Health gathers years of hints from health reformers. Water supply, drainage, waste, light, and fresh air come first. Dry walls and floors, stoves, cooking, washing gear, and clean beds all have their place. Sick rooms that do not endanger the well, plain food, and shunning of vice join the plan. Death rates fall where such rules rule, the piece insists.
46811-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Number 683 of Chambers's Journal, the Edinburgh weekly of popular literature, science, and art, is dated Saturday, January 27, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal, then in its fourth series. The number opens with The Banffshire Naturalist, an account of Samuel Smiles's new life of Thomas Edward, the Scotch naturalist.

Edward, born in 1814, was a working shoemaker at Banff whose passion for living things began in childhood. He was scolded and cuffed for keeping jackdaws and beetles, and thrown out of one school for a bird in his pocket. The journal abridges Smiles's book for readers who had not seen it, praising the kindliness that told so obscure a life. Such numbers mixed biography, fact, and tale for a penny-a-week readership.
46885-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal took up the ask of what work women may do. Issue 684 of the fourth series is dated February 3, 1877. It sold for one and a half pence from the Chambers house. William and Robert Chambers ran the paper at that time. Talk of fit work for women had stirred heat for years, it says.

Shall women train as doctors or not, the piece asks first. May they vie fair with men where strength and skill suit? The paper claims a calm, even hand in the fight. It turns to nature's broad light for its last test. More tale and fact parts fill the rest of the issue. Town readers got a grave talk in a cheap wrap.
46886-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
William and Robert Chambers ran a weekly paper of tales, facts, and art for wide sale. Number 685, dated Saturday, February 10, 1877, sold for a penny and a half. The lead piece, The Wooden Leg, starts as a letter from a dull seaside town. Its writer had promised news to an old lady and her two girls at home.

The letter tells of two young ladies who each walk with a wooden leg. One leg is a plain black pin, worn with grace and high spirits. Fine notes on dress, pace, and nerve fill the sketch. Readers of the time got light, kind fare mixed with facts and verse.
46897-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 686, is one weekly issue of a popular Scottish magazine. William and Robert Chambers conducted it. The issue is dated Saturday, February 17, 1877. It belongs to the journal's fourth series. The price was three halfpence. Literature, science, and art share its pages.

An article called Derelicts leads the number. Abandoned ships drift on every ocean, it observes. Some float keel upwards. Some, laden with timber, will not sink. A rescued cat on a waterlogged hulk earns a tender paragraph. The article then tells of a famous find. In September 1855 an American whaler boarded a silent ship in Davis Strait. Papers in her cabin named her the Resolute. Her story fills the rest of the piece.
46954-the-story-of-siena-and-san-gimigna:
Edmund Gardner wrote The Story of Siena and San Gimignano, published by Dent in London in nineteen two with illustrations by Helen James, to whose memory the book is dedicated. Reproductions from Sienese painters and sculptors fill its pages. The contents open with the republic of Siena itself, then turn to Saint Catherine, the city's people, and the Petrucci lords.

Later chapters walk the city in detail. The sculptors and painters come first, then the Campo and the palace of the commune, the cathedral and baptistery, and a walk in Saint Catherine's footsteps. The republic's last days precede a tour through the city of the Virgin and its convents. San Gimignano, the town of the beautiful towers, closes the book. Siena, Gardner writes, stays the most perfectly medieval of Tuscany's larger cities.
46955-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal number six hundred eighty seven is a week sheet of February twenty fourth, eighteen seventy seven. William and Robert Chambers led the sheet in its fourth run of years. Its full name adds trade in books, science, and art for the folk. Price stands at a penny half on the front leaf of the sheet. A lead talk asks how to live to a hundred years of age.

Most folk would take that span if it came with ease, the talk opens. Work on hand, kids to school, and funds to grow all plead for time. Death seems a far jest till his call comes close and hard. An old Dance of Death book shows bone men at feast and play. Each grinning guest must march at once, his glass left full.
46959-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 688 of its fourth series, is dated Saturday, March 3, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly. Rob Graham, a Tweedside reminiscence by W Chambers, leads the number. Chambers recalls his schooldays at Peebles, a small town on the Tweed. The burgh school drew pupils from miles around. Farmers' children trudged in all weathers to sit with townsfolk.

Rob Graham was one of the country lads. He was a sturdy boy of twelve, well knit and barefoot in summer. Coarse red hair crowned a brow so large it promised brains. His dress was dingy corduroys and a Galashiels blue coat; Chambers values the whole outfit at twenty shillings. Yet Rob outshone boys in frills and shoes. At duck, pitching a stone at a mark, none showed more dexterity. At shinty on the school green he ran with greatest vigour.
47049-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
William and Robert Chambers ran this weekly journal of tales, science, and art for a wide public. Number 691, fourth series, came out on Saturday, March 24, 1877. The price was a penny and a half, and a piece on names leads the number.

Names argues that family names are a late growth in England. Six or seven hundred years back, it says, men had one name and no more. Surnames came in after the Conquest, from France, and spread down from great houses by slow steps. One spur, the writer jokes, was love: young ladies balked at wedding men with a bare John or Thomas. Single-name lands like Turkey show the old way still at work.
47066-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 693, for Saturday, April 7, 1877, sold for three halfpence and was conducted by William and Robert Chambers. The leading article, The High-Mettled Racer, looks back at the trained horses of Astley's Amphitheatre in London.

The writer recalls the acts of thirty or forty years before, under the manager Ducrow, when the horses seemed almost human in intelligence. In one play a lady's horse, hearing her screams from its stable, rushed into a burning house on stage. It climbed the stair through flame and smoke, and carried her down on its back to loud applause. A white horse named Prince starred in another play that traced a racer's fall through stages of degradation. The journal mixed such memories with its usual fare of fact and story.
47083-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 694, is the issue of Saturday, April 14, 1877, in the fourth series conducted by William and Robert Chambers. Its lead article, The Coming Obelisk, takes up Cleopatra's Needle, the obelisk lying on the shore at Alexandria.

For more than fifty years, the article recounts, schemes to bring the stone to England had come to nothing. British officers leaving Egypt in 1801 claimed it as a memorial of Abercrombie's victories, planned its stowage through a ship's stern port, and subscribed days of pay, but the plan was abandoned. Mehemet Ali later presented the obelisk to the Prince Regent, and the government, deterred by an estimate of ten thousand pounds for the removal, took no steps. A Crystal Palace scheme for Sydenham fell through. The stone, the journal notes, has suffered little by its burial in the sand.
47094-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 695 of the fourth series, came out on Saturday, April 21, 1877, at three-halfpence. William and Robert Chambers conducted it. The lead article, A Marvel of Artistic Genius, tells of John Carter of Coggeshall in Essex, a silk-weaver's son. Coggeshall boasts a fine church and antiquarian ruins, and takes pride in Carter's parentage.

The boy drew horses and dogs on his slates, copy-books, and cottage walls, to his neat mother's annoyance. Bright and high-spirited, he fell in with wild young men and led their daring enterprises. At twenty he married a quiet, respectable young woman, yet did not steady. The article follows the gang's midnight rooking expedition to Holfield Grange in May 1836, with signals agreed to avoid suspicion. The tale is a cautionary life told as popular journalism.
47099-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal number 696 is one weekly issue of a famed Scots magazine. William and Robert Chambers ran the journal in its fourth series run. The issue bears the date Saturday, April 28, in the year 1877. It sold for three halfpence and opens with a piece called Making Pretend. Little girls play at being ladies, and grown folk copy them, it opens.

Court life gets held up as full of such polite pretence in the piece. The Queen's Speech is not the Queen's at all, the writer points out. The prime minister writes it, and the Lord Chancellor reads it aloud. In old days the king spoke his own words as his own master. Now ministers answer for all the Crown's public acts and words. Symbols like regimental colours draw the same point about shared forms. Even at night an officer salutes the quarter-deck by rote habit.
47223-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for May 12, 1877 is number 698 of the journal's fourth series, priced at three halfpence. William and Robert Chambers conducted it. The issue opens with The Twelfth Rig, a tale in six chapters. Its first chapter is called The Charm Suggested.

The story begins in a district of Ireland, at the foot of a tall mountain. Patrick Daly keeps a comfortable farm-house there, well sheltered from the wind. By thrift and industry he has risen above the class of small farmers and counts as a wealthy man. His barns are full and his farm well stocked. He has no family beyond a daughter of nineteen. The serial tale unfolds from that house.
47230-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art was a penny weekly run by William and Robert Chambers. This number, 697 in the fourth series, came out on Saturday, May 5, 1877, price three halfpence.

Its lead piece recalls Sir Walter Scott out strolling with his dogs near Abbotsford in the summer of 1824, before misfortune clouded his mind. The essay traces Scott's love of animals to his childhood at Sandyknowe, where shepherds and collies surrounded him and a Shetland pony walked into the house to be fed from his hand. It argues his pets were treated as friends with rights to be respected. Readers get a warm portrait of the novelist at home.
47235-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science and Art was a weekly run by William and Robert Chambers. Number 699 is dated Saturday, May 19, 1877. The price was just over a penny.

The number opens with the story of Charley Ross of Germantown, near Philadelphia. On July 1, 1874, Charley, aged four, played by the road with his brother Walter. Both boys loved candy, and that taste led to grave trouble. The piece tells how a sweet treat drew the child into danger. Such true tales of loss and search were a staple of the journal. The journal mixed such tales with science, art and verse each week.
47387-fissure-of-the-anus-and-fistula-in:
Fissure of the Anus and Fistula in Ano is a medical monograph by Lewis Adler, printed in 1892. Adler taught diseases of the rectum at the Philadelphia Polyclinic. Davis of Detroit published the book. Its contents split into two parts matching the title. The first part treats anal fissure, or irritable ulcer. Definition, location, and the ages and sexes affected open it.

Symptoms, examination, diagnosis, and prognosis fill the second chapter. Treatment, both soothing and operative, closes the first part. The second part gives fistula the same fourfold treatment. Adler's preface aims at a concise yet thorough account. No organ, he argues, is more neglected than the rectum. Neglect by laymen springs from carelessness of habit and cleanliness. That neglect, he holds, causes many rectal maladies.
47687-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, volume six for 1900, is a plate series for architects. Its list of text illustrations opens with carving from the churches of Italy. A carved arm piece of a choir stall of the sixteenth century, from Genoa cathedral, stands first. 

A long section treats the cathedrals of England in photographs for the student. Canterbury, Chichester, Hereford, Lincoln, Norwich, and Peterborough cathedrals appear by choir or front. Saint Albans abbey, Wells, Winchester, and Worcester complete the English set in the list. The chateau of Chambord in France is treated with its great staircase lantern and plan in turn. Such brochure series gave American architects a cheap picture library of European models. Before the age of the art book, these plates were the working reference on many a drafting room shelf in the United States.
47688-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, volume six, number two, is the February 1900 issue. Its subject is Japanese gardens. A plate shows a daimio's garden at Shinjuku. The text insists that such a garden is not a flower garden. In nine cases of ten, it says, no flower bed appears. Some gardens hold scarce a sprig of green. Rocks, pebbles, and sand can make the whole.

Scale runs from many acres down to ten feet square. A carved box on a veranda can hold hills, ponds, and tiny bridges. On any scale, the garden models a real landscape. More than that, it must carry a mood: peace, wildness, or solitude. Custom shapes the model, like the art of Hokusai. Western readers are told the code takes long study to learn.
47689-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration for March 1900 is one number of a monthly plate series for architects. This number is given to Spanish wrought-iron screens. A plate of the screen in the Royal Chapel of Granada Cathedral leads the set. The text traces Spain's iron craft from the earliest times. The iron mines of the Cantabrian provinces fed the art, it says. Fine work in metal has been a Spanish gift in all ages. Little early work survives, since iron rots and was little prized.

One key at Valencia gets a close tale. It is nine and a half inches long and once was gilt. Its wards bear words in Cufic letters, and round the handle the maker's name can be read: Ahmel Ahsan. Twelfth-century capitals from the monastery at Monreale fill the rest of the number.
47815-francisco-the-filipino:
Francisco the Filipino, a school reader by Burtis Little, was issued by the American Book Company. Little had been principal of the provincial school at Albay in the islands. The contents open with Francisco’s home and his work. Rice, abaca, and coconuts take the next three chapters in order.

Francisco’s pleasures and his days at school follow in the list. What he learned of Philippine history and government stands near the end. His graduation and a trip to Manila close the little book. Francisco lived between the towns of Albay and Camalig on Luzon. American schoolbooks of that age taught the islands through such a boy. The reader joins geography, farming, and civics in one story.
47879-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
Brochure Series number four treats the Petit Trianon at Versailles here. The April 1900 issue shows the chateau as plate twenty seven. Louis the Fourteenth tired of Saint Germain in his early reign. Windows there viewed Saint Denis, the royal tomb house, it is said.

He chose Versailles, a desolate, waterless, empty site near Paris. Cost in money passed one thousand million francs for the palace. In 1681, twenty two thousand soldiers and six thousand horses worked there. Workmen died by thousands at the unhealthy site, the sketch says. English carved fireplaces share the April issue with the Trianon plates and text.
47893-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
A plate set on home art gives its May 1900 number to Chippendale chairs, with a full plate of fine forms. First pages trace how rare chairs were till late years, when ease and wealth spread their use. Seats in stone and paint from Egypt, Greece, and Rome show the shape in grand homes and shrines of old.

In England chairs were so rare in the 1500s that wills and deeds name them as wealth to pass down. Kings and queens sat in chairs at feasts while the rest sat on plain benches at the board. Dutch sway, French craft, and inlay work then reshaped the chair for the age of ease.
47894-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration for June 1900 is volume six, number six of a pictured study set. The number treats the Duomo and the Campanile at Florence, plus grotesques from Notre Dame in Paris. Plate forty three shows the Florence dome and tower.

The text quotes Symonds on the mid 1200s, when the free cities of Lombardy and Tuscany fought the Empire and the nobles. In that strain, he says, some of the most lasting and splendid public works rose. The domes and towers of Florence and Pisa climbed over the city walls as burghers paid for them with common funds. Sismondi is quoted that these great works were republican. Building fans get fine plates and proud civic history in one slim number.
47904-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
One issue of an architecture picture series from July 1900 shows the house of Jacques Coeur at Bourges in France. The issue gives plates of the house and a long note on its past. The house is praised as the most full and pure case of a great town house left from the Gothic age in France.

The note tells the life of Jacques Coeur, son of a rich fur dealer born in 1395. It tells of his mint work at Bourges, a fine for bad coin, and his rise as a bold man of trade. Readers get both the carved stone work of the house and the strange life of the man who built it.
47914-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
August 1900 in the Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration takes up the guild halls of London, with plates of the great rooms, Haberdashers' Hall among them.

The text traces the trade guilds to the earliest records of the city. About one hundred such bodies still stand. The twelve greatest are styled the Twelve Great Livery Companies. From old charter rights their members, though self-chosen, still pick the Lord Mayor of London from the twenty-six aldermen. The account lingers on the rite: aromatic herbs strewn on the Guildhall floor, scarlet gowns, and the robes that give the liverymen their name. The series served architects and draughtsmen who needed sound plates of fine rooms, and this number mixes civic history with its views.
47915-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, volume six number nine, dated September nineteen hundred, is an issue of a plate series. Its subjects are the ducal palace at Venice and types of Italian garden fountains. A plate of the court of the ducal palace heads the number. The text opens with a judgment from Ruskin on that palace.

Considered as the chief representation of the Venetian school, the palace is the Parthenon of Venice, Ruskin wrote. To know its history would be to know the whole history of the republic, the text says. It was at once the doges' residence, senate house, court of justice, and prison. A passage from Taine pictures the first sight of it. Like a magnificent jewel in a brilliant setting, it effaces its surroundings, he wrote.
47916-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
The October 1900 number of the Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration takes up the Chateau of Chambord in France. It is number ten of the 1900 run. A plate shows the southern front of the chateau. The piece on Chambord opens with praise drawn from Jules Loiseleur, who calls the palace one of the most singular of its age.

Loiseleur calls Chambord the Versailles of the feudal kings. It stood to Blois, the chief seat of the Valois line, as Versailles stood to the Tuileries: the country seat of the crown. Tapestries from Arras, Venetian mirrors, carved chests, crystal lamps, and great silver goods filled the palace through eight reigns, the piece says. All were scattered in a single day by the storm that came after. The number is a study piece for readers of old French buildings.
47921-the-brochure-series-of-architectur:
Brochure Series number eleven treats the work of Sir Christopher Wren. The November 1900 issue shows Saint Paul's Cathedral as plate eighty three. English Renaissance style shed Gothic traits under James the First. Inigo Jones brought Palladio study from Italy to his design work.

Jones held near sole sway in the profession till the Commonwealth. Wren took up the work and surpassed even Jones sway after. No great building rose in late Stuart England without Wren hand. American colonial church style rests much on his models, it says. Wren was born at East Knoyle, Wiltshire, on October 20, 1632, the sketch records.
48189-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal was a cheap weekly of tales, lore, and art for all. Number 703 is dated Saturday, June 16, 1877. It cost one penny and a half in that day's coin. William and Robert Chambers ran the fourth run of the sheet. A Holiday in the Lake-Country leads this week's bright list.

Those who have not yet chose a summer rest are bid there first. Charm in change waits at each turn in that fair land, it says. Hill winds fan the worn brow back to boyhood's glad zest there. Steep roads, green slopes, and calm lakes fill its first page. More tales, facts, and verse fill the back of the week. Home guests prized the sheet.
48207-lays-and-legends-of-the-english-la:
John Pagen White wrote Lays and Legends of the English Lake Country, with copious notes, printed in London and Carlisle in 1873. White, a surgeon, spent years of a busy working life on the book. He died suddenly in 1868, before he could revise it, and his brother published the manuscript as he left it.

The poems sing of Cumbria, the lake country of north-west England. Long notes add history and local lore about the places and events in the verse. The brother's introduction says the notes aim to serve both residents and the many visitors to the lakes. A preface maps the district from Cross-Fell and the Solway Firth to Morecambe Bay and the Irish Sea. The book blends local pride, poetry, and guide-book fact.
48221-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of popular literature, science, and art, number 704, for Saturday, June 23, 1877, conducted by William and Robert Chambers and priced at a penny-halfpenny. Its lead story is called Seventy Years Since.

The narrator publishes true stories of an old Scotch house, names slightly changed, now that the actors are gone. In the winter of 1816, three young officers ride ahead of their regiment into Edinburgh for lodgings. A gaunt gipsy woman seizes the lieutenant's bridle and prophesies a bonnie bride waiting in the first house he enters. The officers laugh, ride on, and knock at a shuttered house, where a stalwart maid storms at them for asking lodgings. Family readers get the famous weekly's mixture of tale and fact.
48348-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal number 705 appeared on Saturday, June 30, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly in its fourth series. The price was three halfpence. Its lead tale is Faithful Unto Death, a fireside story. A Highland snowstorm drives the opening scene.

The narrator sits by a crackling fire in his wife's Highland house. Snow falls so fast that a yard ahead is hidden. His wife hopes no poor creature is out on the moor tonight. Past eleven, a whining and scratching comes at the door. Their dog Laddie is loose, but he will not come in. He takes the narrator's coat in his mouth and pulls him outward. Laddie, his wife recalls, once found a man in the snow before. Brandy and blankets are readied for a rescue.
48714-cape-gloucester-the-green-inferno:
Cape Gloucester, The Green Inferno, by Bernard Nalty, is a Marine Corps history of a World War Two landing. The book belongs to the Marines in World War Two commemorative series. A photograph shows a patrol crossing a flooded stream in the forests of New Britain. It probes for the enemy as it wades.

On the morning of 26 December 1943, Marines waded ashore at Cape Gloucester. They came through heavy surf onto a narrow beach of black sand. Beyond a curtain of growth lay swamp forest and the Japanese defenders. Mount Talawe, a mile high, bulked against the dawn sky. Nalty writes the official short history of that wet and savage fight. The green inferno of his title is the jungle itself.
49237-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 706, came out on Saturday, July 7, 1877, for a penny halfpenny. William and Robert Chambers ran the fourth series of their famed weekly. The lead piece tells the Story of the Fairbairns of Kelso. Andrew Fairbairn began as a ploughboy and gardener, fond of books. In the American war he was pressed to sea, fought under Lord Howe off Gibraltar, and helped save men when the Royal George sank in 1782.

Home again, he wed a Jedburgh girl of rare grit. She spun wool and flax, wove cloth, and made the clothes for the whole house while her health failed. Their eldest son William rose to note from that hard school. Fans of old weeklies get a true clan tale of press gangs, thrift, and rise.
49246-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science and Art, Number 707, is the weekly issue dated Saturday, July 14, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal, here in its fourth series. The price was 1½d. The number opens with an article called A Village Home.

The article weighs how England should house its poorest children. Industrial schools gather hundreds of waifs in large asylums, fed and taught trades. Scotland boards pauper children out among rural families instead. The writer praises the boarding-out plan for keeping the family home at the centre. Then comes Dr Bernardo's English scheme. His Village Home at Ilford in Essex takes orphan and destitute girls. Each cottage has a Mother at its head. Babies of twelve months are admitted when rescue cannot wait. The piece argues charity's shape, not just its size.
49262-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
William and Robert Chambers ran this weekly journal of tales, science, and art for a wide public. Number 708, fourth series, came out on Saturday, July 21, 1877. The price was a penny and a half, and a Cornish travel piece leads the number.

A Cornish Haven starts with a call: come away to the sea. Cornwall's air and water are the purest, the writer swears, and the train runs west to Launceston. The old town and its frowning castle are left behind in the rush shoreward. A box seat on the coach is the goal. Summer readers of 1877 got a bright taste of the Cornish coast, salt air and all, for a penny and a half.
49374-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 709 of Saturday, July 28, 1877, is one weekly issue of the famed Edinburgh magazine. It belonged to the fourth series, conducted by William and Robert Chambers. The price was a penny halfpenny. The lead article treats Peter Botte, a mountain in Mauritius.

In that island in the southern ocean stands Pieter Both, one of the strangest shaped and most inaccessible mountains in the world, the article begins. Its quaint shape towers over the rugged mass above Port Louis. Its name dates from 1616, when a Dutch admiral of that name was shipwrecked there and drowned in its shadow. Travellers' tales of ascents have lent the little mountain a grandeur and mystery rivalling the Alps.
49387-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal for a day in the summer of eighteen seventy seven is one issue of a cheap weekly of tales, science, and art. Two named brothers ran the sheet in its fourth run. Its price is set on its head in old pence.

Its lead piece takes on a plain saw: seeing is belief. That saw goes scarce called in doubt, the piece says, and yet it is most false. A great host of sights that seem true to the eye are not true at all. Lack of lore and bent thought have led to most strange slips. We speak of the sun as it rises and sets, it notes. It does no such thing. The earth turns in front of it, like a roast at a fire.
49535-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 711, came out on Saturday, August 11, 1877, at a penny and a half. William and Robert Chambers conducted this fourth series. The lead piece is a warm sketch of Charles Kingsley at home, at Eversley Rectory.

Kingsley, the author of Hypatia, Westward Ho, and Alton Locke, is praised less for his books than for his home life. The writer calls him a hero to his wife and children, quick to take pain on himself and give joy to them. He built the children an outdoor nursery on the Mount, the high point of the glebe, and joined them there with finds from his walks: wild flowers, ferns, beetles, even a lizard.
49539-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 712, is the issue dated Saturday, August 18, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly, sold for three halfpence. The lead article attacks air and water pollution. The writers had stayed at a fine seaside resort. Houses and sands pleased them, but factory smoke spoiled the air. Bottle works sent out dense black clouds with the wind. They call such smoke a theft of the common air.

Sheffield and Wigan stand as grim cases of soot and blight. On Sundays, they note, the chimneys rest and children breathe cleaner air. The piece argues that pure air is a public right. Industry that fouls it for private gain does a public wrong. The journal mixed such reform talk with tales and science for a broad public.
49673-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
William and Robert Chambers ran this weekly journal of tales, science, and art for a wide public. Number 714, fourth series, came out on Saturday, September 1, 1877. The price was a penny and a half, and a plea for beasts leads the number.

Treatment of Animals looks back to the writer's youth in the century's early years. Then, he says, small heed was paid to planned kindness to beasts. Horses were worked past mercy, ill fed and with wounds that should have stirred pity. If they sank in their pain, they were left to die where they fell. The piece marks how far public feeling had come by 1877, and how far it had to go.
49703-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art was the famous cheap weekly of William and Robert Chambers. This copy is number 715 of the fourth series, dated Saturday, September 8, 1877, priced at three halfpence. The issue leads with an essay called Foreigners' English.

The essay gathers the comic English that hotels abroad wrote for British guests. A visitors' book at the Three Moors in Augsburg records Wellington's arrival in 1815 as a great honour descended upon the house. A Salzburg landlord begs leave to recommend his hotel opposite the birth home of Mozart, with all comforts at the meanest charges. Prepositions, the writer notes, are the great stumbling blocks. The piece keeps a straight face over page after page of earnest blunders. Victorian readers bought the journal for this mix of instruction and quiet fun.
49741-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 716, came out on Saturday, September 15, 1877. The weekly, in its fourth series, was run by William and Robert Chambers and sold for three halfpence. Its pages mixed essays, tales, and notes for general readers who wanted sound fare at a low price.

The lead piece, Youthful Prodigies, asks whether the greatest works come in the flush of youth or the calm of age. It lists young writers at speed: Pope wrote some Pastorals at sixteen, and Poe wrote Helen at scarcely eleven. Cowley and Bacon get their turns as well. The piece weighs bright starts against the slow work of later years.
49781-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 717, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, September 22, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conduct the paper, in its fourth series. The price is three halfpence, as the masthead shows.

Burial Eccentricities leads the issue. In all times and lands, it says, folk have held queer views on burial. Wilkinson, a founder of the iron trade in Britain, loved iron so well that he took it to the grave. He was buried in his garden in an iron coffin, under an iron tomb of twenty tons. The coffin proved too small, and the poor man was buried three or four times over.
49804-the-mentor-famous-american-sculpto:
Lorado Taft, the sculptor, writes on famous American sculptors in this number of the Mentor. Volume one, number thirty-six, names six men on its cover page at the front. Ward, MacMonnies and Barnard stand there with French, Saint Gaudens and Bartlett in the list.

The story of American sculpture is brief beside the chronicles of other lands, Taft begins. Greenough and Powers, the first professionals, were both born in 1805, he notes at the start. From a kindergarten stage to pride of place at the Paris Exposition of 1900 took seventy years, a rise Taft, himself a sculptor, tells with pride.
49874-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, Number 718, is a weekly number dated Saturday, September 29, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal. The price was three halfpence. Its lead article takes up the green flag of the Prophet.

The war between Russia and Turkey had just begun. Already, the piece says, the world had several times been startled by word that the Prophet's flag was to be unfurled in Stamboul. Such a raising would proclaim a crusade. It would bind all true Mussulmans everywhere. The writer weighs the dread appeal and its menace over the Mohammedan world. Set against it stands the Red Cross banner of the old Crusaders, an emblem of mercy under which dark deeds were also done. The number is Victorian popular journalism at its most topical.
50061-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 719, for Saturday, October 6, 1877, is one weekly number of the fourth series, conducted by William and Robert Chambers. The number opens with A Word on Rich Folks, an essay against the stock pulpit attack on wealth. Preachers, it says, call the rich man all that is bad and the poor man a saint by rule.

The essay answers that in western Europe riches now come, as a rule, from patient industry, not from robbery and armed oppression as in old days or in Turkey. Fraud and jobbery exist, but they are the exceptions, and ill-gotten wealth seldom lasts or wins respect. Every man, it argues, owes it to himself and his household to better his lot by lawful means. The number shows the journal's mix for family reading.
50183-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
William and Robert Chambers ran a weekly journal of popular literature, science, and art. Number 720 came out on Saturday, October 13, 1877, at a price of three halfpence. Its lead piece, Thrift and Unthrift, argues that rich folk are not the monsters preachers claim. Without thrift and honest trade, it says, the world would stay backward.

The essay praises the artisan who saves enough for old age. It notes that savings banks now hold close to thirty millions sterling. Friendly societies take in much more. Yet it warns that vast numbers still live from hand to mouth. The issue shows the self help creed of its age.
50486-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal number seven hundred twenty one is a week sheet of October twentieth, eighteen seventy seven. William and Robert Chambers led this fourth run of the famed sheet. Its price stands at three half pence on the front page head. Toys heads the scheme of this count with a trade piece at start. Brit toy craft is no small theme, that piece holds from the first line.

London counts spring up in that count of the toy trade at once. Eleven horse toy shops and ten bulk shops stand in its town count. A cent wood toy shop is a man, his wife, and his kids at one bench. Tin toys eat a ton of old ware a month at one town house. Tea sets beat meal sets near thirty to one in that count.
50680-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 722 of its fourth series, is dated Saturday, October 27, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly. The number leads with Sea-Monsters, an article on the sea-serpent question. Its opening is cautious. Only the capture of such a visitor, it says, will settle whether the ocean holds one. True sea-snakes, the Hydrophidae of the Indian Ocean, certainly exist.

The article blames the ocean itself for the legends. Its vastness and unexplored depths invite the wildest flights of fancy. Minute deep-sea organisms keep turning up under research. Animals of enormous unknown size, by contrast, almost never do. Trapping a monster of great strength is far harder than netting the small. Old accounts follow as evidence to weigh. A 1629 botanical work reports a fifty-foot serpent stranded near Sandwich. The finders ate it, then stuffed its skin with hay. Crantz's 1766 History of Greenland supplies the kraken.
50787-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, fourth series, number 724, for Saturday, November 10, 1877, conducted by William and Robert Chambers and priced at a penny-halfpenny. Its lead article celebrates the royal game of golf.

For ages, it begins, golf has been pre-eminently the national game of Scotland, linked with football in old fulminations against unprofitable sports. The writer explains the game for southern readers: links, weighted clubs, the small gutta-percha ball, and holes won in fewest strokes. The enthusiasm of its votaries, men of all classes, is the article's real subject, and it praises a new volume gathering what has been said and sung in the game's praise. Family readers get Scotland's pastime explained at the moment it spread south.
51100-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 726, is a weekly issue of popular literature, science, and art dated Saturday, November 24, 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted it, in the fourth series, at a penny and a half. The lead article, War and Telegraphy, laments how much discovery and skill go to the murderous purposes of war.

Armies grow larger, the writer notes, and science aids attack and defense ever more fully. Gun carriages now let a six hundred pounder be worked as fast as a small gun of old. Photography serves the War Office with plans of battles and forts, copied fast by zinc based printing for officers in the field. Torpedoes managed by electric current point to a strange future for naval war.
51191-nooks-and-corners-of-lancashire-an:
James Croston wrote wayfarer's notes on nooks and corners of Lancashire and Cheshire. John Heywood issued the work at Manchester in 1882. Six hundred copies were printed, all taken by subscribers before issue. Croston held fellowship in the Society of Antiquaries, the title page notes.

The notes mix history, legend, family lines, and plain description throughout. Croston warns the book is no full history of the places it walks. Samlesbury, Prestbury church, and old Manchester stand among his past works. Local readers gain a rich ramble through two palatine counties' hidden spots.
51542-the-just-wed-cook-book-a-present-f:
The Just Wed Cook Book was a present from the merchants of Reno, Nevada, in nineteen seventeen. E F Kiessling compiled it, and the Just Wed Cook Book Company of Reno published it. The book is presented free to the bride and groom, its front page says. The compliments of the advertisers make the presentation possible, it adds.

Merchant pages fill much of the volume. The Nevada Credit Company, leading home furnishers of the state, offers everything in furniture for cash or credit. Homes furnished complete for cash or small weekly or monthly payments, it promises. We make a specialty of furnishing homes for newlyweds, it says. A directory with new recipes would be mailed monthly, free, the front page promises. Brides got recipes wrapped in a whole town of wedding trade ads, a snapshot of Reno commerce.
51677-the-mentor-the-national-gallery-lo:
John Van Dyke wrote on the National Gallery in London for The Mentor of April 1, 1916, at fifteen cents a copy. Serial number one hundred four of volume four treats the great galleries of the world, fine arts number four. Knowledge gives power, says the philosopher, a front page essay opens. Knowledge enriches, says the scholar.

But the practical individual exclaims: special expert knowledge is a personal asset, but how does general knowledge enrich? Knowledge makes life fuller and more interesting, the essay answers. Through it we learn to appraise things at their true value. Our eyes open to other colors than purple and gold, our ears to other sounds than the roar of traffic or the shriek of an automobile horn. Van Dyke then walks the reader through London's great picture rooms, master by master.
51785-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 728, fourth series, for Saturday, December 8, 1877, is one weekly issue of the Edinburgh magazine of William and Robert Chambers. One copy cost three halfpence. A tale of the Covenanters, The Hidden Box, opens the number.

Near two centuries before, while the persecution against the Covenanters raged in Scotland, many were forced for conscience sake to give up all. They retired to out of the way places, out of reach of their enemies. A well to do farmer named MacWilliam, cut to poverty by fines and the loss of his lands, withdrew from the home of his youth. He rented a moorland farm named Hillfoot in a remote parish. A burn ran through the farm and joined a river two miles on. Magazine fans get cheap weekly reading of 1877.
51786-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
William and Robert Chambers ran this weekly journal of tales, science, and art for a wide public. Number 729, fourth series, came out on Saturday, December 15, 1877. The price was a penny and a half, cheap for its bulk of print.

A Bunch of Keys leads the number, told by a London professional man of the West End. His assistant finds dropped keys near Oxford Street one morning. Should they go to the police, or should an ad in the Times seek the owner? The teller wishes he had picked the police at once, for his own plan cost him dear. The tale opens with that rueful note and runs on in the journal's house style.
51841-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, December twenty-second, eighteen seventy-seven, is number seven hundred and thirty of the fourth series. William and Robert Chambers ran the weekly, priced at three halfpence. The lead piece is called Christmas-Time.

The writer grants that men differ on the feast as on all things. To some, Christmas is a string of small tortures, from forced greetings to the last glass of punch. Rough boys home from school spoil furniture, tease dogs, and lame horses. A married daughter brings spoiled babies and a husband with strong views. Others find pure pleasure in the same season. Both camps get a fair hearing.
52100-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 731, is the issue dated Saturday the twenty ninth of December 1877. William and Robert Chambers conducted the penny and a half weekly in its fourth series. Its lead piece, The Romance of Accident, argues that great finds often spring from trivial causes. Inventions and discoveries culled at random make up the amusement offered readers.

One tale turns on the trial of two robbers in the Basses Pyrenees in France. Highway attacks and burglaries had spread terror round Sisteron before their capture. No trace of the plunder could be found until one man gave a clue. That clue led, by chance, to a find of archaeological interest in the case.
5252-the-voyage-of-verrazzano:
Henry C. Murphy's study examines the claim that Giovanni da Verrazzano discovered America for France, and finds it without real foundation. Printed separately in 1875 from a larger work on early exploration, it argues that the famous Verrazzano letter is neither genuine nor true.

Murphy tests the letter against geography, showing misrepresentations of the coast, Cape Breton, and Newfoundland, and questioning whether any such voyage was made for the French king. The book offers readers a sharp example of historical detective work, in which documents, maps, and dates are weighed against a cherished story.
52762-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chamberss Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number seven hundred and thirty-two, is the print of that week sheet for the fifth of January in eighteen seventy-eight. Two kin of the name led the sheet. Its price was a coin and a half. Its lead piece is a tale in parts by a named hand, past a lady of rank.

That tale opens past a young school wife of past twenty years in a church town school room. Her plain dress and grave mien hide a rare grace of form and face, the tale says. Two men of rank stand past her past the rows of young ones. One is the old earl whose park gates stand near the school. They ask her of a swart man of ill look who hangs past the plot gate.
52833-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 733 of the fourth series, is dated Saturday, January 12, 1878, priced at three halfpence. William and Robert Chambers conducted the Edinburgh weekly. The leading article is called The Jubilee Singers, named for the famous Black concert company then touring Britain.

The article opens with a memory the writer calls one of the most vivid of his life: a slave auction in the United States, some 20 years before. He describes buyers examining the men and women like horses, testing fingers, looking into mouths for teeth, stripping coats to scan bare backs for the lash. Cowhide whips stood close by, and a jail waited across the way. What surprised him was the good humour of the sold. From that memory the article turns to the singers. Victorian readers got slavery recalled by an eyewitness.
55808-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Number 734 of Chambers's Journal came out on Saturday, January 19, 1878, at a penny and a half. William and Robert Chambers ran the paper. The Story of Thiers leads the number: the life of France's famed statesman, told as a tale.

In a thick street of Marseilles, the sea port, dwelt a poor locksmith and his kin. Rent and taxes for their wretched rooms ran weeks behind. Yet the man, son of a ruined cloth merchant and sunk to a dock porter, bore life as if born to wealth. His name was Thiers. His wife came of the poet Chenier's line. Their ungainly child, laughed at by the neighbours, would be Louis Adolphe Thiers.
57647-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 735 of the fourth series, was dated Saturday, January 26, 1878. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly. The lead article, Queen's Messengers, looks back more than forty years to a hard ride told by Baillie Fraser in a book on a winter trip from Constantinople to Teheran.

Fraser was sent with urgent orders when strain grew between Russia and Turkey and no fast route but horseback existed. The article explains the Tatar courier, a tough rider, guide, and translator used on such runs. One famed ride carried news of Napoleon's escape from Elba toward Persia, a trip of near two thousand miles done in seventeen days.
57759-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 736, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, February 2, 1878. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal in its fourth series, and the price was a penny and a half. Its lead piece remembers Miss Stirling Graham of Duntrune.

The writer recalls meeting her fifty years earlier in Edinburgh society: a lively, small, unmarried lady of middle age, at home in high circles. Her speech kept a Scottish seasoning, like that of Lady Anne Lindsay, who wrote Auld Robin Gray. Her line ran back to John Graham of Claverhouse, the persecutor of the Covenanters who fell at Killiecrankie in 1689.
58045-travels-in-the-interior-of-brazil-:
George Gardner, a Scottish botanist, traveled through Brazil from 1836 to 1841 and published this account at London in 1849. The second edition came from Reeve, Benham, and Reeve. Gardner dedicated the book to Sir William Jackson Hooker, director of the Royal Gardens at Kew, whose kindness and encouragement had made the journeys possible. Gardner himself later superintended the Royal Botanic Gardens of Ceylon. The Organ Mountains front the volume.

His preface is modest. He does not claim a better account than other travellers, only an account of a large portion of the country not yet described. He promises a faithful picture of the physical aspect and natural productions of Brazil. His routes ran principally through the northern provinces and into the gold and diamond districts.
