Along the way he notes the character, habits, and condition of the races, native and immigrant, who made up the population.
58096-a-trip-to-the-chain-bridge-near-ba:
A Trip to the Chain-Bridge, Near Bangor records a four-day tour of North Wales made from July 26 to July 29, 1825. Its author signs himself only a Gentleman of Liverpool. The account first appeared in the Kaleidoscope magazine that August, and this second edition was printed at Liverpool in 1826, priced at sixpence.

The writer had never crossed into Wales beyond the border counties. Business called him north-west, and curiosity drew him to the new chain bridge over the Menai Straits. He sailed from Liverpool on the Llewellyn steam packet on a busy Mersey morning. The trip takes in Beaumaris, Carnarvon, the lakes of Llanberris, Conway, Llanrwst, and Llangollen. An appendix adds particulars of remarkable objects and places mentioned on the way.
620-sylvie-and-bruno:
Lewis Carroll mixes fairy tale, satire, and nonsense in this strange, charming novel. Sylvie and Bruno, fairy children, wander between a fairy court and Victorian England, where a narrator watches plots, professors, and a warden's breakfast room. Chapters run from less bread and more taxes to a ride on a lion and a visit to Dogland.

Carroll writes with logic games, songs, and sudden tenderness, letting dream and waking blur. The book baffled some readers, yet it holds some of Carroll's most inventive play. It endures as a late Carroll work, where a child's wonder meets an adult's wit.
62125-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number seven hundred thirty eight, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, February sixteen, eighteen seventy eight. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal. Its price was three halfpence. A picture headpiece opens the number, and its lead piece treats sociable and unsociable people.

The lead essay calls the pleasures of company among the best and truest enjoyments of life. The wish for the friendship of others is inborn, it argues. Yet thousands with every chance to enjoy society fail to gain from it, the essay notes. Such folk are called unsociable, though many of them like company well enough. Obstacles they plead stand in their way, the writer says. The piece likens them to a hedgehog that rolls into a ball.
62226-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, the Edinburgh weekly of popular literature, science, and art, reached number 739 of its fourth series on Saturday, February 23, 1878. William and Robert Chambers conducted it, and the price held at three halfpence. The leading article is A Word About Bird-Keeping.

The writer owns a doubt at the start: caged birds look like prisoners, flitting between two or three spars. Yet the practice covers the civilised world, and the keepers have their answers. Most cage birds, canaries and goldfinches, were bred in confinement and never knew liberty. Turned loose, they would perish at once. Many live 12 or 13 years in the cage, singing to the last. Their song also cheers invalids and the housebound. The essay weighs the case fairly, as the journal loved to do.
62545-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal number 740 appeared on Saturday, March 2, 1878, in the journal's fourth series. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly, priced at three halfpence. Its lead article is The Gaelic Nuisance, a second piece on the same theme. The topic is language teaching in the Scottish Highlands and Islands.

The editors restate their position with care. They raise no objection to Gaelic itself. Their charge is against fostering Gaelic in a way that shuts out English. Gaelic alone, they argue, keeps poor Highlanders ignorant and tied to their birthplace. It shuts them out of work in the wider world. Fans of Gaelic poetry and antiquity miss the point, the article says. Learn Gaelic by all means, but alongside English.
62808-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 741, fourth series, conducted by William and Robert Chambers, appeared on Saturday, March 9, 1878, at the price of three halfpence. The number opens with an essay, In the Gloaming, on the twilight hour.

To northerners, the essay says, few expressions carry such peace and beauty as in the gloaming. The hour has had its singers ever since poetry found a voice, and its tenderness answers in the soul so long as human nature stays impressionable and yearning. Between the light and the dark, between the gloaming and the mirk in the old local tongue, lies a world of precious memories and holy suggestions. The French phrase, between dog and wolf, is judged a poor equivalent, and in the sunny south the thing itself is as absent as the expression.
62849-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal number 742, dated Saturday, March 16, 1878, was a weekly of popular writing, science, and art run by William and Robert Chambers and sold for a penny and a half. The lead piece tells the life of George Cruikshank, who had died not long before at the age of eighty six. Cruikshank was born in London on September 27, 1792, the son of a caricature artist, and his brother Robert drew as well.

The piece traces his start as a boy making etchings for booksellers. It notes his sketch of Lord Nelson's funeral car in 1805 and his prints of the Old Price riots at Covent Garden in 1809. By the end of the reign of George the Third he was a famed caricaturist.
62863-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, fourth series, number seven hundred forty three, for Saturday, March twenty third, eighteen seventy eight, cost three halfpence. William and Robert Chambers conducted the weekly. A lead story, Toby, opens the number. Toby was a sheep of middling size, lightly built and finely limbed, as agile as a deer. An old sailor tells his history.

Bound from Cork to Galatz on the Danube, the brig Reliance reached the Grecian Archipelago and was detained by adverse winds, he says. At Tenedos the current from the Dardanelles ran out like a mill stream, he adds. The captain went ashore for fresh water, of which they were scarce. Wanting fresh meat too, he strolled through the town, but butchers were unknown in Tenedos. A man came up with a sheep, he says. Family readers got tales, science, and verse weekly.
62970-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal for a day in the spring of eighteen seventy eight is one issue of a cheap weekly of tales, science, and art. Two named brothers ran the sheet in its fourth run. Its price is set on its head in old pence.

Its lead piece goes ashore in the straits of the east. A royal war ship, the text says, lies at anchor off a river mouth. A long, heavy ground swell rolls her slow from side to side. It is as if the sea too found the clime too hot for much work. A white beach frilled with bright leaf stands in view, and a cone hill clad in thick wild wood. On deck the fierce sun makes the tar ooze from the seams.
63031-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 745, came out on Saturday, April 6, 1878. William and Robert Chambers conducted the fourth series of the weekly, priced at three halfpence. The lead piece is called Borlum, and starts at Peebles long ago, in 1808. Schoolchildren there bombarded a defaced stone figure with stones, as a game. The figure stood in the wall of a ruinous old church, and bore the name Borlum.

No one on the spot could say who Borlum was, till the writer read it years later. Borlum was Brigadier Mackintosh, who led Highlanders in the rising of 1715. His bold march toward the Border threw the south of Scotland into alarm. Five hundred of his clan, banners flying, marched even to Inverness in the tale. The terror of his name lived a century on the Tweed, in a children's game.
63079-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, Fourth Series, Number 746 for April 13, 1878, was conducted by William and Robert Chambers and sold at three halfpence. Ottoman Gipsies leads the issue. The piece calls the Ottoman gipsy independent and savage in the terms of the day. Some two hundred thousand souls are counted in that group, it says.

The gipsy is unrecognised by the people in whose midst he lives, the piece holds. He has neither political nor literary history of his own, it claims. He is religious when it suits his convenience and submissive to law from fear, it charges. Yet secure in his tent he defies the world, it grants. Even those who have left tents for fixed dwellings are no less despised, it notes.
63247-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, April twenty-seventh, eighteen seventy-eight, is number seven hundred and forty-eight of the fourth series. William and Robert Chambers ran the weekly at three halfpence. The lead piece treats the folk who live on English canal boats.

A watcher lets surly barges pass, then finds a friendly pair at a lock. The cleanly dressed wife smiles up, and her husband talks sense on saving water. They invite the watcher aboard for the ride to Brentford. Room at the tiller is tight, and the cabin is tiny. Nine feet by six, the cabin holds all a family's goods in cupboards, lockers, and hooks. Plain witness drives the piece.
63507-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, fourth series, number 749, for Saturday, May 4, 1878, was conducted by William and Robert Chambers and priced at a penny and a half. The number opens with an essay, The Power of Draw. Draw, the essay argues, is a force for good and evil that pervades the whole social system.

Every centre of industry draws people to it for employment, and by draw the uttermost ends of the earth are peopled. But the same pull draws the idle, who mean to live at the cost of others, and mistaken charity has fed them. The poor, however they became poor, have been extolled as superior beings. Monasteries gave without judgment first, then the poor-laws made relief a duty, and now voluntary giving so dominates as to amount, in its working, to a kind of communism.
63533-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 750, is the issue for Saturday, May 11, 1878. William and Robert Chambers conducted the popular weekly. It sold for three halfpence. The lead article reviews a voyage in the yacht Sunbeam. The journal calls it a lively and interesting book. Its author, a Mrs Brassey, sailed round the world with her husband and children. Her husband navigated the yacht himself.

The Sunbeam carried three masts, sail, and a screw with steam power. A crew of at least twenty seamen worked her. Stewards, cooks, a nurse, and a lady's maid made up the household. A library of seven hundred volumes served the elegant saloon. The journal envies the family's splendid chance at a world tour. Diary form and untiring energy earn the author praise.
64243-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 753, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, June 1, 1878, priced at a penny and a half. William and Robert Chambers conducted the journal of popular literature, science, and art in its fourth series. The lead piece is a life of Charles Bianconi, the Italian who became famous in Ireland.

Bianconi was born on September 24, 1786, near Lake Como, and was thought a dunce at school because his impulse was to work, not study. Bound to a dealer in prints and barometers who promised London, he was taken instead to Dublin in 1802. Friendless at sixteen, knowing one English word, buy, he was sent out weekly to sell pictures with fourpence for his keep.
64273-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 754, for Saturday, June 8, 1878, is one issue of the cheap weekly conducted by William and Robert Chambers. The price was three halfpence. This is the fourth series of the long lived Edinburgh journal. Tales, essays, and short pieces for the general reader fill its pages.

The lead piece, Pixy-Led, roams the green lanes of Devonshire. Pixies, it says, still lead mortals astray there, as the little folk do in Scotland and Ireland. To be pixy-led is to see withered leaves as shining gold and folly as grace. The essay turns the old belief on modern life: lovers, fools, and dreamers still walk under the same glamour.
66216-curiosities-of-music-a-collection-:
Louis Elson gathered odd facts about music across lands and ages, in a book first held under an 1880 right and reissued in 1908. He had first run the pieces in a magazine, so he kept the tone light and the search brief. Full weight goes to Chinese music, which he calls a much missed field in English books.

Chapters move from India and Egypt through Hebrew, Greek, and Roman music and dance. Sounds of stone, metal, silk, wood, and bamboo sort the tools of China by the stuff they are made of. Japan, the peoples of Africa, and the early Christian church close out the grand tour.
6885-the-indolence-of-the-filipino:
Jose Rizal answers the charge that Filipinos are idle by nature, in an essay rendered into English by Charles Derbyshire. Derbyshire had already put Rizal's great novels into English, and he brings the same care to this shorter work. Notes by James Robertson, librarian of the Philippine Library, show the breadth of Rizal's learning in history.

Rizal argues from records and from life under colonial rule, not from slur or slogan. The editor notes only one small error, blamed on a faulty reprint where the true text was out of reach. The essay thus reads as a defense of a people, built on study and on pride in their past.
72469-the-journal-of-prison-discipline-a:
The Journal of Prison Discipline and Philanthropy for January 1860 is volume fifteen, number one, of the Philadelphia prison society's quarterly. The society, founded in 1787 to ease the miseries of public prisons, sold the journal at one dollar a year. The lead article welcomes a new gaol for the city of Baltimore, with plans drawn by the Dixon brothers.

The editors warn that most city and county gaols breed crime. A thief waiting trial, they say, serves an apprenticeship to adepts inside. Other articles treat the Texas penitentiary, the criminal statistics of England and Wales for 1858, and Irish convict prisons. Short notices gather escapes, pardons and prison news from many states.
7402-c-sallusti-crispi-de-bello-catilina:
Sallust, the Roman historian, wrote two short histories that have been read for two thousand years: the conspiracy of Catiline against the Roman Republic, and the war against Jugurtha, king of Numidia. This edition presents both works in their original Latin, in the Classical Series edited by Schmitz and Zumpt. It is a scholar's text, not a translation.

The preface explains the editor's problem frankly. Many manuscripts survive, and they differ, so no single text commands general agreement. The edition weighs those manuscripts, especially the Codex Leidensis, and draws explanatory notes from Kritz while often differing from him. Students of Latin will find here a careful, critical text of two masterpieces of Roman prose.
78201-daphne-bruno:
Ernest Raymond wrote this novel, copyrighted by Doran in New York in 1926. Raymond had written 'Tell England' and 'Damascus Gate' before Daphne's story. The end of the long prologue opens the book, before part one begins in the contents.

Bruno, the father, sits beside his writing table in that prologue's first scene. His legs stretch past the drawers and his arm rests on the blotting pad as he stares. A pained mouth and lifted brows show thoughts tethered to a fixed anxiety, Raymond writes, and Daphne's schooldays and romance grow out of her father's shadow.
alps-and-sanctuaries-of-piedmont-and-the:
Samuel Butler walks the mountain sanctuaries of Piedmont and the Canton Ticino in this enlarged edition of 1913, with an introduction by R. A. Streatfeild calling the book the Cinderella of the Butler family. Chapters take the reader to Faido, Giornico, Piora, and the great sanctuary of Oropa. Etchings and photographs mark chapels and passes along the way.

Butler writes on frescoes, priests, innkeepers, and the decline of Italian art with the same dry independence he brought to his novels. He loves these high shrines and the peasants who keep them, and he distrusts every system, including the church's. The book is a walking tour, an art notebook, and a quiet comedy in one.
britannica-1911-albino:
Albino, a biological term, is explained at great length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. From the Latin albus, white, it names a pigmentless individual of a normally pigmented race, a creature lacking its kind's usual colouring. A true or complete albino has no pigment at all. In some flowering plants, and in animals such as the polar bear, partial albinism has become a fixed character of the kind.

Without pigment, a vertebrate's eyeball shows pink, since transparent eye parts leave the red blood in tiny vessels unmasked. In humans the lack of pigment also brings the albinotic facies, a squinting, blinking look caused by light striking the retina too strongly. Much of the long article turns to breeding experiments. Cuenot showed with albino mice that colour hidden in an albino's ancestry can reappear in its offspring when crossed with a coloured individual, and Allen in America confirmed the same result.
britannica-1911-avellino:
Avellino is a city and episcopal see of Campania, capital of its province, set 1,150 feet above the sea east of Naples at the foot of Monte Vergine. Its 1901 population was 23,760. Ruins remain of a castle built in the 9th or 10th century.

In that castle the antipope Anacletus II crowned Count Roger II as king of Sicily and Apulia. The town's name comes from ancient Abellinum, whose ruined walls and amphitheatre in early imperial brickwork lie near Atripalda. Above the city, Monte Vergine carries a sanctuary of the Virgin founded in 1119, holding a picture ascribed to Saint Luke and drawing its great festival each September.
britannica-1911-avezzano:
Avezzano is a town of the Abruzzi in Italy, in the province of Aquila, east of Rome by rail and south of Aquila by road. Its 1901 population was 9,442. The town sits on the main line from Rome to Castellammare Adriatico, with a branch line diverging toward Roccasecca.

A fine, well-kept castle dominates the entry: built in 1490 by Gentile Virginio Orsini, it is square in plan with round towers at its corners. Twelve miles east lies Lago Fucino, the lake that gives the district its setting. Rail links, the castle, and the nearby lake are the facts the entry chooses to record about Avezzano.
britannica-1911-baldi-bernardino:
Bernardino Baldi (1533–1617) was an Italian mathematician and wide-ranging writer, born at Urbino on 6 June 1533. He studied at Padua with great zeal and is said to have learned as many as sixteen languages in his life. Plague at Padua drove him home to Urbino.

Baldi tutored Ferrante Gonzaga, who gave him the rich abbey of Guastalla, which he held for twenty-five years. The 1911 Britannica entry calls him perhaps the most universal genius of his age, with more than a hundred works to his name, most still unpublished. His Cronica dei Matematici, printed in 1707, sums up twelve years of work on the lives of mathematicians.
britannica-1911-balmes-jaime-luciano:
Jaime Luciano Balmès (1810–1848) was a Spanish churchman famed as a political writer and philosopher. He was born at Vich in Catalonia on 28 August 1810 and died there on 9 July 1848. Exiled for attacking the regent Espartero, he came home to found a Catholic, conservative weekly, El Pensamiento de la Nación.

His fame rests chiefly on a three-volume defence of Catholicism against Protestantism, printed in 1842–1844, which cast the one as the spirit of order and the other as revolt. The 1911 Britannica entry judges that work able but weak as history. It rates his philosophy books higher: the Filosofia Fundamental of 1846 and his elementary course of 1847, clear accounts of scholastic thought.
britannica-1911-banchieri-adriano:
Adriano Banchieri (about 1557–1634) was a Bolognese composer for church and stage, an organist, a writer on music, and a poet. He founded the Accademia Florida of Bologna. Like Orazio Vecchi, he worked to turn the madrigal, a part-song form, toward drama and the stage.

The 1911 Britannica entry is short, and its sharpest point is a quarrel. Banchieri disliked the monodists, singers of solo song, and all their new, daring harmonies. He said so with force in his Moderna Practica Musicale, printed at Venice in 1613. In the same work he set out orderly rules for the lawful use of thorough-bass, the figured bass line that guided players of his day.
britannica-1911-bassano:
Bassano is a city of Venetia, Italy, in the province of Vicenza, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands at the foot of the Venetian Alps on the Brenta river, which a covered wooden bridge crosses there. The town held 7553 people in 1901, its commune 15,097. A castle built by the Ezzelini in the thirteenth century stands in the upper town above the river.

Art and a contested past fill the rest. The museum and churches hold pictures by the da Ponte family, painters surnamed Bassano after their birthplace, Jacopo being the most eminent. The museum also keeps drawings and letters of the sculptor Canova. Bassano arose around AD 1000, was disputed between Padua and Vicenza, and passed to Venice in the early 1400s. Its printing and majolica pottery then flourished. In 1796 the French defeated the Austrians in a battle at the town.
britannica-1911-bauer-bruno:
Bruno Bauer (1809–1882), a German theologian and historian born at Eisenberg, is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The son of a porcelain painter, he studied at Berlin. There he joined the “Right” of the Hegelian school under Marheineke. In 1834 he began to teach theology at Berlin. In 1839 he was moved to Bonn, and his 1838 book on the religion of the Old Testament still shows his early orthodox, or church-true, stand.

Reversal cost him his post and set his life. In books on the Fourth Gospel and the Synoptics, in 1840 and 1841, Bauer cast off his old faith. He argued the gospel tales were not plain history. In 1842 the government took back his licence to teach. He withdrew to Rixdorf near Berlin for life. There he wrote as a free critic on the gospels, on politics, and on modern history.
britannica-1911-baveno:
Baveno is a town of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Novara, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the west shore of Lago Maggiore, thirteen miles north-north-west of Arona by rail. Its people numbered 2502 in 1901. The town is much visited as a resort in spring, summer, and autumn, when the lake shore draws guests from the cities of the plain. Many fine villas line its shore, built for that season traffic.

Stone is Baveno's lasting export. To the north-west of the town lie its famed quarries of red granite. That stone, cut in great blocks, has gone into some of the proudest buildings of Italy. The entry names the columns of Milan cathedral and the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele among works raised from Baveno granite.
britannica-1911-belli-giuseppe-gioachino:
Giuseppe Gioachino Belli (1791–1863) was an Italian poet born at Rome. He spent a stretch in poorly paid literary work and lived in narrow means. Marriage to a woman of property freed him to follow his own bent in writing.

Belli is remembered for his lively popular verse in the Roman dialect. His satirical sonnets, sharp pieces in the speech of Rome’s streets, stand alone of their kind, says the entry, and Morandi’s edition of I sonetti romaneschi gathered them in the 1880s. The note is short: a poor clerk’s start, a lucky marriage, and a body of dialect sonnets that kept his name alive.
britannica-1911-belluno:
Belluno, the ancient Bellunum, is a city and bishop’s see of Venetia, Italy, capital of its own province. It stands in the Piave valley where the Ardo joins the river, 1,285 feet above the sea among the lower Venetian Alps. In 1901 the town held 6,898 people and the commune 19,050.

Belluno was a Roman municipium, passed through many hands in the middle ages, and came under Venice in 1511, staying Venetian until 1797. Its buildings keep a Venetian stamp, above all the Palazzo dei Rettori in early Lombard Renaissance style. Tullio Lombardo rebuilt the cathedral after 1517; the quake of 1873 hurt it badly, but the tall campanile stood firm.
britannica-1911-benno:
Benno (1010–1106) was bishop of Meissen, son of Werner, count of Woldenburg, and educated at Goslar. The emperor Henry IV named him to the see in 1066. In the great fight between empire and papacy that followed, Benno took the pope’s side against the emperor.

The synod of Mainz deposed Benno in 1085, but after Gregory VII’s death he submitted and was restored on the word of the imperialist pope Clement III. He held Meissen until his death, reforming his diocese on Hildebrandine lines and building up its wealth. Long honoured locally as a saint, he was formally canonised in 1523, which drew a fierce pamphlet from Luther against the “new false god.”
britannica-1911-bertani-agostino:
Agostino Bertani (1812–1886) was an Italian revolutionist born at Milan. He joined the rising of 1848 in Lombardy. In the Roman republic of 1849 he ran the ambulance service as medical officer. After Rome fell he withdrew to Genoa. There he aided Neapolitan political prisoners. In 1859 he joined Garibaldi's corps as surgeon.

The 1911 Britannica entry makes him the organizer behind the Sicily expedition. From Genoa he raised four volunteer corps for Garibaldi. At Naples he became the dictator's secretary-general. He rebuilt the police, founded twelve infant asylums, and planned the city's sanitary reform. Later he led the extreme left in parliament. His inquiry into peasant health shaped the later sanitary code.
britannica-1911-bixio-nino:
Nino Bixio (1821–1873) was an Italian soldier, born on 2 October 1821. His parents forced him into a sea career as a boy. After many adventures he returned to Italy in 1846 and joined the Giovine Italia movement. At Genoa in 1847 he seized the bridle of Charles Albert's horse in the street. He cried for the king to cross the Ticino, with all Italy behind him. He fought through the campaign of 1848 that followed.

Under Garibaldi at Rome in 1849 he captured a whole French battalion as captain. A gold medal for valour marked that service. In the Marsala expedition of 1860 he turned the day at Calatafimi for Garibaldi. Wounds at Palermo and Volturno, where his leg broke, did not stop him. The 1911 Britannica entry follows him to Custozza in 1866 and the taking of Rome in 1870. He died of cholera in Sumatra in December 1873, on a trade expedition.
britannica-1911-boccalini-trajano:
Trajano Boccalini, an Italian satirist who lived from 1556 to 1613, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Loretto, he was the son of an architect and took up that trade himself. He came late in life to literary work as a main pursuit. Study at Rome won him the friendship of cardinals and other great men of his day.

By their sway Boccalini won posts in the church states, and Pope Gregory the Thirteenth made him governor of Benevento. He acted there without due care and was soon recalled to Rome. There he wrote his chief work, the Ragguagli di Parnaso. In that book Apollo hears the complaints of all who come before him and deals out justice on the merits of each case. The text calls the book full of light and playful satire on the great men and writers of his age.
britannica-1911-bruno:
Bruno, or Brun (925–965), was archbishop of Cologne, third son of the German king Henry I, the Fowler, by his second wife Matilda. Educated for the church at Utrecht, he distinguished himself by studious zeal. In 940 his brother, King Otto, afterwards the emperor Otto the Great, made him chancellor. Later arch-chaplain, and under his lead the chancery was reformed into a training ground for capable administrators.

He gave his brother valuable help against the risings of the reign's early years, rewarded in 953 when he was made archbishop of Cologne and about the same time duke of Lorraine. Bruno is chiefly renowned as a scholar and patron of learning. He courted learned foreigners, sought a better education for the clergy, made his brother's court a centre of intellectual life, built many churches and worked to purify monastic life.
britannica-1911-bruno-giordano:
Giordano Bruno (about 1548–1600) was an Italian philosopher of the Renaissance, born near Nola in the village of Cicala. Little is known of his life. Christened Filippo, he took the name Giordano only on entering a religious order, joining the Dominicans at Naples in his fifteenth year. He is said to have composed a treatise on the ark of Noah.

That discipline sat ill on his fiery spirit. Accused of impiety over his views on transubstantiation and the immaculate conception. He endured persecution for years, then fled from Rome about 1576 and wandered through city after city, reaching Geneva in 1579. Calvin's home was no resting place either, and he travelled on through Lyons, Toulouse and Montpellier to Paris in 1581.
britannica-1911-camerino:
Camerino is a city and bishop seat in the Marches of Italy. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in Macerata province, high above the sea on a hill. An electric tram links it with the rail stop at Castelraimondo near by.

The modern cathedral replaced one that fell in seventeen ninety nine by quake. A citadel from fifteen o three may rest on plans by Leonardo da Vinci. The site is old Camerinum, whose folk allied with Rome in three ten before Christ. Two cohorts of its men fought with honour under Marius later. No old buildings stand now, as Roman ground lies deep below.
britannica-1911-cantacuzino:
Cantacuzino is a family article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a great Rumanian house. The family claims descent from the Byzantine emperors and writers of the same name. From his two sons sprang lines that included rulers of Walachia and Moldavia. Under its influence Rumanian letters reached their highest growth in the seventeenth century.

The article then picks out leading members. Sherban Cantacuzino, ruler of Walachia from 1679, died suddenly in 1688. His lasting work was at home: he brought maize into Rumania and founded its first school. The list ends with Gheorge Cantacuzino, head of the Conservative party and prime minister from 1905 to 1907.
britannica-1911-capponi-gino:
Gino Capponi (1792–1876) was an Italian statesman and historian. He was a marquis of an old Florentine house. This 1911 Britannica entry traces his life. The Capponi are named as early as 1250. They grew rich in trade and banking in Florence. Gino was born on 13 September 1792. His father served the grand duke Ferdinand III closely. When the French deposed Ferdinand in 1799, the family followed him. They lived in exile at Vienna until 1803.

The Capponi then returned to Florence. Gino married Giulia Riccardi in 1811. In 1813 he went to Paris to pay homage to Napoleon. Ferdinand returned to Tuscany in 1814. His restoration was milder than in most of Italy. Court life did not satisfy the young marquis. He turned to serious study and foreign travel instead. Trips to Paris and England deepened his interest in institutions. The article follows his later public career from there.
britannica-1911-carpini-joannes-de-plano:
Joannes de Plano Carpini is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on the first notable European explorer of the Mongol empire in the thirteenth century. A native of Umbria and a companion of St Francis of Assisi, he rose high in the Franciscan order. He served as warden in Saxony and as provincial of Germany, Spain, and Cologne, spreading the order's teaching across northern Europe.

He held the Cologne post when the Mongols crushed eastern Europe at Liegnitz in April 1241. Four years later Pope Innocent IV sent the first formal Catholic mission to the Mongols, to protest the invasion and gather sound news of the hordes and their aims. The pope placed Friar Joannes at its head. His account became the earliest important Western work on northern and central Asia and the Tatar lands. The entry frames the mission as fear, diplomacy, and reporting in one journey.
britannica-1911-carupano:
Carúpano is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town and port of the state of Bermúdez, Venezuela, 65 miles north east of Cumaná. Its population was estimated at 8600 in 1908. The town stands on the Caribbean coast where two valleys open to the sea, and several regular steamship lines call there. The mean annual temperature is 81 degrees Fahrenheit, yet the climate is healthy thanks to the open coastal site.

The country right behind the town is rough, but trade is considerable. Exports listed in the entry are cacao, coffee, sugar, cotton, timber, and rum, the produce of the valleys and hills behind the port. The short entry thus fixes the town's place, its shipping links, and the farm goods that paid its way. Readers get a plain port profile rather than a history, since the entry offers no account of the town's past.
britannica-1911-casino:
Casino is a word study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that covers two very different topics under one name. The word is the small form of the Italian word for a house. It first named a pleasure house set in a garden.

The article gives the house sense its due first. Such houses grew into halls for concerts, plays, balls, and gaming at spa towns. In England of the 1700s great homes built them in their parks. The rest of the piece deals with a card game of the same name. Four cards go to each player and four lie face up. Players match cards, build sums, or lay cards down. Points come from set cards and from sweeps of the table.
britannica-1911-concini-concino:
Concino Concini, count Della Penna and marshal of Ancre, was an Italian adventurer who died in 1617 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a native of Florence. He came to France in the train of Marie de Medici. He wed Leonora Dori, called Galigai, a lady in waiting to the queen.

His wife stood high with the queen, and his own wit and boldness did the rest. By 1610 he had bought the marquisate of Ancre and a top court post. He gained the rule of Amiens and of Normandy in turn. In 1614 he rose to marshal and in effect to first minister. He dropped the plans of Henry the Fourth and let the treasury be looted, earning hate from all classes.
britannica-1911-conegliano:
Conegliano is a town and episcopal see of Venetia in Italy, in the province of Treviso. It stands 17 miles north of Treviso by rail, 230 feet above sea level. The town held 5,880 people in 1901, and its commune 10,252. A large castle looks down over the place. One famed son gives the town its chief art link.

That son is the painter Cima da Conegliano. A fine altarpiece by his hand stands in the cathedral and dates from 1492. Wine brings the town its trade fame. Its wine is noted in the entry, chiefly a sweet champagne. The hosted segment is short and gives no more than place, count, castle, painter and wine. Those five facts form the whole of what can be said from the text itself.
britannica-1911-conversano: Conversano is a town in Apulia in Italy, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands south east of Bari. About thirteen thousand people lived there in 1901. The town has a fine Romanesque cathedral from the close of the eleventh century. A castle there belonged from 1456 to the Acquaviva family. Near the town lies the site of the ancient town of Norba.
britannica-1911-della-bella-stefano:
Stefano della Bella, an Italian man who cut plates in metal, born in sixteen ten, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Florence, he was put to learn the gold trade as a boy. Prints by a famed French hand fell into his hands by chance. Those prints turned his mind in full to the cut plate art.

He learned that art from a master who had taught that same French man. By the free gift of a lord of the Medici house, he spent three years in study at Rome. In sixteen forty two he went to Paris. There a great church lord of France set him to draw the siege and the fall of a town by the royal host. Past a long stay in Paris he came home to Florence.
britannica-1911-della-colle-raffaellino:
Raffaellino della Colle, an Italian painter born near 1490 in Tuscany, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Colle, near Borgo San Sepolcro. He was a pupil of Raphael and is held to have helped him at the Farnesina and the Vatican. After Raphael died, he aided Giulio Romano at Rome and Mantua.

In 1536 Della Colle took service at Florence under Vasari. In his later years he lived at Borgo San Sepolcro and kept a school of design there. His pupils of note list Gherardi and Vecchi. His works stand at Urbino, Perugia, Pesaro, and Gubbio. The best are kept in churches in his home town.
britannica-1911-el-reno:
El Reno is a city in Oklahoma and the seat of Canadian county, as a 1911 Britannica entry records. It stands on the north fork of the Canadian river west of Oklahoma City. Growth was swift, from 285 people in 1890 to 7872 in 1910. Three rail lines serve the town on the rolling prairie land.

Corn, wheat, oats, and cotton grow round it, with dairy farms as well. A large grain lift, a cotton press, and mills for flour and canned goods mark its trade. A Carnegie library serves readers, and a lake in town draws guests for rest. A state boarding school for Native children stands near the city.
britannica-1911-fabriani-severino: Severino Fabriani was an Italian writer and teacher who lived from seventeen ninety-two to eighteen forty-nine. He was born at Spilamberto and joined the church. He took up school work, but full loss of his voice changed his path. He chose to teach those who can not hear or speak, and set up a small school for them. The duke made that school an institute, and nuns were sent to teach. His method is summed up in Logical Letters on Italian Grammar.
britannica-1911-fabriano:
Fabriano, a town of the Marches in Italy, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It lies in the province of Ancona, south-west of that city by rail. It stands 1,066 feet above sea level. Its people in 1901 numbered 9,586 in the town. The wider commune held 22,996.

The town has been noted since the thirteenth century for its paper mills. Those mills still make the best paper in Italy, the text says. A school of painting also arose there. One of its early masters was Allegretto Nuzi. Several churches hold works by him and other local masters. His pupil, Gentile da Fabriano, had greater skill and wider knowledge. Yet no major work of his stands at Fabriano. The gallery of the town holds a collection of pictures. Paper and painting together give this small town its name.
britannica-1911-faliero-marino:
Marino Faliero, doge of Venice, who lived from 1279 to 1355, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from one of the oldest great families of Venice. He served the republic with honour in many posts. In 1346 he led its land forces at Zara and beat the Hungarians in full.

Faliero was chosen doge in September 1354 while he was away on a mission. His reign began in disaster, as Genoa wrecked the Venetian fleet. Plague and falling trade made the mood worse. Bound by tight limits on ducal power, he grew bold and harsh. He joined a plot to kill the chief nobles and make himself prince. The plot leaked, guards seized the leaders, and Faliero confessed at trial. He was put to death in April 1355.
britannica-1911-ferentino:
Ferentino, a town and episcopal see of Italy in the province of Rome, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands 48 miles east-south-east of Rome by rail. Its people numbered 7,957 in the town and 12,279 in the commune in 1901. The town sits prettily on a hill 1,290 feet above the sea. It keeps large remains of ancient defences.

The lower outer walls are built of rough blocks of limestone that splits in flat layers. Above them in places stands walling of squared tufa blocks. Two gates survive, the Porta Sanguinaria and the double Porta Santa Maria. Outside the second gate is the rock-cut tomb of a citizen, with a long inscription. The acropolis above is also fortified, with massive retaining walls. At its eastern corner, under the bishop's palace, the building work is more careful.
britannica-1911-filangieri-gaetano:
Gaetano Filangieri, who lived from 1752 to 1788, was an Italian writer on law and rule. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica starts with his birth at Naples. His father meant him for the army, which he joined at age seven. He soon left it to study law. Skill at the bar won him court posts and royal favour.

His great work on the science of law making began in 1780. The first books set rules for laws in general and for trade. He urged free trade with no limits. He also attacked the old rules that held back work and wealth. A third book, on crime and courts, came in 1783. It called for change in the church and was banned in 1784. Three more books on schooling and morals followed in 1785. Ill health cut the work short.
britannica-1911-foligno:
Foligno, in ancient times Fulginiae, is a town and episcopal see of Umbria, Italy. It stands 771 feet above sea-level in the province of Perugia, 25 miles south-east of that city by rail. Its population in 1901 was 9,532 in the town and 26,278 in the commune. It lies in a fertile plain on the Topino, a tributary of the Tiber. Almost square in shape and ringed by walls, it is a picturesque town of painted churches.

Several churches hold works by Umbrian masters, above all Niccolo Alunno, whose chief altar-piece stands in San Niccolo. The cathedral has a Romanesque south front of 1133, restored in 1903, while its interior was modernized in the eighteenth century. An octagonal chapel by Antonio da Sangallo the younger dates from 1527. The Palazzo del Governo of 1350 has a chapel frescoed by Ottaviano Nelli. The entry tours these buildings and the town's art in detail.
britannica-1911-fossano:
Fossano is a town and episcopal see of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Cuneo. It stands 15 miles north-east of Cuneo by rail and 1,180 feet above sea-level. Its population in 1901 was 7,696 in the town and 18,175 in the commune. An imposing castle with four towers, begun by Filippo d'Acaia in 1314, dominates the place. Its cathedral was rebuilt at the end of the eighteenth century, and the town lies on the main line from Turin to Cuneo, with a branch to Mondovi.

Fossano began to matter in the thirteenth century. It appears as a commune in 1237, but in 1251 it had to yield to Asti. In 1314 it finally surrendered to Filippo d'Acaia, whose successor handed it over to the house of Savoy. The short entry thus gives a Piedmont town in outline: its castle, its rebuilt cathedral, its railway, and three centuries compressed into a struggle between commune, Asti and Savoy.
britannica-1911-fresno:
Fresno is a city and the county-seat of Fresno county, California, set in the San Joaquin valley near the centre of the state at about 300 feet. Its growth was swift: 1112 people in 1880, 12,470 in 1900, and 24,892 in the census of 1910. Two railways serve it, and the county joins arid plains to mountains.

Water brought from King river, 20 miles off, fed a wide irrigation system, with 500 square miles watered by 1905. The farms yield grain and fruit, and Fresno is called the only place in America where Smyrna figs have been grown with success, at the heart of the state finest raisin country. Dried fruit packing is the chief manufacture, worth near seven million dollars in 1905. The county was organised in 1856, the town laid out when the railway came in 1872, and the city chartered in 1885. The hosted file also holds neighbouring entries.
britannica-1911-geinitz-hans-bruno:
Hans Bruno Geinitz, a German geologist who lived from 1814 to 1900, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Altenburg in October 1814, he studied at Berlin and Jena. He gained the ground of his science under Quenstedt. In 1837 he took his doctorate with a thesis on the Muschelkalk of Thuringia. In 1850 he became professor at the Royal Polytechnic School at Dresden.

From 1857 Geinitz also directed the Royal Mineralogical and Geological Museum at Dresden. He held both posts until 1894. He was known for his work on the coal-bearing and chalk rocks and fossils of Saxony. His studies of the Permian formation, its plants and animals, won special note. He also described local graptolites and the coal flora of Altai and Nebraska. He edited a leading journal for many years. In 1878 the Geological Society of London gave him the Murchison medal.
britannica-1911-gentile-da-fabriano:
Gentile da Fabriano is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was an Italian painter who lived from about 1370 to about 1450. He was born at Fabriano. He is said to have learned from Allegretto di Nuzio. His style is also linked to that of Fra Angelico. About 1411 he went to work in Venice.

In Venice he painted wall scenes for the hall of the ducal palace. The work pleased the doge and senate so much that he won a pension for life. About 1422 he moved to Florence. There he painted a famed scene of the Magi in 1423. That work is called his best one still kept. Calls then came from Siena, Perugia, and Rome. Michelangelo praised his work as fine as his name. The entry notes his calm joy and his love of gold trim.
britannica-1911-giottino:
Giottino, an early Florentine painter, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Vasari is the main source for his life. The painter's real name seems to have been Tommaso di Stefano. Vasari gives his dates as 1324 to 1357. The article warns that those dates rest on shaky ground. He is said to have died young, of consumption.

His father Stefano was a famed painter in his own day. Contemporaries called Stefano the ape of nature for his true-to-life work. The son learned from his father at first. He then turned to the works of the great Giotto. He formed his style on those works, and so gained his nickname. Some even claimed he was a son of Giotto. Vasari credits him with frescoes in a chapel of Santa Croce. They show the miracles of Pope Silvester from the Golden Legend.
britannica-1911-giudici-paolo-emiliano:
Paolo Emiliano Giudici (1812-1872) was an Italian writer, born in Sicily. The 1911 Britannica entry is short: his History of Italian Literature of 1844 brought him to the front. In 1848 he became professor of Italian literature at Pisa, but lost the chair within months for his liberal politics.

When the Italian kingdom was re-established he became professor of aesthetics at Florence and secretary of its Academy of Fine Arts, resigning the chair in 1862. In 1867 he was elected to the chamber of deputies. His other works include a history of the theatre of 1860, a history of the Italian communes of 1861, and a translation of Macaulay's History of England of 1856. He died at Tonbridge in England on 8 September 1872.
britannica-1911-giulio-romano:
Giulio Romano, or Giulio Pippi (about 1492-1546), headed the Roman school of painting in succession to Raphael. The 1911 Britannica entry calls him a prolific painter, modeller, architect and engineer, named for Rome, his birthplace. His family name was Giannuzzi; Pippi came from his grandfather Filippo.

His birth year is unsure: Vasari's figures give 1492, other accounts 1498. Either way he was young when he became Raphael's pupil, and no more than twenty-eight when Raphael died in 1520. Raphael loved him as a son and set him on leading works, above all the Vatican Loggie. Much of the series called Raphael's Bible there, the entry says, is Giulio's hand. The long article follows his vast output at Rome and Mantua until his death on 1 November 1546.
britannica-1911-guarini-camillo-guarino:
Camillo-Guarino Guarini (1624–1683) was an Italian monk, writer and architect. He was born at Modena in 1624. He was also a learned mathematician. He taught literature and philosophy at Messina. From the age of seventeen he served as architect to Duke Philibert of Savoy. The entry is brief and factual.

His building work spread across Europe. He designed many public and private buildings at Turin. The duke of Savoy's palace was among them. So was the prince of Cacignan's palace. He also worked at Modena, Verona and Vienna. Prague, Lisbon and Paris saw his designs too. He died at Milan in 1683. The short account rests on that wide building record.
britannica-1911-guarino:
Guarino, also called Varinus or Favorinus, was an Italian scholar. He was born at Favera near Camerino about 1450. He died in 1537. He studied Greek and Latin at Florence under Politian. He later became a pupil of Lascaris. He entered the Benedictine order. Then he gave himself with zeal to Greek lexicography.

In 1496 he published his Thesaurus cornucopiae et horti Adonidis. That work collects thirty-four Greek grammatical tracts. He tutored Giovanni dei Medici, the future Leo X. He also kept the Medicean library at Florence. Leo made him bishop of Nocera in 1514. His Etymologicum magnum appeared in 1523. That Greek thesaurus was often reprinted. Later scholars owed it much, acknowledged or not.
britannica-1911-kladno:
Kladno, a coal town of Bohemia, is placed in a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands eighteen miles west of Prague by the rail line. In 1900 its folk came to over eighteen thousand, most of them Czechs. Iron and coal fields of great wealth wrap the town round. Some of the largest iron and steel works of Bohemia stand there.

Buschtehrad, a mine town in rich coal ground, lies close by. Its castle was once the whole place that bore that name. Kladno was a mere village of no weight for long years. Sold in 1705, it passed to a cloister that still holds it. Work in the mines began there in the year 1842. From that start the town grew into a seat of heavy trades.
britannica-1911-lanciano:
Lanciano is a town and bishop's see in the Abruzzi of Italy. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it in the province of Chieti on three hills. It stands 984 feet above the sea, eight miles from the coast. Its count in 1901 was 7,642 in town and 18,316 in the commune. Broad, straight streets and fine houses mark the town, it says.

The cathedral stands on brick bridges that span a gorge below. Those spans may date from Roman times, the entry suggests with care. The church is named Our Lady of the Bridge for that cause. A Gothic church of St Mary Major dates from the year 1227. Its front shows a portal of 1317 by a home sculptor's hand.
britannica-1911-larino:
Larino is a town and bishop seat in Molise, Italy, near Campobasso. Its town entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands north east of Campobasso by rail, high above the sea. Counts from nineteen o one put its people at just over seven thousand.

The cathedral, done in thirteen nineteen, has a good Gothic front face. Its bell tower rests on a Gothic arch built in fourteen fifty one. The town hall holds a courtyard from the sixteenth century in its build. Old Larinum stood close by and lived before Roman rule spread there. Coins prove that early life, and wall and bath remains still stand.
britannica-1911-locarno:
Locarno is a small town of Italian appearance in the Swiss canton of Ticino, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It is built at the north end of Lago Maggiore, near the point where the Maggia enters that lake. It lies by rail 14 miles south west of Bellinzona. Its height above the sea is only 682 feet, the lowest spot in Switzerland.

Until 1881 Locarno was one of the three capitals of its canton in turn. Its count in 1900 was 3,603, mainly Italian speaking and Roman Catholic in faith. The Swiss took it from the Milanese in 1512 and ruled it till 1798. In 1555 a number of Protestant inhabitants were expelled for their faith. They went to Zurich and founded the silk industry there, the text notes. Above the town stands the sanctuary of the Madonna del Sasso in a romantic site.
britannica-1911-lugano:
Lugano is the largest and most thriving town in the Swiss canton of Ticino. It stands 906 feet high on the north shore of the lake of Lugano. Its people numbered 9,394 in 1900, near all of them Italian in speech and Roman Catholic in faith. Monte Salvatore rises to the south of the town, and Monte Generoso stands across the lake to the south-east. Both hills can be reached by railways, and Generoso is a famed view point.

By rail, Lugano is 124 miles from Lucerne and lies on the main St Gotthard line. That ease of reach brings many guests, largely German, in spring and autumn. Though Swiss in rule since 1512, the town is Italian in look and in character. Of late years many works have raised the town. It has two chief suburbs, Paradiso to the south and Cassarate to the east.
britannica-1911-luini-bernardino:
Bernardino Luini, born at Luino on Lago Maggiore in about 1465, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the most famed master of the Lombard school of painting. That school rested on the style of Leonardo da Vinci. Luini wrote his name as Bernardin Lovino, but Luini is now the common form.

Few facts of his life are known for sure. Many of his works were long given to Leonardo by mistake. He studied at Vercelli and reached Milan near the year 1500. Whether he knew Leonardo in person stays unclear. Later works show some pull from Raphael as well. He hardly ever left Lombardy. His two sons followed him as painters, the younger one skilled in landscape.
britannica-1911-magliani-agostino:
Agostino Magliani (1824-1891) was an Italian financier from near Salerno. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his start in the Naples treasury after study. A book on law thought won him that post in his youth. The Senate took him in 1871 as a known finance expert there.

His work on coinage in 1874 fixed his name in the field. Finance minister from 1877, he served in four Liberal cabinets in turn. He ended the grist tax in 1880, to start in 1884. High costs with weak taxes pushed him to unsound finance tricks. Italian credit bore the strain for years after he left in 1888.
britannica-1911-martos-christino:
Christino Martos, a Spanish politician, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Granada in eighteen thirty, he was educated there and at Madrid University. His radical views soon got him into trouble at the university. He narrowly escaped expulsion for his part in student riots against the government.

He made his name as a journalist on a paper called El Tribuno. In eighteen fifty four he joined leaders against a revolutionary cabinet. He later turned against one of those leaders to back democratic movements under Prim and others. Those movements failed, and the entry follows his part in them.
britannica-1911-melegnano:
Melegnano, once called Marignano, is a town of Lombardy in Italy, in the province of Milan, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives it a short entry. It stands south east of Milan by the railway to Piacenza, with 6,782 people in 1901. Remains of a castle of the Visconti survive there. Its military weight came from its position at the crossing of the river Lambro. Melegnano was a stronghold of Milan in her great struggle against Lodi. 

It is famous for the victory of Francis the First of France over the Swiss in 1515, the battle of Marignan. It also saw a fight between the French and the Austrians in 1859.
britannica-1911-milanesi-gaetano:
Gaetano Milanesi, an Italian scholar who lived from 1813 to 1895, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He wrote on the history of art and was born at Siena, where he studied law. In 1838 he gained a post in the public library there. In 1856 he joined the Accademia della Crusca and helped with its famous dictionary.

The entry follows his move to Florence as a keeper of the Tuscan archives. There he took charge of the Medici archives and gathered a vast body of material on Italian art. He became director of the archives in 1889 and retired in 1892. His chief work was an edition of Vasari in nine volumes, issued from 1878 to 1885 with full and valued notes.
britannica-1911-monte-cassino:
Monte Cassino is a lone hill that looks down on a town, set half way past Rome and Naples. Saint Benedict came here from Subiaco in the first years of the sixth age. He set up the church house that became the chief home of monks in the west. That house had a hard tale of loss and new birth.

Lombard hosts sacked it, and the monks fled to Rome. It was built once more, razed by Saracen hosts, and built yet once more. Its peak of wealth came past a great abbot who rose to be pope. The house holds rich writs and a school.
britannica-1911-murano:
Murano, an island in the Venetian lagoon about one mile north of Venice, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It runs five miles in circuit, and gardens cover a large part of it. Its people numbered 5436 in 1901. Once it held far more, as many as 30000 in its great days.

Venetian nobles loved it as a resort before they built villas on the mainland. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries its gardens and casinos held wide fame. Literary clubs with names like the Vigilanti and the Occulti used to meet on the isle. The town is built on one broad main canal where the tide runs with great force. Smaller canals cut the rest of the ground. Its cathedral of San Donato is a fine basilica of the twelfth century.
britannica-1911-oristano:
Oristano, a town and archiepiscopal see of Sardinia, is described in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. It stands 23 feet above the sea, about three miles from the shore of the gulf that bears its name. Cagliari lies 59 miles to the south by rail. Its people numbered 7,107 in 1901. The town keeps scanty remains of its late thirteenth-century walls.

Two gates survive, one crowned by a tall square tower. The houses are largely built of sun-dried bricks and are low. The town thus covers much ground for its population. The cathedral was rebuilt in 1733 in the baroque style, with slight traces of the twelfth-century church. Slabs from its pulpit may be the work of Andrea Pisano. Older carvings, of the eighth or ninth century, appear on their backs. The sacristy holds fine silverwork.
britannica-1911-orizaba-volcano:
Orizaba is the subject of a peak entry in the 1911 Britannica. Orizaba is a dormant volcano in Mexico. Its Aztec name means star mountain in that tongue. It stands on the line of Puebla and Vera Cruz states. It rises from the south east edge of a great plateau. Its height is the top height in all Mexico. It ranks as the second highest peak in North America. Snow in patches was found high on its slopes.

Tree growth stops high up on its cold slopes. The first climb to its top was made in 1848. More climbs since then have met with mixed fate. Its last burst of fire ran from 1545 to 1566. The peak is now held to be extinct in full. Smoke was still seen from its top in the early 1800s. Gauges of its height by three teams are compared.
britannica-1911-parmigiano:
Parmigiano, a painter of the Lombard school, opens a bright art life in the 1911 Britannica. His full name was Girolamo Francesco Maria Mazzuoli of Parma. He went by Francesco and by a name drawn from his home town. Born in fifteen oh four, he was the son of a painter. Two uncles of the same craft raised him when his father died.

His gift showed at a boy age in clear and strong form. He took the style of Correggio as his base, but made it his own. At age fourteen he had painted a Baptism of Christ of ripe skill. Chapels in a Parma church bore his wall work by age nineteen. A self portrait in a round mirror won the pope as a fan at Rome.
britannica-1911-paterno:
Paternò, a town of Sicily in the province of Catania, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands by rail west-north-west of Catania, at the south foot of Mount Etna. In 1901 its commune held close to twenty-three thousand people. The town crowns the rock of an old Greek town, Hybla Minor.

A castle first raised in 1073 tops that rock, with a square tower and a chapel of old wall paintings. Mosaic floors still lie beneath houses in one street of the town. Ruins of baths and of an old bridge over the Simeto can be seen close by. The entry notes one grim date from the far past. In the summer of 415 before Christ, the men of Athens laid siege to the place and failed.
britannica-1911-piombino: Piombino is the subject of a short 1911 Britannica entry on a seaport of Tuscany, Italy. Old walls ring the town on its sea site. The town count for 1901 is 5,979 folk in all. Fine works of the Renaissance age stand within its walls. It is the port of sailing for the isle of Elba. The town first belonged to the city of Pisa.
britannica-1911-pirano: Pirano is a seaport of Austria, in Istria, south west of Trieste. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its people as mostly Italians, over thirteen thousand in 1900. Wine growing and olive farming support the town, with shipbuilding and fishing. Salt works nearby are the largest in Istria for sea salt. They yield about fifty thousand tons each year, the entry says. Venice beat an imperial fleet there in 1177. The town passed to Venice in 1283 and to Austria in 1813.
britannica-1911-pitigliano:
Pitigliano is a town article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Pitigliano is a town in Italy, in the province of Grosseto. It is the cathedral city of a bishopric named for nearby Sovana. The entry notes its cathedral, built in the sixteenth century, and an older church.

Most of the article tells the town's feudal past. Pitigliano began as a fief of the counts of Sovana. In 1293 it passed by marriage to the great Orsini family. Siena took Sovana in 1410, but a peace of 1417 left Pitigliano to the Orsini. Its most famous count was Niccolo the Third, a noted captain of his age. Later counts fell into family feuds and killings. In the end the Medici of Florence seized part of the land and gained the rest by exchange. The Orsini stronghold still stands in the town.
britannica-1911-rossano:
Rossano, a city of Calabria in Italy, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands in the province of Cosenza, on a steep spur of the Sila hills above the Gulf of Taranto. Its highest part reaches 975 feet above the sea. Its people numbered 13,354 in 1901.

The article calls it the seat of an archbishop. Its cathedral keeps a famed book of the Gospels of Matthew and Mark, written in silver letters on purple skin. Twelve small paintings adorn it, and the entry calls it a prize for the study of Byzantine art of the sixth century. Marble and alabaster pits are worked nearby. The town was a strong place under Latin rule, was taken by Totila in 548, and clung fast to the empire at Constantinople.
britannica-1911-rovigno:
Rovigno is a seaport of Austria in Istria, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies on the west coast of Istria, seventy-five miles south of Trieste by rail. Its people numbered 10,205 in 1900, and most of them were Italian. On a headland above the town stands the cathedral of St Eufemia.

The bell tower of the church copies the famed tower in Venice and bears a bronze statue of the saint, whose remains rest in the church. The town holds a station of the Berlin Aquarium with a fine stock of Adriatic sea life. Vineyards near it yield the best wine in Istria, and its hazel nuts are said to be the finest in the world. Rovigno is the chief seat of the Austrian tunny and sardine fishery. Its trades add ship building, fish curing, tobacco, cement, and flour.
britannica-1911-sarno:
Sarno is a town of Campania, Italy, in the province of Salerno, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes its site and trades. It lies at the foot of the Apennines, thirty miles east of Naples, near the sources of the river Sarno. Its commune held 19,192 people in 1901.

The entry notes the ruins of a medieval castle once held by Count Francesco Coppola, a leader in the barons' plot against Ferdinand of Aragon in 1485. Paper, cotton, silk, linen, and hemp are made in the town. The soft stone that forms round the Sarno springs was used as building material even at Pompeii.
britannica-1911-saronno:
Saronno is a town of Lombardy, Italy, in the province of Milan. It lies thirteen miles north-west of Milan by rail. The town had 8,729 people in 1901, and the commune 9,533. Its church of pilgrimage, the Madonna dei Miracoli, was begun in 1498. The church has a dome of rich form on the outside. Its bell tower dates from 1516, while the rest of the church is of later date.

Inside, the church holds fine wall paintings by Gaudenzio Ferrari that show a concert of angels. The choir holds works by Bernardino Luini that rank among his finest. The town is well known for its gingerbread, called amaretti. It is also a town of workshops and trade. Rail lines run from it to Milan and Como, with branches to Seregno, Busto Arsizio, and Varese.
britannica-1911-solferino:
Solferino, a village of Lombardy in Italy, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the province of Mantua. It stands four hundred and ten feet above the sea, on hills that rim Lake Garda. Its count in nineteen hundred and one was one thousand three hundred and fifty.

The village is famed for one day of war. On the twenty fourth of June in eighteen fifty nine a great battle was fought here. A French and Sardinian host met an Austrian host. Past a hard fight the Austrians fell back past a river. One wing fight of that day bears the name of the hamlet where it was fought.
britannica-1911-spinello-aretino:
Spinello Aretino was an Italian painter born at Arezzo in the fourteen hundreds era of early masters. His father was a man of Florence who had fled there in exile with his party. Spinello learned from a follower of Giotto, and his own style forms a link between the school of Giotto and that of Siena.

The 1911 Britannica entry tracks his fresco work town by town. He helped his master paint church walls in Florence, then spent years on frescoes in and round Arezzo, most now lost. After the sack of Arezzo he went back to Florence. There he and his aides filled a chapel store room with scenes from the life of a great saint, works that still stand, though much restored.
britannica-1911-steffani-agostino:
Agostino Steffani, a priest who wrote operas, is drawn in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Castelfranco in 1653, he sang as a boy at St Mark's. His fine voice drew a count's eye in the year 1667. That count bore him to Munich for a rich man's schooling. The elector of Bavaria paid his keep and gave him a post.

Kerl taught him at Munich, then Rome gave him Bernabei as master. Six motets from that Rome time still live in a Cambridge hoard. Back at Munich in 1674 he put out his first printed work. Court organist in 1675, he turned in time to the stage as well. His first opera, Marco Aurelio, was staged in the year 1681. Court and altar shared his strange, split career of note.
britannica-1911-talcahuano: Talcahuano, a seaport of the province of Concepcion in Chile, is the subject of a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the bay of Concepcion, eight miles north west of the city of that name, sheltered by the island of Quiriquina. The entry gives it 13,499 people by estimate in 1902. It has the best harbour on the Pacific coast of South America and is a key port of southern Chile. The Chilean government set its chief naval depot there.
britannica-1911-telesio-bernardino:
Bernardino Telesio, an Italian philosopher and natural scientist who lived from 1509 to 1588, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The hosted text opens with short entries on other names, then gives Telesio's own article in full. Born of noble parents at Cosenza, near Naples, in 1509, he was taught at Milan by his uncle Antonio. He went on to study at Rome and Padua.

Telesio's studies covered the full range of classics, science, and philosophy taught in his day. So armed, he began his attack on the medieval teaching of Aristotle then strong at Padua and Bologna. Pope Pius the Fourth offered him the archbishopric of Cosenza, but he gave it to his brother. He lectured at Naples instead and founded the academy of Cosenza. The article dates the next stage of his work to the early 1560s.
britannica-1911-volcano:
Volcano is an opening in the crust of the earth through which heated matter rises. A 1911 Britannica entry notes that the flow most often builds a cone shaped hill. A hollow crater crowns that hill in the common picture men hold of it. The hill is not the core of the process, the entry is careful to say.

The name first fit Etna and the Lipari islands, seats of the fire god in myth. All action tied to such vents is grouped under the name vulcanism in science. Study of that action forms its own branch of natural knowledge today. The entry calls vulcanicity the chief surface sign of forces deep within earth.
britannica-1911-weyler-y-nicolau-valeria:
Valeriano Weyler y Nicolau, a Spanish soldier born in 1839, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was born at Palma in Majorca, of a family first Prussian that served in the Spanish army for generations. At sixteen he entered the military college of infantry at Toledo. On gaining a lieutenancy he passed into the staff college and came out head of his class.

Two years later he was a captain and was sent to Cuba at his own request. He stood out in the expedition to Santo Domingo, above all in a daring scouting raid with few men. For that he won a high cross of honour. From 1868 to 1872 he served with distinction against the Cuban rebels. He came back to Spain in 1873 as a brigadier general and fought the Carlists.
c-sallusti-crispi-de-bello-catilinario-e:
Sallust's De Bello Catilinario et Jugurthino presents the Latin text of his two histories: the conspiracy of Catiline and the war against Jugurtha. The Classical Series edition, edited by Schmitz and Zumpt, addresses a text whose form no editor had yet settled.

The preface explains that many manuscripts differ, and that editors disagree over which reading deserves acceptance. Corte's Leipzig edition of 1724 abandoned the vulgate in many passages, while Haverkamp's Hague edition of 1742 returned to it. Later editors, including Gerlach, continued the debate. Students of Latin will find this a scholarly, working text of Sallust's masterpieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-mont:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Monte Cassino describes the abbey nullius eighty miles south of Rome, the Benedictine Order's cradle. In about 529 Benedict quit Subiaco to escape the jealous priest Florentius, travelling with a chosen band including Sts. Maurus and Placid to Monte Cassino.

The town of Cassinum below had been destroyed by Goths some thirty-five years earlier, yet an Apollo temple still topped the peak and the few inhabitants remained sunk in idolatry. Benedict broke Apollo's image, destroyed the altar, and built a church to St. John the Baptist with an oratory to St. Martin of Tours. In a tower of the old citadel he took up his abode, and that tower's preservation is owed to his dwelling there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albano:
Albano is a suburban diocese near Rome, taking in seven towns in the province of Rome. Its chief town stands ten miles from Rome on the Appian Way, the great Roman road, and grew from a military post where Christian soldiers served very early. Nearby lie Appii Forum and the Three Taverns, where St. Paul was met by fellow Christians on his way to Rome.

The entry recalls Albano's Roman past, including the consul Acilius Glabrio, forced by the emperor Domitian to fight a bear unarmed in the local amphitheatre. Its first known bishop is Dionysius, who died in 355, followed more than a century later by Romanus in 463. Its cemetery, found in 1720, holds frescoes tracing Christian art from the fourth to the ninth century. Later titular bishops include future popes Sergius IV, Adrian IV, and Alexander VI, alongside St. Bonaventure, and the diocese counted 12 parishes and 41,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alberic-of-mo: Alberic of Monte Cassino, who died in 1088 and had been a cardinal since 1057, was a Benedictine monk, perhaps born at Trier. He fought the teaching of Berengarius and defended the measures of Pope Gregory VII. He wrote works on theology and science as well as lives of saints, and his treatise on letter-writing, De dictamine, is the earliest medieval work of its kind. Many of his letters survive among the writings of St. Peter Damian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-bo:
Alessandro Bonvicino, called Il Moretto or Moretto da Brescia, was among the finest sixteenth-century painters of northern Italy. He was born at Brescia about 1498 and died there in 1555. He studied under his painter father and under Floriano Ferramola, felt the influence of Romanino, and later taught the portrait painter Giambattista Moroni. His manner is natural and attractive, his colour fresh and rich, and his figures sympathetic and graceful.

Bonvicino helped Ferramola paint an altar screen for Brescia's old cathedral and worked for Romanino at San Giovanni Evangelista, where he painted the Massacre of the Innocents. His church works at Brescia include the Coronation of the Virgin and Christ in Glory at Santi Nazzaro e Celso, the Ascension of the Virgin and St. Ursula at San Clemente, and Christ in the House of Simon at Santa Maria Calchera. Works of his also hang in Venice, Florence, and Milan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alonso-cano:
Alonso Cano, or Alexis, was a Spanish painter, architect, and sculptor, born at Granada in 1601, dead there in 1667. His father Miguel Cano, an architect, taught him first; he then studied sculpture under Montañés, painting under Pacheco. He went to Madrid in 1637 and, chiefly by merit, was made Master of the Royal Works and Painter to the King. He ranked first among Don Balthasar's instructors.

Cano was a greater sculptor than painter, though famed as a painter alone. His early colour work was tentative and eclectic, but his later pictures fill Granada's and Málaga's churches. After entering the Carthusian convent to paint alone, he returned to Madrid, restored to royal favour. He took orders and settled at Granada. In 1652 Philip IV made him a canon of Granada cathedral. His works include St. Agnes at Berlin, The Dead Christ at Madrid, and a Madonna and Child at Lebrija.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrogio-cale:
Ambrogio Calepino, Italian lexicographer born about 1440 at Calepio near Bergamo, died 1510 or 1511. He joined the Augustinian Order in 1458. His Latin dictionary, Cornucopiae, first appeared in 1502 at Reggio, reprinted many times in the sixteenth century, the Aldi alone issuing eighteen editions from 1542 to 1592.

Later editions grew, adding other languages to the Latin: the Basle edition of 1590 holds eleven languages, and Facciolati's seven-language edition of 1718 was often reprinted. Calepinus became a common word for dictionary or lexicon, as in Septem linguarum calepinus, a Latin lexicon. Calepino also wrote St. John the Hermit's life, printed in the Acta Sanctorum for 22 October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-castag:
Andrea Castagno, a Florentine painter, was born near Florence in 1390 and died at Florence in 1457. Little is known of his life. Vasari says his father was a labourer, and Castagno began keeping cattle. No one knows what led him to art or who first taught him. In 1434, after the Medici returned, he painted the executed Albizzi and Peruzzi on the palace facade, winning the name Andrea degli Impiccati.

In 1454 Pope Nicholas V commissioned him to decorate rooms in the Vatican. Vasari tells that Andrea learned oil painting's secret from Domenico Veneziano and murdered him to keep it alone. The tale fails, since Domenico outlived him by four years. With Uccello and Lippi he furthered the Masaccio revolution, under the influence of the Brancacci frescoes and Donatello. His Niccolo da Tolentino in Florence Cathedral, his Last Supper at Sant'Apollonia, and his Villa Carducci frescoes show his strength in form and drawing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-cesalp:
Andrea Cesalpino, a physician, philosopher, and naturalist, ranks as a botanist. He was born at Arezzo in Tuscany in 1519 and died at Rome in 1603. At Pisa he studied medicine under Colombo and botany under Luca Ghini. He then taught philosophy, medicine, and botany at Pisa, exploring plants across Italy.

Europe's first botanical gardens rose in his time, at Padua in 1546 and Pisa in 1547 under Ghini. Cesalpino succeeded Ghini in charge of the Pisan garden from 1554 to 1558. Late in life he moved to Rome as medicine professor at the Sapienza and physician to Clement VIII. His writings show genius and deep thought, though his style runs heavy, with passages of great beauty. On the blood's circulation he went further than any physiologist before Harvey, without grasping its full course. His De plantis libri XVI, published at Florence in 1583, made him immortal. Linnaeus later named the genus Caesalpinia for him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-contuc:
Andrea Contucci del Sansovino was born at Monte San Savino, near Arezzo, in 1460 and died in 1529. A sculptor of the transition between the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, he shows that transition in his style. He worked first in his native town and at Florence, then for about eight years in Portugal. His best sculpture came after his return, at Florence and Rome.

His Baptism of Christ, a marble group in the Florence baptistery, sets finely contrasted figures with great effect. The tombs of Cardinals Basso and Sforza Visconti at Santa Maria del Popolo join antiquity's lessons to mature Renaissance art. At Venice he turned pictorial, in small statuettes of Pallas, Apollo, Mercury, and Pax, and in Saint Mark's bronze reliefs and sacristy doors, and a Bacchus of antique grace. Venetians ranked him a master of the first rank.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-pisano:
Andrea da Pontadera, known as Andrea Pisano, was an Italian sculptor and architect, born in 1270 and dead in 1349. A pupil of Giovanni Pisano, he first learned goldsmithing, which served his later work well. He helped his master on Saint Maria della Spina at Pisa and worked on Saint Mark's and the Doge's palace at Venice before going to Florence.

There he made his work: the first of the three bronze doors for the baptistery's south side. He spent years on it before it was set up in 1336. The date 1330 on the door marks the wax model, not the casting. Its quatrefoil panels hold single figures and scenes from Saint John the Baptist's life. Giotto's influence shaped his style. After Giotto's death Pisano built two stories of niches above Giotto's Campanile work. From 1347 to 1349 he was chief architect of Orvieto's duomo. His pupil was Andrea da Cione, known as Orcagna.
