catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angel-de-saav:
Angel de Saavedra Ramirez de Baquedano, Spanish poet and statesman, was born at Cordova in 1791 and died at Madrid in 1865. Second son of the Duque de Rivas, he succeeded to the title when his elder brother died without issue in 1834. At eleven he entered Madrid's Seminario de Nobles, leaving at sixteen to join the army. From 1808 to 1813 he fought in the Spanish War of Independence.

From 1813 to 1820 he lived in Seville, writing, then sat in the Cortes to 1823. Siding with the revolutionaries, he fled when Ferdinand VII came to power, escaping to Gibraltar, London, Malta, and France. On Ferdinand's death he returned to Spain. In 1836 he became minister of the interior, and in 1844 ambassador to Naples until 1850. A poet and painter, he earned a living in French exile by a painting school and selling pictures. His front-rank works are El moro exposito (1834) and Don Alvaro (1835), his best work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-di-ma:
Florentine sculptor Antonio Rosselino was the youngest of five sculptor brothers of the Gamberelli family. He lived from 1427 to 1478 and won praise for sharp, fine low relief, carving that rises only slightly from its background. Said to have studied under Donatello, he made his most important work, the tomb monument of Cardinal Jacopo of Portugal in San Miniato al Monte, Florence, between 1461 and 1467. A signed portrait bust of Matteo Palmieri, held in the Bargello, dates from 1468.

In 1470 he built the monument for Mary of Aragon, Duchess of Amalfi, at Monte Oliveto in Naples, with a Nativity relief over the altar probably also his. Other works include a boy St. John the Baptist, Madonna and Child reliefs, an Ecce Homo, plus a bust of Francesco Sassetti. Working with Mino da Fiesole, he also carved reliefs of the Assumption, the taking up of Mary into heaven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-monte:
Spanish Dominican Antonio Montesino had an unknown birth date and died in the West Indies in 1545. He became the first voice in America to denounce the enslavement of Indians in public. He entered the Dominicans at Salamanca and landed in Hispaniola in September 1510 with the first band of his order, under Pedro de Cordova. Noted for piety, strict observance, eloquence, and moral courage, he preached in 1511 that enslaving and oppressing Indians was sinful and disgraceful to Spain.

Censured for the sermon, he was summoned to Spain in 1512, where he pled the Indian cause so well that the king at once moved to ease their condition. In June 1526 he sailed with colonists under Ayllón to Guandape, near the later Jamestown site. There, the article says, Mass was first celebrated in what is now the territory of the United States.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ariano:
Ariano is a diocese in the archdiocese of Beneventum, covering seven towns in Avellino province, four in Beneventum, and one in Foggia. The town, very ancient, of the Hirpini people, stands on hills fifteen miles from Beneventum, and its name comes from pagan Ora Jani, the shrine of Janus. No documents fix the date of its conversion to Christianity. The gospel may have reached it from Beneventum, whose bishop was among nineteen prelates at the Synod of Rome in 313.

Ariano had been an episcopal city from the tenth century, perhaps earlier. It first appears in Pope John XIII's bull of 965 to 972 erecting the archdiocese of Beneventum, where it is named a suffragan see. Its first known bishop was Menardus, whom Ughelli believed a native not of Padua but of Poitiers. The entry traces a hill town from pagan shrine to suffragan diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascendente-do:
Ascendente Domino is a bull of Gregory XIII, dated 24 May 1584, in favour of the Society of Jesus. It confirms its constitution and privileges already granted by Paul III, Julius III, Paul IV, plus Pius V. It recalls and confirms those means Ignatius prescribed for the Society to reach the end for which he founded it.

Candidates first make two years' novitiate, or trial, then take three simple vows, ceasing to be novices and joining the Society's body. Those simple vows bind their makers for life, but bind the Society only while the general sees fit to keep them as members. Unformed temporal coadjutors, or lay brothers, may after some years become formed temporal coadjutors, while scholastics, after studies, must pass further stages before becoming professed or formed spiritual coadjutors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ascoli-piceno:
Ascoli Piceno is a diocese of sixteen towns in Ascoli-Piceno province, two in Aquila, and two in Teramo, Italy, under the Holy See's immediate jurisdiction. Harnack calls it one of Italy's cities which, by importance, may be believed to have held a Christian community and bishopric from the mid-third century. That was when sixty bishops attended Pope Cornelius's Roman synod. Traces of the bishopric, however, appear only in the fourth century.

Emidius, martyred under Diocletian, and Claudius, present at Rimini's synod in the Arian controversy of 359, were bishops of Ascoli. So was Lusentius in the fifth century, present at Milan's synod that sent the famous letter to Leo I. Worth noting for art is its twelfth-century baptistery, and one later bishop, Giulio de' Medici, rose higher in church history. The entry joins early bishops to a town's artistic heritage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-avellino:
Avellino is an Italian diocese in the province of Naples, suffragan, or subordinate, to Benevento. St Sabinus, martyr, founded it at the start of the second century, and its list of bishops runs from 1124. The Diocese of Frigento, whose list runs from 1080 to 1455, was joined to Avellino on 9 May 1466. That union lasted until 27 June 1818, when Frigento was suppressed.

Avellino itself stood vacant from 1782 to 1792, a decade without a bishop. In the author's day it counted 118,649 Catholics in 41 parishes, served by 243 secular priests and 11 regulars, with 80 seminarians. It held 90 churches and chapels. The entry cites the Annuario Ecclesiastico of 1907, Cappelletti's Churches of Italy, and Zingarelli's history of Avellino's see and pastors for these facts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basle-lugano:
Basle-Lugano is Switzerland's largest Catholic diocese, joining the dioceses of Basle and Lugano under one common bishop. Basle replaced old Augst, whose bishop attended a Cologne council in 346. When Augst decayed amid the migrations, the see moved to Basle, founded by Valentinian I in 374. Its most important early bishop was Hatto of Reichenau, Charlemagne's friend, bishop from 805.

Hatto issued a capitulary of great importance for his diocese, resigned in 822, and died at Reichenau in 836. Under Adalbert (999-1025), Rudolph III of Burgundy laid the bishops' secular jurisdiction with towns, territories, coinage, and hunting rights. Adalbert rebuilt the Magyar-pillaged cathedral and consecrated it in 1019 before Henry II and his wife. His successors Ulrich II and Dietrich ranked among the Holy Roman Empire's spiritual princes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedetto-da-:
Benedetto da Majano, a Florentine sculptor and architect of the Renaissance, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Majano in 1442 and dead at Florence in 1498, he began with wood mosaic, inlaid pictures in wood at which he was unusually skilled. A ruined shipment bound for the King of Hungary pushed him toward stone, a more lasting material.

His carving fills the rest of the entry, from the Faenza altar of 1471 to a lifelike bust of Pietro Mellini and the carved doorway frame of the Palazzo Vecchio. Churches, tombs, and palace work show a craftsman moving easily between sculpture and building. The piece is a short working life of a busy Renaissance hand.

Benedetto da Rovezzano, a sculptor and architect, is the subject of this short 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1490 near Florence, or by some accounts near Pistoia, he died at Florence in 1530. His family name is given as Gratini or Grazini, and his career belongs to the late Renaissance in Florence.

Tombs dominate his known work, most of them architectural in design with sculpted ornament. Fragments of his carving for the church of St. John Gualbertus survive in the Bargello, damaged in the siege of Florence. Monuments for the Altoviti and Soderini families show the same blend of building and carving that marks his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardo-ross:
Bernardo Rossellino, properly Bernardo di Matteo Gambarelli, was a Florentine architect and sculptor of the early Renaissance, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born at Florence in 1409, he died in 1464, standing first among the second-rank masters of his generation. His Rucellai palace at Florence followed the plans of Leon Battista Alberti, with Rossellino working out the details.

At Arezzo his façade for the Fraternity of Mercy rose on a Gothic base. Greatest fame came in papal service under Nicholas V and Pius II, including work at Pienza, the pope's rebuilt hometown. The entry presents a capable builder who turned great men's designs into stone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernhard-bolz:
Bernhard Bolzano, an Austrian mathematician and philosopher, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Prague in 1781, he died in 1848 after a career that joined mathematics with the philosophy of religion. Against his father's wish he entered the priesthood and was ordained in 1805, the year he became professor of religious philosophy at Prague.

His lectures, tinged with rationalism, drew denunciation, and the Prince-Archbishop's protection kept him in post only until 1820, when dismissal came. Later work in logic and mathematics, long neglected, won him posthumous fame. The entry presents a priest-scholar punished for independent thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-albert-ber:
Blessed Albert Berdini of Sarteano, a Franciscan preacher and missionary, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Sarteano in Tuscany in 1385, he died at Milan in 1450. He joined the Conventuals in 1405, then passed to the stricter Friars Minor under the influence of St. Bernardine of Siena.

As Bernardine's disciple and companion, Albert's preaching fame grew until men called him the King of Preachers. Missions in Italy and the East, including work for church unity with the Greeks, filled his later years. The entry presents an orator formed by a master, carrying the Holy Name devotion abroad.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-angela-of-:
Blessed Angela of Foligno, an Umbrian penitent and mystical writer, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Foligno in 1248 to a rich family, she died in 1309. Married young, she loved worldly pleasures and, by the entry's frank account, fell into sin and a disorderly life.

Sorrow for her sins turned her, little by little, toward perfection and the deepest mysteries of faith. Her Book of Visions and Instructions, seventy chapters dictated from her own account, records that conversion. The entry presents a sinner turned mystic whose book still guides readers of the spiritual life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-francis-of:
Blessed Francis of Fabriano, a Franciscan priest, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1251, he died in 1322, with signs of future holiness marking his birth and childhood, the entry says. Gifted in mind, he finished humanities and philosophy and entered a nearby Franciscan convent in 1267.

Under able masters he grew fast in religious life, then gave himself to theology and to mission preaching in Fabriano and its neighbourhood. As a preacher he became a shining example to Franciscan missioners. The entry presents a local saint whose life stayed close to home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-pacificus-:
Blessed Pacificus of Ceredano, also called Pacificus of Novara, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cerano in Lombardy in 1420, supposedly of the respected Ramati family, he died in 1482. He joined the Observant Franciscans at Novara in 1445 and preached widely, sharing in his order's preaching of a crusade against the Turks.

In 1481 the Observants' general chapter at Ferrara sent him as commissioner to Sardinia to govern and inspect the Franciscan houses there. He is famed as author of the Summa Pacifica, an Italian treatise on hearing confessions, first printed at Milan in 1479 and later in Latin at Venice. His feast falls on 5 June.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boccaccino:
Boccaccino covers two Cremona painters, father and son: Boccaccio, born in 1460, and Camillo, born in 1511. Boccaccio trained near Ferrara among followers of Mantegna and painted frescoes at Sant'Agostino in Cremona. His Coronation of the Virgin in Rome was mocked, and he returned to Cremona, where his cathedral frieze on the Virgin's life won praise.

Lanzi ranked him with Perugino, calling him modern among ancients and ancient among moderns. His Marriage of the Virgin and Madonna with Saints Vincent and Anthony were often mistaken for Perugino's work. Light grey eyes with a dark rim mark his pictures. Camillo, his son and pupil, died young in 1546 but surpassed his father, approaching Correggio in works like the Four Evangelists at San Sigismondo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boiano:
Boiano, a diocese in Benevento province, Italy, occupies the site of the Roman colony Bovianum at the foot of Monte Matese. Its see is ancient, though an early claim for a sixth-century bishop Laurentius rests on error. The first recorded bishop is Adalberto, named in 1071.

Later bishops left their mark on the cathedral of Saint Bartholomew. Poliziano consecrated it in 1215, Giovanni adorned its facade in 1226, and cardinals Orsini and Carafa furnished it richly. After a vacancy from 1774 to 1836, caused by disputes between Rome and Naples, Giuseppe Riccardi took the see. The diocese then counted 90,300 people, 33 parishes, and 134 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-borgo-san-don:
Borgo San-Donnino, a diocese in Parma province, Italy, takes its name from Saint Domninus, martyred there during Maximian's persecution. It stayed under a provost with full faculties, directly subject to Rome, until Clement VIII made it a see in 1601. The last provost, Papiro Picedi, became its first bishop. Its twelfth-century cathedral stands as a fine Romanesque monument, though its facade stays unfinished.

Notable bishops include Alfonso Pozzi, learned and zealous, and Ranuccio Scoti, nuncio to Switzerland under Urban VIII. Filippo Casoni urged Ughelli to write Italia Sacra, Gaetano Garimberti enriched the cathedral, Gerardo Giandemaria held a synod whose wise decrees still stand, and Girolamo Baiardi founded a hospital. The diocese counts 60,400 people, 54 parishes, 76 churches and chapels, and 100 secular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bovino:
Bovino, a diocese in Foggia province suffragan to Benevento, sits on a gentle slope with a city of over 30,000. Its first known bishop, Joannes, appears in a deed of 971. Later bishops built and adorned its churches: Roberto raised Saint Michael's shrine in 1190, Pietro built a new cathedral, and Paolo Tolosa founded the seminary in 1601 before becoming Archbishop of Chieti.

Scholars mark Bartolomeo della Porta, a noted jurisconsult of 1404, and Gian Domenico Annio, called the greatest canonist of his time. Cardinals Accolti and Marini held the see in the 1530s, and Angelo Ceraso, bishop from 1685, always visited on foot. After political strife left it vacant from 1792 to 1818, the diocese counted 32,710 Catholics, 10 parishes, and 76 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calvi-and-tea:
Calvi is the ancient Cales in Campania, near Capua. It was certainly a bishopric by the end of the fifth century, since Valerius of Calenum sat at the Roman council of Pope Symmachus in 499. Saracens destroyed it in the ninth century. Atenulfo, Count of Capua, rebuilt it, likely restoring the see, which surely had a bishop by the end of the eleventh century.

Notable bishops include Odoardo, who sat at Lyons in 1245, opposed Frederick II, and was slain on his return, and Gennaro Filomarino, a monk, in 1623. In 1818 Calvi joined with Teano, a small city once held by the Gaetani, whose first bishop was Saint Paris, ordained by Sylvester I.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-camerino:
Camerino is a city in the Apennines, about 40 miles from Ancona, which passed to the Holy See when the Exarchate of Ravenna was given to the pope. It suffered under Frederick II for backing the pope. Manfred's siege failed when Gentile Varano saved the city, which then became a papal fief and later a fief of the Farnesi. Under Decius's persecution in 249, the priest Porphyrius and Bishop Leontius died as martyrs there.

Later bishops include Saint Ansovinus in 816 and Alberto degli Alberti, made cardinal at Florence and peacemaker between Alfonso of Aragon and René of Anjou. Berardo Buongiovanni served as legate in Poland and a learned voice at Trent. The Capuchin Order was born at Camerino, and its diocese counts 182 parishes and 45,900 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conversano:
Umberto Benigni's entry covers the Diocese of Conversano, Cupersanensis, suffragan to Bari. Conversano, in Bari province, Apulia, Southern Italy, stands as ancient Cupersanum, a Peucetian city. Its history runs practically with Apulia's. After the Norman invasion it served for a while as a duchy's seat, later becoming a fief of Atri's dukes. The first bishop of certain date, Hilarius, attended the Roman synod of 501. Local tradition preserves an earlier bishop, Simplicius, who died in 492. No other names appear until Leo, mentioned in a 1088 document.

Later bishops worthy of mention include the Cistercian Stefano about 1266, Giovanni de Gropi about 1283, Antonio Guidotti, died 1433, and Paolo de Torcoli, died in the odour of sanctity in 1482. Romolo de' Valenti died 1579, Giuseppe Palermo was appointed 1658, and Andrea Brancaccia served 1681. The diocese counts 95,521 people, seven parishes, 130 churches and chapels, 132 secular and eight regular priests, two religious houses of men and eight of women.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-desiderio-da-:
A life of Desiderio da Settignano, a Tuscan sculptor born in 1428 who died at Florence in 1463. Said to be a stone-cutter's son, he joined the stone-workers' association in 1453 and studied under Donatello. Fineness, joy, elegance, and distinction mark his work, and it is often confused with his master's. His brief life still ranks him among the great artists of his day.

Chief works include the sculpted tomb of Carlo Marsuppini in Santa Croce, a tabernacle at San Lorenzo with a standing Child Jesus, and a bust of Marietta Strozzi. A Madonna relief, a girl's bust in the Bargello, and a wooden Magdalen finished by Benedetto da Majano follow. Other pieces, from a Louvre Beatrice to a London Saint Cecilia relief, are claimed for him by some judges and for Donatello's school by others.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diano:
Diano is a small city and diocese in the province of Salerno in Italy. It stands where the ancient town of Tegianum once stood, home to the Tegyani tribe of Lucania. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how Pope Pius the Ninth set up the see in 1850. King Ferdinand the Second of Naples had asked for it, joining Diano first to Capaccio.

Under the second bishop, Capaccio was cut away again and joined to Vallo. Diano took the name Teggiano in 1882 and answered to the archbishop of Salerno. It counted forty-four parishes and about two hundred and fifty secular priests. Its people, roughly one hundred thousand, fill out a compact picture of a small south Italian see.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diario-romano:
The Diario Romano, Italian for Roman Daybook, was a small book put out each year at Rome. It came with papal approval and laid down the feasts, fasts, and church functions to be kept in the city. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry built around the 1908 issue shows how it guided clergy and faithful through the Roman year.

Beyond feast days and moon phases, it lists when each Roman congregation met. It gives the hour of the evening Angelus bell as sunset shifted through the year. It also names which images of the Virgin were put out for veneration. Its day-by-day directory of Masses and devotions opens a window onto Rome at prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diego-francis:
Diego Francisco Altamirano was a Jesuit born at Madrid in 1625. He spent his career in Peru and died at Lima in 1715. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry treats his History of the Peruvian Province of the Society of Jesus. Only the twelfth book ever reached print, issued in 1891 with a short life of the author.

A second work, a brief note on Jesuit missions among the unbelievers of Peru and the Mojos provinces, followed with the same editor. The History's original manuscript rests in Lima's National Archives, now badly decayed. The entry is thus as much a story of a book nearly lost as of the missions it records.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-pass:
Domenico Passignano, born Domenico Cresti at Passignano near Florence in 1558, belongs by style to the Venetian school. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he lived at Florence and Pisa, then took up Venetian ways at Venice and kept them for life. Charming in manner and delightful in talk, he won knighthood and many commissions from Pope Clement the Eighth, with fresh honors from Urban the Eighth.

Florence loved him on his return and counted him chief of its Academy, even though all knew his style as Venetian and foreign to Florentine methods. He painted with rare speed, and his work fills churches at Rome and galleries at Paris, London, and Vienna. His own portrait hangs in the Uffizi, and he died at Florence in 1638.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-brun:
Eusebius Bruno was Bishop of Angers in eleventh-century France, a prelate caught between loyalty to his teacher and loyalty to the Church's faith. He was trained under the famed Berengarius of Tours and became bishop in December 1047. His fame rests on his long, uneasy tie to Berengarius, who taught that the bread and wine in the Eucharist are only a figure of Christ's Body and Blood.

Eusebius at first defended his master against condemnation at Rome and Vercelli in 1050, and he stayed away from the Paris synod of 1051 for fear of censure. Yet at Tours in 1054 he pressed Berengarius to swear in writing that after consecration the bread and wine truly are the Body and Blood of Christ. Whether he changed his mind or had misunderstood his master from the start remains, the entry says, an open question.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-kino:
Eusebius Kino, born Kuhn in the Tyrol in 1644, was a Jesuit missionary, mathematician, and mapmaker whose work opened up the American Southwest. After teaching mathematics at Ingolstadt, he reached Mexico in 1680 and founded the mission of Lower California. Working from 1687 in Sonora, he entered Upper Pimeria and won his first convert at Nuestra Señora de los Dolores. He crossed the Rio Colorado on a bold exploring voyage that proved California was a peninsula reached by an overland route.

His reports and maps gave Europe its first exact knowledge of a vast, little-known country. He crossed it time and again, covering more than twenty thousand miles by the account of Clavigero. He built missions, learned the ways of the native peoples, and drew the celebrated map of California printed in 1702. It notes the claim that rebel Indians shot him on 15 March 1711.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fano:
Fano is an Italian city and diocese on the Adriatic coast of Italy. Its Roman name, Fanum Fortunae, recalls a temple of Fortune. Claudius Nero beat Hasdrubal near the city in 207 BC. Augustus later made it a Roman colony called Julia Fanensis.

Aurelian fought the Alamanni there in 271, and Vitruvius built its basilica. An arch of Augustus, enlarged in 340, still marks the old city. Fano passed to the Holy See in the eighth century with the Pentapolis. The Malatesta ruled it from 1306 to 1463, and its bishops included several men of Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferentino:
Ferentino is an Italian town in the province of Rome, subject to the Holy See. In ancient times the Hernici's chief place, it kept massive cyclopean walls near its fortress. Rome made it a municipium in 487 after early wars with the Volscians. Legend credits Peter and Paul with the first preaching of the Gospel there.

Its first known bishop, Bassus, attended Roman synods in 487 and 492. Later bishops served as legates to emperors, popes, and crusade princes. The town counted 19 parishes and some 45,000 souls in 1909. Six monasteries and eight convents still marked its busy religious life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernando-aven:
Fernando Avendano was a Peruvian priest and keen scholar of Lima's Indian past. Born at Lima near the turn of the seventeenth century, he died in 1665. He studied survivals of the old rites and customs of Peruvian Indians. His valuable notes survive only in fragments within Arriaga's work.

His Sermones de los misterios, published in 1649, hold great value for students of language. Delivered in Quichua, they appeared beside Spanish translations in print. Lima's archbishop ordered their publication for the Church. Avendano died at Lima in 1665, shortly after his appointment to Santiago.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-foligno:
Foligno is a diocese in Perugia, on the river Topino, under the Holy See at once. It rose on the site of a cemetery around the basilica of St. Felician, outside old Fulginium. After the Lombard invasion it passed to Spoleto's duchy and then to the Holy See. Ghibelline in the thirteenth century, it fell to the Trinci in 1305, who ruled to 1439.

Art bloomed under the Trinci, whose palace halls Nelli and Fabriano painted. Its cathedral, rebuilt in 1133, gained a carved wing in 1201, restored in 1903. The Sassovivo house of 1229 boasts a cloister of 120 columns. The diocese counts 55 parishes and 31,000 people, with schools, houses of religious, and a weekly paper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fossano:
Fossano is a town and diocese in Piedmont in northern Italy, suffragan to Turin, set in a fertile plain on the Stura river. It trades in farm produce and livestock, with silk weaving, paper making, basket making, and mineral springs nearby. An independent commune in the early Middle Ages, it passed to the Marquesses of Saluzzo, then to the House of Savoy. It was sacked or captured repeatedly, by Facino Cane in 1396, by the French in 1535 and 1796, and in the wars that followed.

The painter and architect Ambrogio da Fossano, called Il Borgognone, who designed the Certosa at Pavia, was born here. The bishop's see dates from 1592, was suppressed from 1801 to 1817, and then restored. At the time of writing the diocese held 25 parishes and 36,000 people. It had religious houses for men and women, schools for boys and girls, charitable institutions, and a weekly Catholic paper.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-faa:
Francesco Faa di Bruno, born at Alessandria on 7 March 1825 and dead at Turin on 26 March 1888, was an Italian mathematician and priest of noble birth. He once held the rank of captain on the staff of the Sardinian army, but in Paris he resigned his commission. He studied under Cauchy and Leverrier, who shared in the discovery of Neptune, and grew close to Abbe Moigno and Hermite. Returning to Turin, he was ordained and spent the rest of his life as professor of mathematics at the university.

Paris and Turin both gave him the degree of Doctor of Science. Beyond devotional writings, sacred melodies, and scientific apparatus of his own invention, he published about forty mathematical articles in leading journals. He wrote a general theory of elimination in 1859, a calculus of errors in 1867, and the first half of a planned three-volume treatise on elliptic functions, its theory and uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-adorn:
Francis Adorno, born in 1531 and dead at Genoa on 13 January 1586, was a celebrated Italian Jesuit preacher from the family of Genoa's last doge. Born three years after the Adorni name was suppressed and the dogeship abolished by Andrea Doria to end 165 years of strife with the Fregosi. He entered the Society of Jesus in Portugal, where he had been sent to study. Recalled to Rome, he taught theology and won a reputation as one of Italy's greatest orators.

He became the first rector of the College of Milan and later administered several houses of the order, serving as friend, adviser, and confessor to St. Charles Borromeo. At Borromeo's request he wrote two volumes on ecclesiastical discipline. His remaining works include sermons, Latin verse, counsels on illustrating Ligurian history, and a treatise on usury kept in the Ambrosian Library.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-gar:
Francisco Garcia Diego y Moreno, born at Lagos in Jalisco on 17 September 1785 and dead at Santa Barbara on 30 April 1846, was the first Bishop of California. He took the Franciscan habit at the missionary college of Guadalupe, Zacatecas, in 1801 and was ordained at Monterey in 1808. He spent twenty years preaching missions, compiling a small Method for Giving Missions.

When Mexico resolved to expel Spanish friars from California, his college sent eleven Mexican Franciscans in April 1832, Diego as commissary. They reached Monterey in February 1833 and took the missions from San Antonio to Sonoma. Diego chose Santa Clara, then visited Mexico to press for a bishop to preserve the Church in California. The government petitioned Rome in 1836. Diego, consecrated bishop, made a visitation of all his churches from Santa Barbara, dying worn out and disheartened at conditions he could not remedy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francisco-med:
Francisco Medrano was a Spanish lyric poet of Seville, not to be confused with Sebastian Francisco de Medrano, another poet of about the same time. His birth and death dates are unknown, but he lived in the later sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, and little is known of his life except his visit to Rome. His poems were published at Palermo in 1617 as an appendix to Pedro Venegas's imitation of Ovid's Remedy of Love.

Critic Adolfo de Castro calls Medrano the best of the Spanish followers of Horace, comparing favourably even with Fray Luis de Leon. His Prophecy of the Tagus closely follows Horace's ode that would separate Mark Antony and Cleopatra, so closely as almost to translate it. Leon's ode on the same theme departs from Horace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-napo:
Francois-Napoleon-Marie Moigno, born at Guemene in Morbihan on 15 April 1804 and dead at Saint-Denis on 14 July 1884, was a French physicist and scientific writer. Educated at the Jesuit college of Sainte-Anne d'Auray, he entered the novitiate in 1822 and studied theology at Montrouge while giving leisure to mathematics and physics with much success. He fled to Brieg in Switzerland in the Revolution of 1830. There his remarkable memory won him several foreign languages, including Hebrew and Arabic.

In 1836 he became professor of mathematics at Sainte-Genevieve College in Paris, widely known as scholar, preacher, and writer, esteemed by Cauchy, Arago, Dumas, and Ampere. He was writing Lessons on differential and integral calculus on Cauchy's methods, with a first volume out, when he left the Society in 1843.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriel-garci:
Gabriel García Moreno, an Ecuadorian patriot and statesman, was born at Guayaquil on Christmas Eve 1821 and assassinated at Quito in August 1875. His father died while he was young, and his mother, aided by the Mercedarian tutor José Betancourt, schooled him well. Despite lost family fortune, he took his law degree at Quito in October 1844 and soon entered politics.

García Moreno first shone as a satirist in El Zurriago and as a useful Quito councilman, then as advocate from 1848. Exiled after the fall of the Roca government, he returned to find Jesuits expelled from New Granada seeking shelter. At Panama he shielded them, slipped ashore ahead of their pursuers at Guayaquil, and won them a foothold in Ecuador, a deed that marked him for lifelong foes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaetano-sanse:
Gaetano Sanseverino, restorer of scholastic philosophy in Italy, was born at Naples in 1811 and died there of cholera in 1865. Schooled at Nola under his rector uncle, he was ordained, taught logic and metaphysics, and became a canon of Naples Cathedral and a writer in the National Library. Descartes ruled the schools of his youth, but wider reading won him to Saint Thomas.

From then on, restoring Christian philosophy was his life's work, by pen, lecture, and talk, and he greatly aided Leo XIII. In 1840 he founded the journal Science and Faith, carried on by disciples until 1887. His chief book, Christian Philosophy Compared with Ancient and New, ran to five volumes but covered only logic and psychology. He also answered Hume and Gioberti on the test of truth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gentile-da-fa:
Gentile da Fabriano, an Italian painter born about 1378 in the Marches, worked in a haze of uncertain dates that scholars have only lately cleared. Vasari's tales need caution, but Milanesi, Ricci, and Venturi fixed key points. An altarpiece at Venice in 1408 proves years of residence there, and the doges' palace council hall followed between 1411 and 1414.

From 1414 to 1419 Gentile painted at Brescia for Pandolfo Malatesta, and Pope Martin V invited him to Rome on meeting Malatesta. Delayed, he stopped at Florence, joined its painters' guild in 1422, and signed the Strozzi Adoration for Santa Trinità in 1423. Siena took him in 1425, Orvieto that August, and he probably died in 1427, his early life still unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giangiorgio-t:
Giangiorgio Trissino was an Italian poet and scholar of a patrician Vicenza family, born in 1478 and dead at Rome in 1550. Trained in Greek at Milan and philosophy at Ferrara, he served Leo X as nuncio to Germany in 1515 and Clement VII as ambassador. Charles V made him a count palatine in 1532. A Catholic Encyclopedia article places him high in modern European letters for his classical regularity.

His tragedy Sofonisba of 1515 was the first Italian tragedy to follow the classic rules. His epic Italia liberata dai Goti, on Belisarius's campaigns, tried to prove the vernacular could carry a classical epic. It came out cold and colorless. He also argued, in his Castellano of 1529, that literary Italian was a courtly blend rather than Tuscan at root, and he proposed new letters to mark open and close vowels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giordano-brun:
Giordano Bruno was an Italian philosopher born at Nola in 1548, who died at Rome in 1600. Born Filippo, he entered the Dominicans at fifteen and was ordained a priest in 1572. Accused of heresy in 1576, he fled Rome, left his order, and wandered through Geneva, Toulouse, Paris, London, and Germany. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a restless mind that found peace nowhere.

In London he published his Expulsion of the Triumphant Beast in 1584 and defended the Copernican universe. Lured to Venice in 1591, he was denounced to the Inquisition, sent to Rome in 1593, and held six years. Condemned in January 1600, he was burned at the stake in the Campo dei Fiori on 17 February. His system joined God and world in one infinite, living universe, a material pantheism his judges condemned for theological error.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gioseffe-zarl:
Gioseffe Zarlino was an Italian musical theorist born at Chioggia in 1517, who died at Venice in 1590. Ordained a deacon in 1541, he gave himself to music under Willaert at Venice. In 1564 he succeeded di Rore as first maestro di cappella at St. Mark's, a post he held until his death. A Catholic Encyclopedia article rests his fame on theory rather than on composition.

Between 1558 and 1589 he published three remarkable treatises at Venice. He admitted only twelve modes, beginning with the Ionian, and so laid the ground for the modern major and minor scales. He proposed dividing the octave into twelve semitones and equal temperament for keyed instruments. His pupil Galilei disputed his theories, but Zarlino, the article says, was right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anto:
Giovanni Antoniano was a patristic scholar born at Nijmegen in Holland early in the sixteenth century, who died there in 1588. From his entry into the Dominican Order, his patience, industry, and love of the Fathers marked him as an editor their writings needed. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar who served twice as prior of Nijmegen, in 1566 and again in 1587.

He preached learned sermons against the principles of Protestantism and worked beside Henry Gravius, whose pupil he was. He succeeded Gravius as editor of the Fathers. His editions include Gregory of Nyssa on the creation of man and Basil's Hexameron, both printed at Cologne in 1537. Paulinus of Nola followed in 1560, and the letters of St. Jerome at Antwerp in 1568.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Cima da Conegliano was a Venetian painter born at Conegliano in 1459 or 1460, who died in 1517 or 1518. His father, a cloth-shearer who died in 1484, gave the family its name. At work in Vicenza by 1488, he settled at Venice in 1492 and returned home by the summer of 1516. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a calm, undramatic master of Madonnas.

His earliest dated painting, the Madonna of the Arbour of 1489, already shows the serious calm that marked his whole career. Under Giovanni Bellini he became an able successor and a link between that master and Titian. He gave landscape a set place in modern painting, shaping laws of atmosphere, light, and shade, and his silvery color ripened into delicate gold. Madonnas enthroned among saints, in gently animated symmetry, fill his output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-da-v:
Giovanni da Verrazano was a navigator born about 1485 at Val di Greve near Florence, who was executed at Puerto del Pico in Spain in November 1527. In French service under Francis I, he won fame as a corsair against Spain and Portugal. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his 1524 voyage of discovery to the North American coast.

Sailing in January 1524, he explored the coast from thirty to fifty degrees north, giving the first post-Columbian description of it, including New York Bay and the Hudson River. He noted Long Island Sound, Block Island, and Newport, and returned to Dieppe in July 1524. His brother Girolamo drew a 1529 map from his log, still in Rome, whose accuracy shaped later cartography. Spanish records say he was captured off Cadiz and executed in 1527.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giulio-romano:
Giulio Romano, properly Giulio dei Giannuzzi, also known as Giulio Pippi, was a famous architect and painter, the best-known of Raphael's pupils. Born at Rome in 1492, he died at Mantua in 1546. At nineteen he placed himself under Raphael, who had just finished the Halls of the Segnatura and Heliodorus. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the unique representative of the so-called Roman School.

As Raphael's right hand he enlarged and executed in fresco or on canvas the master's drawings. Within eight years he completed the Fire in the Borgo, the cartoons of the Acts of the Apostles, the Vatican loggias, and the Farnesina frescoes. He had no originality, only manual dexterity and prodigious industry, and Raphael's graceful figures often turned in his hands into coarse muscular giants. His brick-colored tones and plaster flesh-tints marred many of Raphael's later works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humbert-guill:
Humbert-Guillaume de Precipiano was a churchman and diplomat, born at Besançon in 1626 and dead at Brussels in 1711. He studied classics at Constance, philosophy at home, and theology at the Jesuit college in Louvain, graduating in law and theology at Dôle. He rose through canon, archdeacon, and dean of Besançon's chapter, commendatory abbot of Bellevaux, and ecclesiastical councillor at Dôle under Philip IV of Spain.

In 1667 Philip sent him as plenipotentiary for Burgundy to the imperial Diet of Ratisbon, and after 1672 he served at Madrid as chief councillor for the Netherlands and Burgundy. Made bishop of Bruges in 1682, he laboured seven years for purity of faith and church rights against Jansenism. In 1690 he accepted Mechlin only on the pope's express order, and there fought Jansenist doctrines spread by French refugees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-il-parmigiano:
Il Parmigiano, the Parmesan, was the current name of Francesco Mazzuola, Italian painter born at Parma in 1504 and dead at Casal Maggiore in 1540. Son of the painter Filippo Mazzuola, who died in 1505, he was brought up by his uncles Michele and Pierilario. The boy loved painting strongly and grew especially keen on Correggio, who founded the Parmesan school.

His St. Bernard for Parma's Observantines and other early works show him an eager follower of Correggio. At twenty he headed for Rome, eager to study Michelangelo's masterpieces, and his early talent quickly made him famous there. Vasari reports a Roman saying: Raphael's soul had moved into the Parmesan's body. Clement VII commissioned a Circumcision, but the sack of Rome in 1527 checked this bright beginning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-jandu:
John of Janduno was a fourteenth-century Averroist philosopher linked to the Defensor Pacis against Pope John XXII. Born about 1300, he took his arts degree at the College of Navarre in Paris and praised Paris in his De Laudibus Parisiis. With Marsilius of Padua he composed the celebrated Defensor Pacis, for which both authors were condemned in 1327.

He must be distinguished from John of Gand, born about 1270, theologian of the Sorbonne and canon of Paris. Yet many philosophical works ascribed to Johannes de Ganduno may belong to either man. They include commentaries on the Sentences, on Aristotle's Physics, Metaphysics, and Soul, and a question on Averroes. The author defends twofold truth, a single intellect common to all men, and determinism, belittles St. Thomas in favor of Averroes, and fits the turbulent anti-papal writer better than the quiet canon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-monte:
John of Montecorvino was the Franciscan founder of the Catholic mission in China. Born in southern Italy in 1246, he first served the Persian mission. When Argun Khan asked the pope through the Nestorian bishop Bar Sauma for missionaries to Kublai Khan's court, Nicholas IV entrusted John with the mission to Farther China. He set out in 1289 with letters to khans, kings, and patriarchs.

Preaching thirteen months in India and baptizing about a hundred, he reached China in 1294 to find Kublai dead and Timur Khan on the throne. Unopposed by the new ruler despite Nestorian hostility, he built churches at Peking in 1299 and 1305. He bought and trained some 150 boys for choir and Mass, learned Chinese, preached in it, and translated the New Testament and Psalms. Among his six thousand converts was a Nestorian king named George.

John of Montesono was a Spanish Dominican theologian condemned at Paris for denying the Immaculate Conception. Born at Monzon, dates unknown, he joined the Dominicans probably at Valencia, lectured on theology there in 1383, and taught at the Paris convent of St. James, taking his mastership in 1387.

Declaring it heretical to hold that the Virgin was conceived without sin, he drew the Paris faculty's censure of fourteen claims from his lectures. Warned in private and in public to take his words back, he refused. The Bishop of Paris then cut off defenders of the banned theses from the Church. Montesono appealed to Clement VIII at Avignon, then, foreseeing defeat, fled against orders to Aragon and Sicily, switching allegiance to Urban VI, Clement's rival. He later served on a legation for the Aragonese succession in 1412 and wrote against Clement's papal claim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jordanus-of-g:
Jordanus of Giano was an Italian Franciscan whose memoirs are a chief source for the order's early years in Germany. Born at Giano in the Spoleto valley about 1195, he entered the Franciscans about 1220. He was sent to Germany a year later under Caesarius of Speyer, first Minorite provincial of Germany. Ordained in 1223, he became guardian at Mainz in 1225 and custos of the Thuringian houses, doing much to spread the order in northern Germany.

Sent to Italy on order business in 1230 and 1238, he attended a chapter of German Franciscans at Halberstadt in 1262. There he dictated his early memoirs of the first friars sent to Germany to Brother Baldwin of Brandenburg. Beginning in 1207, the memoirs break off abruptly at 1238 in the sole manuscript, carefully edited in the Analecta Franciscana. A German translation of 1870 carried many erroneous notes. Jordanus died after 1262, his exact end unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-klemens-maria:
Klemens Maria Brentano (1778-1842) was a German poet of the Romantic School, born at Thal-Ehrenbreitstein. After failing as a merchant, he entered Jena University in 1797 and met the Schlegel brothers and Ludwig Tieck, founders of the movement he joined.

At Heidelberg with Achim von Arnim and Joseph Gorres, he led the younger Romantics and issued with Arnim the folk-song collection Des Knaben Wunderhorn in three volumes from 1805 to 1808. It fixed the folk song's place in German letters and stirred poets abroad, Longfellow among them, though its texts were not exact. After his wife's death in 1806 and a disastrous second marriage, an unreturned love for Luise Hensel turned him to fervent Catholic devotion. He spent six years at Dulmen recording the visions of the stigmatic nun Katharina Emmerich.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-larino:
Larino, ancient Larinum, belonged to the Frentani, a Samnite tribe. It ranked as a Roman town with its own charter, a municipium, in Campobasso province, southern Italy. Today's city, a mile from ancient Larinum, ruined by war and epidemic, first appears as an episcopal see in 668.

Noted bishops include Giovanni Leone, a canonist and theologian of 1440, Fra Giacomo de' Petruzzi, a saintly philosopher, and Belisario Baldovino, present at Trent, who founded the seminary and episcopal palace. Gian Tommaso Eustachi won fame for sanctity in 1612, Carlo Pianetti restored the cathedral with its fine marble front in 1706, and Gian Andrea Tri wrote Larino's history in 1726. The diocese, suffragan of Benevento, holds 21 parishes with 79,000 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leghorn-livor:
Leghorn, Italian Livorno, is a Tuscan port, suffragan of Pisa and capital of Italy's smallest province. Built on marshy ground and cut by canals, it earns the name Little Venice. A larger canal joins it to Pisa. It has an old Medici port and a new port built in 1854.

Once Tuscany's chief port, it is still outranked only by Genoa and Naples. It holds a naval academy, an 1881 observatory, a notable public library, and a prehistoric museum of Etruscan and Roman finds. It also holds a picture gallery and historic archives. Shipbuilding, ironworks, and alabaster and coral trade drive its industry. Its sixteenth-century cathedral stands beside Greek, Maronite, and Armenian churches and a 1603 synagogue second only to Amsterdam's. Ancient Portus Liburni, it passed from Pisans to Genoese, and Florentines bought it in 1421 for 100,000 florins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luca-giordano:
Luca Giordano was a Neapolitan painter, born in 1632 and dead in 1705, marvelled at for the speed with which he covered ceilings, domes, and walls across Italy and Spain. His father kept urging haste, and the nickname Luca Fa Presto, make haste, stuck.

Chief of the Machinisti, Italy's quick-painting decorators, he left more pictures than perhaps any painter of his age. Pupil of Ribera, then of Pietro da Cortona, and constant copyist of Raphael, he worked at Naples, Florence in 1679, and Madrid in 1692, painting the Escorial's vast ceiling and stair. Sixty pictures stand at Madrid, about thirty at Naples, with more in Dresden, Munich, Paris, and Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-lippoma:
Luigi Lippomano was a Venetian cardinal and writer of saints' lives, born in 1500 and dead in 1559. Of noble birth, he mastered classics, then sacred learning, and joined Cajetan's Oratory of Charity, a leaven of reform inside the Roman Curia.

Made titular Bishop of Methone in 1538 and coadjutor at Bergamo to his uncle, he followed him to Verona in 1544 and succeeded him in 1548, returning to Bergamo in 1558. Paul III sent him to Portugal to announce Trent, and he later presided at the council from 1551, when decrees on Eucharist, penance, and extreme unction passed. Nuncio to Poland in 1556, he faced Protestant threats to his life, and his eight-volume Lives of the ancient Fathers crowns his scholarship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-macerata-and-:
Macerata and Tolentino form a diocese in the Marches of central Italy. Macerata, a hill capital between the Chienti and Potenza with a sea view, takes its name from maceries, ruins. It rose on Helvia Recina, founded by Septimius Severus and destroyed by Alaric in 408.

Nicholas IV restored the town and founded its university in 1290, renewed by Paul III in 1540, and Malatesta and Sforza fought for it until the Sforza were expelled in 1441. Its cathedral holds a St. Michael mosaic by Calandra and a Madonna by Pinturicchio. Tolentino, ancient and martyred under Trajan in St. Catervus, keeps the Augustinian church of St. Nicholas, tomb of its patron, and joined Macerata in 1586.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mariano-armel:
Mariano Armellino was a Benedictine historian, born in Rome, or by other accounts Ancona, in 1657 and dead at Foligno in 1737. At twenty he entered St Paul's monastery in Rome, then went to Monte Cassino to finish his studies. From 1687 to 1695 he taught philosophy in Cassinese houses.

From 1697 to 1722 he gave himself to preaching and won fame across Italy for Lenten sermons. In 1722 Innocent XIII made him abbot at Siena, in 1729 moved him to St Peter's at Assisi, and in 1734 to St Felician near Foligno. His chief book, the Bibliotheca Benedictino-Cassinensis, lists and sketches every author of the Cassinese Congregation with care. A few other historical and hagiographical works on the same congregation complete his output, which Hurter and later Benedictine scholars cite as a solid guide.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mario-pagano:
Mario Pagano was a jurisconsult and man of letters, born at Brienza in 1748 and dead at Naples in 1799. At twenty he lectured on moral philosophy at Naples University while practising law. He wrote on criminal procedure, became law professor in 1787, and published political essays in 1792 on barbarian peoples and the rise and fall of civilised societies, following Vico.

As early as 1768 he had reviewed all Roman legislation, applauded for its Montesquieu flavour and current philosophy. His novel, partly daring theories won enemies, and despite court favour he was jailed. When France set up the Naples republic in 1799, Pagano stood among its most active men and wrote its constitution on the French Constitution of 1793. On monarchy's return he held Castel Nuovo to the last with fellow republicans. In prison he wrote aesthetic discourses and lyrics and dramas, of which only Gerbino and Agamemnon were printed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marsilio-fici:
Marsilio Ficino was a philosopher, philologist, and physician, born at Florence in 1433 and dead at Correggio in 1499. Son of Cosimo de' Medici's physician, he served the Medici for three generations and gained a villa at Monte Vecchio. Cosimo chose him to turn Plato into Latin.

The 1439 Council of Florence brought Greek scholars to the city, and the Platonic Academy, which Ficino headed, spurred Greek and Plato study. He praised Plato past measure, urged reading him in churches, and called Socrates and Plato forerunners of Christ. Ordained in 1477, he became a Florence cathedral canon. His Plato translation came out before Plato's Greek text appeared, and he also rendered Plotinus, Porphyry, Proclus, Homer's Hymns, and Hesiod. His chief work, Theologia Platonica of 1482, treats the soul as God's image in a great chain from God and back to God. His lasting merit was bringing Platonic thought to Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-cano:
Melchior Cano, Dominican bishop and theologian, was born at Tarancon in Cuenca, Spain, in 1509 and died at Toledo in 1560. His father, the learned jurist Ferdinand Cano, sent him young to Salamanca. There in 1523 he joined the Dominicans and was professed at St. Stephen's in 1524. Francis de Vitoria, holder of the first theology chair, taught him from 1527 to 1531.

Cano then studied at St. Gregory's, Valladolid, under Bartholomew of Carranza, taught philosophy, and rose to the second theology chair in 1536 and the first at Alcala in 1542. After Vitoria's death he won his master's Salamanca chair in 1546 and held it until 1552. Sent by the emperor to the Council of Trent early in 1551 with Dominic Soto, he served the council with historical learning and mastery of scholastic and positive theology. Charles V then presented him for the Canary bishopric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montalcino:
Montalcino is a small Tuscan town twenty miles from Siena, some 1,900 feet above sea level overlooking the Ombrone valley. Mineral springs and chalk quarries lie nearby. In the ninth century it belonged to the abbey of San Antimo. Its later story is a tug between Siena and Florence, changing hands after battles and sieges.

Taken by Siena in 1212, it declared for Florence, then fell back to Siena after Montaperti in 1260. In 1555 it became the last refuge of a free Sienese republic under Pietro Strozzi with French help. It submitted to Cosimo I in 1556. Its diocese, created in 1462 under Giovanni Cinughi and once administered by the future Pius III, counts 34 parishes and 39,130 souls, directly subject to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montepulciano:
Montepulciano, a diocese in the province of Siena, crowns the summit of Monte Poliziano. It descends from the ancient Etruscan city of Nocera Alfaterna, which allied with Rome against the Samnites in 308 BC. Florence held its allegiance in the Middle Ages until Siena conquered it in 1260. Its cathedral rose in 1619 from plans by Scalzo.

Notable buildings include the Madonna di San Biagio, planned by Antonio da Sangallo, the Tarugi and Contucci palaces, and a fourteenth-century town hall holding Sienese and Umbrian art. Its famous sons include Cardinal Bellarmine, Pope Marcellus II and the humanist Poliziano, and Saint Agnes died there in 1137. The see, created in 1561 under Spinello Benci, grew from a collegiate church whose archpriest became a mitred abbot in 1400.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-muro-lucano:
Basilicata's province of Potenza holds Muro Lucano, a town built where ancient Numistro stood, below the Apennines. Hannibal and Marcellus fought a Second Punic War battle on this ground. A fine cathedral graces the town, and its castle saw Queen Joan of Naples put to death at the command of Carlo of Durazzo, the son she had adopted.

Leo, in 1049, is the first Bishop of Muro on record. Antonio, bishop in 1376, sided with the antipope Clement VII; Carlo of Durazzo drove him to Polsino for shelter, and Clement then did away with the diocese. Guiduccio de Porta restored it in 1418, a man versed in civil and canon law. Later bishops of note were Cardinal Flavio Orsini, the poet Gian Carlo Coppola, and Alfonso Pacello, who set up a congregation to tend the diocese's sick.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niccola-pisan:
Niccola Pisano, architect and sculptor, was born at Pisa about 1205 to 1207 and died there in 1278. He was the father of modern plastic art. Barely past adolescence, he caught the notice of Frederick II of Swabia, who took him to his Rome coronation. Frederick then took him to Naples to complete Castel Capuano and Castel dell'Uovo from 1221 to 1231.

In 1233 Niccola was in Lucca, where the Deposition relief over the cathedral's side door may date from then. The marble Arca holding Saint Dominic's body at Bologna, said to be early work, shows maturity, and its Madonna and Child group foreshadows all Italian Madonnas. His designs built Padua's Saint Anthony basilica, and Venice's Frari church is also attributed to him. In Florence he designed Santa Trinita's interior, which Michelangelo loved and called his lady. Ordered to destroy a Guelph baptistery, he toppled its tower without touching the precious edifice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niccolo-alunn:
Niccolo Alunno, real name Niccolo di Liberatore, was a notable Umbrian painter in distemper, born about 1430 at Foligno and dead in 1502. Son of a painter and pupil of Bartolommeo di Tommaso, whose assistant was Benozzo Gozzoli, Fra Angelico's pupil, he blended simple Umbrian feeling with Florentine influence. His earliest known work, dated 1458, stands in the Franciscan church of La Diruta near Perugia.

He painted procession banners as well as altarpieces and other pictures, died rich, and is supposed by Mariotti to have taught Perugino, Pinturicchio and Andrea di Luigi. Some works ascribed to him may belong to a contemporary Alunno called Desiderato. A Madonna Enthroned hangs in Milan's Brera Gallery, altarpieces stand at Perugia, San Severino, Gualdo, La Bastia and Foligno, and one banner survives in a Perugia church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-sten:
Danish scientist and bishop Nicolaus Steno, born at Copenhagen in 1638, stood centuries ahead of his time in anatomy and geology. Studying in the Netherlands at twenty-two, he found the duct of the parotid gland and traced blood flow in the human body.

Passed over for a Copenhagen chair, Steno moved to Florence, where he turned Catholic in 1667 and made geological finds long ignored. Ordained priest and later bishop, he gave up comfort for mission work in northern Germany and died at Schwerin in 1686. His geological discoveries in Italy went unappreciated until modern times caught up with them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oristano:
Oristano, a Sardinian diocese suffragan to Cagliari, was capital of Arborea, the last giudicato to fall to Aragon in 1478. Given to the House of Sardi after Saracen expulsion and subject to Pisa, it was defended valiantly by Mariano against the Aragonese.

Bishops of Arborea appear first in Gregory VII's letters, Tragadorio built the cathedral in 1195, Guido Cattano joined the Franciscan poverty dispute in 1312, and Canopolo founded the seminary in 1588. United with Santa Giusta in 1503, the diocese counts 74 parishes and 97,000 people. Jacopo Serra, bishop in 1492, served as vicar of Rome and became a cardinal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perugino:
Perugino, born Pietro Vannucci at Città della Pieve in 1446, founded the Umbrian school of painting. He learned from the Perugian tradition of pure feeling, added his master Fiorenzo di Lorenzo's decorative taste, and absorbed Piero della Francesca's power. In 1472 he joined Verrocchio's Florence workshop beside Leonardo, mastering construction and perspective under a fixed, much-admired formula.

His earliest surviving work is the Delivery of the Keys to St. Peter of 1482 in the Sistine Chapel, where three companion frescoes later fell to Michelangelo's Last Judgment. Raphael, his great pupil, remembered the Keys in his own Sposalizio. Between 1484 and 1499 Perugino stood at his height, with commissions pouring in for religious houses. He died at Fontignano near Perugia in February 1524.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-colonn:
Pietro Colonna Galatino was a Franciscan philosopher, theologian, and Orientalist who argued the Christian case from Jewish books themselves. He was born at Galatina in Apulia and clothed as a friar by 1480. He mastered Greek, Hebrew, and Jewish Aramaic, taught at Ara Coeli in Rome, and served as provincial of Bari and penitentiary under Leo X.

His chief work, On the Secrets of Catholic Truth of 1516, defended Reuchlin in the quarrel over Jewish writings. He turned the Cabbala, Jewish mystical lore, to Christian proof in a dialogue between Reuchlin and the inquisitor Hochstraten. He admitted the book's faults, blamed haste, and still saw it run through several editions before his death at Rome soon after 1539.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-delfin:
Pietro Delfino, theologian, was born at Venice in 1444 and died 16 January 1525. He joined the Camaldolese house of San Michele on Murano, becoming its abbot in 1479. A year later he rose to lead the whole order, a post he kept until 1513. He then stepped down for his countryman Blessed Paul Giustiniani, to whom he had given the Camaldolese habit in 1510.

Counting from Saint Romuald, who founded the Camaldolese, Delfino stood forty-sixth among its generals, and the last chosen for life. His successors served only three years each. Venice sought him for the cardinalate in 1488, but he turned down the honour from Innocent VIII. More than four thousand of his letters survive, prized for honesty and for what they record of his order and the Church in his day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-sforza:
Pietro Sforza Pallavicino was an Italian cardinal, Jesuit theologian, and historian of the Council of Trent. He was born in 1607 to the noble Parma branch of his house and gave up his birthright as first-born. He took doctorates in philosophy and theology and served Urban VIII at Rome before entering the Jesuits in 1637 against his father's wishes.

He taught philosophy and then theology at the Roman College and sat on the commission that examined Jansen's writings. He defended his order in a long refutation of its critics in 1649. His great history of Trent, written against the Protestant historian Sarpi, and his nine-book dogmatic work made him one of the leading Catholic scholars of his century before his death in 1667.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-puno:
The Diocese of Puno, suffragan of the Archdiocese of Lima in Peru, covers the whole Department of Puno. This encyclopedia entry counts its Catholic population in 1900 at 260,810 souls, served by 85 priests in 62 parishes, with 320 churches and chapels. The bishop lives at the city of Puno. The bishopric arose by a law of the republic on 26 November 1832, and by a Bull of Pius the Ninth dated 6 November 1861, approved by executive resolution in September 1865.

Its first bishop, named on 17 June 1861 and consecrated on 7 April 1862, resigned before taking up his duties. His successor, Juan Ambrosio Huerta, named in June 1865, moved to Arequipa in 1875. Pedro José Chavez followed, consecrated on 25 July 1875, and Juan Estebánes came next. A diocesan seminary in Puno city trains priests, and public and private schools, some tied to parishes, round out a well-supplied diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reginald-of-p:
Reginald of Piperno, Dominican theologian and companion of Saint Thomas Aquinas, was born at Piperno about 1230 and died about 1290. He entered the Dominican Order at Naples, and Thomas chose him as companion and confessor at Rome about 1260. From then on he stayed constantly at the saint's side, and his testimony recurs in the process for Thomas's canonization. Thomas dedicated several works to this disciple.

In 1272 prayer from Thomas cured him of a fever, and that year he began teaching beside Thomas at Naples. He stood at the doctor's deathbed, heard his general confession, and gave the funeral oration in 1274. Back at Naples he probably took his master's chair, and he gathered all of Thomas's works together. Four short works survive as his notes from the saint's lectures. A book printed at Bologna in 1529 under his name belongs to the humanist Flaminius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rossano:
Rossano is an archdiocese in Calabria, in southern Italy, near the Gulf of Taranto. It was the ancient Roscianum, a Roman colony ravaged by Totila, which the Saracens failed to conquer. In 982 Otto II captured it temporarily from the Byzantines. It kept its Greek character long after the Norman conquest. Its cathedral holds an ancient image of the Madonna not made by hands.

Rossano was the birthplace of St Nilus, founder of Grottaferrata, and St Bartholomew, another abbot there. The first known bishop is Valerianus, of the Roman Council of 680, though Cappelletti names Saturninus. The Greek Rite, introduced in the tenth century or earlier, lasted until the sixteenth, despite attempts to introduce the Latin Rite in 1092 and 1460. It was abandoned in the cathedral in 1571 and throughout the city half a century later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salerno:
Salerno, a diocese in Campania in southern Italy, stands on a gulf of the same name beneath a high rock crowned by an ancient castle. A natural harbour drives trade in farm produce, horses are bred widely, and two mineral springs draw visitors. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with the city and its great cathedral before turning to church history.

Built by Robert Guiscard, the cathedral is reached through a porticoed court of granite and porphyry columns holding ancient sarcophagi, with bronze middle doors richly worked. Inside, a mosaic candelabrum survives from the old basilica, Gregory VII lies in the chapel of Giovanni da Procida, and a Pietà by Andrea Salerno graces another chapel. The entry then traces bishops, schools, and the famed medical tradition of the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-marco-and:
San Marco and Bisignano, a united diocese in Cosenza province, Calabria, joins two Norman-rooted sees. San Marco Argentano, named for nearby ancient Argenta, was founded in the eleventh century by the Norman Drogo, who raised a high tower there. Bisignano, ancient Besidias, became a Norman count's seat and later an Orsini fief. Their short entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gives the union's history in brief.

In 1467 Skanderbeg's daughter, wife of Bisignano's prince, invited many Albanian families who founded colonies, kept their own tongue, and used the Greek Rite. Bishops appear from 1179 at San Marco and from the tenth century at Bisignano, where Federico, bishop in 1331, was killed in 1339. United in 1818 and directly subject to Rome, the dioceses count sixty-four parishes, 256 priests, and 110,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-marino:
San Marino, an independent republic between the Italian provinces of Forlì, Pesaro, and Urbino, covers 38 square miles with 10,000 people living mainly by farming and vines. Two captains-regent, chosen for six months from a General Council of sixty life members drawn equally from nobles, burgesses, and landowners, carry on the government. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes a tiny state that outlasted empires.

The council makes laws, and from its members comes the Council of Twelve, the supreme court. Italy recognised San Marino's independence by acts of 22 March 1862 and has kept friendly relations since. Seven hills make up the territory, with the city of San Marino on the highest, Mount Titano, and nine communes with as many parishes, split between the dioceses of Montefeltro and Rimini.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-martino-a:
San Martino al Cimino, a prelature nullius within the diocese of Viterbo, sits 1,840 feet up on Monte Fogliano's western slope in the Cimini mountains. Amid chestnut forests, it is much visited as a health resort. Its head, titled abbot, rules only the single parish commune of San Martino. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a monastery turned collegiate church.

First a Benedictine abbey mentioned under Benedict VIII, it passed in 1150 to Cistercians of St Sulpice near Belley. In 1207 it came to Pontigny's monks, who under Abbot John raised it to great prosperity. After 1379 its abbots were commendatory, and in 1564 it joined St Peter's chapter mensa. In 1645 Olimpia Pamphili, sister of Innocent X, bought castle and abbey and founded the collegiate chapter that still exists, with its Gothic church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-severino:
San Severino, a small town and bishopric in Macerata province in the Marches of central Italy, owns two cathedrals. The ancient one near the old castle holds precious fifteenth-century paintings and inlaid choir stalls. The new cathedral, dating from 1821, was once the Augustinian church and holds works by Pinturicchio, the Gentile brothers, and Pomarancio. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tours a town of pictures.

Churches of St Dominic and St Francis carry fine pictures too, and Santa Maria in Doliolo, once Benedictine, has a crypt thought to be a converted temple of Feronia. The communal palace, the chief civic building, holds decorated halls and ancient inscriptions. San Severino stands on Septempeda, a Picene town turned Roman colony, and in the eighth century it served as a fortress of the duchy of Spoleto.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santes-pagnin:
Santes Pagnino, also called Xantes, was a Dominican philologist and Bible scholar born at Lucca in 1470 who died at Lyons on 24 August 1541. At sixteen he took the habit at Fiesole, studying under Savonarola and other great teachers, and in Florence's new study of Eastern tongues he showed rare quickness and depth. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a scholar-priest across Italy and France.

His learning won him friends among the Medici cardinals who became Leo X and Clement VII. As a preacher his zeal matched his scholarship. Called to Rome by Leo X, he taught at the new free school for Eastern languages until his patron died in 1521. Three years at Avignon followed, then seven at Lyons, where he helped found a plague hospital and, by preaching, turned away Waldensian and Lutheran inroads from the city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-silvio-antoni:
Silvio Antoniano, cardinal and writer on education, was born at Rome on 31 December 1540 and died there on 16 August 1603. Ferrara University gave him a doctorate in laws in 1556 and made him professor of classical literature. In 1563 Pius IV called him to the belles-lettres chair at the Sapienza, where he befriended Saint Charles Borromeo. He resigned in 1566, studied theology under Saint Philip Neri, and was ordained priest on 12 June 1568.

Sharing the humanist enthusiasm of his day, he turned to problems of education. At Borromeo's prompting he wrote his chief work on the Christian education of children, published at Verona in 1583. Clement VIII made him Secretary of Papal Briefs in 1593 and cardinal in 1599. The work's marks are insight into a child's mind, sympathy with its dangers and needs, and care for moral training, with advice on physical culture as well.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sovana-and-pi:
Sovana and Pitigliano formed a single diocese in the province of Grosseto in central Italy. It joined two towns with very different fates. Sovana, an ancient Etruscan city, stayed important into the thirteenth century as capital of the Aldobrandeschi counts. It withstood a siege by Frederick II in 1240, then faded after passing to the Orsini, who moved to healthier Pitigliano.

Pitigliano, first mentioned in 1081, fell to Siena in 1401. After Count Gentile Orsini was killed at Sovana in 1434, its people sacked Sovana and sealed its decay. By 1833 Sovana held only 64 inhabitants. The diocese also held the famed Vallombrosan abbey of Monte Calvello, and the entry ties church geography to centuries of Tuscan rivalry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-agnes-of-m:
St. Agnes of Montepulciano was a Dominican prioress whose religious life began in childhood. Born near Montepulciano in Tuscany about 1268, she entered a monastery at nine. Four years later Pope Nicholas IV charged her to help found a house at Proceno, where she became prioress at fifteen. She died at Montepulciano in 1317.

At her townspeople's urging she established the celebrated convent of Dominican nuns at Montepulciano in 1298 and governed it until her death. Canonized by Benedict XIII in 1726, with her feast on 20 April, she stands in the entry as a girl abbess who became the spiritual centre of her native town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-andrew-ave:
St. Andrew Avellino, born Lancelotto at Castronuovo in Sicily in 1521 and dead on 10 November 1608, was a Theatine priest famed for chastity and preaching. This entry follows a youth who loved chastity from early years, studied humanities and philosophy at Venice, took the tonsure to escape female admirers. He then went to Naples to study canon and civil law, earning a doctorate and ordination at twenty-six.

For a time he practised as a lawyer at Naples' ecclesiastical court, until one day, pleading a friend's cause, a lie slipped out in the heat of argument. Reading soon after a passage in the Bible that condemned such speech. He resolved to leave the law, and the entry follows him into the Theatines, where he changed his name out of love for the cross.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anno:
St. Anno, or Hanno, was archbishop of Cologne from 1055, and this entry follows a soldier turned churchman of rare force. Entering the Church very young under his uncle, a canon of Bamberg, after first taking up arms, he won notice for sacred and profane learning and unusual virtue. Emperor Henry III called him to court, where his handsome presence, rare eloquence, and gift for great undertakings marked him out.

A lover of right and justice who defended them fearlessly, he accepted Cologne with the greatest repugnance, his consecration a scene of unwonted splendour that tried him sorely. At Henry's death Empress Agnes made him regent of the empire and gave him charge of the young prince, the future Henry IV, already spoiled by flatterers. The entry follows that charge with admiration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-beuno:
St. Beuno was abbot of Clynnog, dead in 660, perhaps, and this entry follows a missioner of Powis-land. According to the Bucced Beuno, he was born in Powis, then educated and ordained at the Bangor monastery in North Wales before becoming an active missioner. Cadvan, king of Gwynedd, was his generous benefactor. Cadwallon, Cadvan's son and successor, deceived Beuno over some land, and when the saint demanded justice, he refused to yield.

Cadwallon's cousin Gweddeint then gave his township to God and Beuno forever, in reparation. There the saint, about 616, founded the abbey of Clynnog Fawr in Carnarvonshire. Beuno became the guardian of his niece, the virgin St. Winefride, and, the entry says, he restored her to life. Her clients still obtain marvellous favours at Holywell in Flintshire. Hardened sinners found him relentless, but those in distress found him full of compassion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-joseph-of-:
Joseph of Cupertino, mystic of levitations and gaping ecstasies, was nicknamed Open Mouth as a schoolboy. Born on 17 June 1603, surnamed from Cupertino village between Brindisi and Otranto, he was son of Felice Desa, a poor carpenter who died before Joseph's birth, leaving debts. Creditors drove his mother Francesca Panara from home, and she bore him in a stable. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Osimo to 18 September 1663.

At eight he had an ecstatic vision at school, renewed several times, and children, seeing him gape and stare, lost to all around him, called him Bocca Aperta. He had a hot, irascible temper his strict mother strove to overcome. Apprenticed to a shoemaker, he sought the Friars Minor Conventuals at seventeen and was refused for ignorance. Accepted as a Capuchin lay brother at Martino in 1620, his continual ecstasies marked a mystic life the entry follows to Osimo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-nicholas-o:
Nicholas of Tolentino, an Augustinian hermit of the March of Ancona, spent his last thirty years preaching almost daily at Tolentino. Born at Sant'Angelo near Fermo about 1246, he was made a canon of St Saviour's while still a student. A sermon by an Augustinian hermit on loving not the world moved him to join that order, with his parents' joyful consent.

He made profession before nineteen and was sent from house to house as a model of generous striving. After ordination he preached with striking success, notably at Tolentino, where he died on 10 September 1306. He is pictured in the black Augustinian habit, with a star, a lily, or a crucifix garlanded with lilies. The entry joins a gentle preacher to a lasting local devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-pacificus-:
Pacificus of San Severino, a Franciscan of the March of Ancona, bore nearly twenty-nine years of lameness, deafness, and blindness with patience. Born at San Severino on 1 March 1653, he lost both parents soon after his confirmation at three and suffered hardship until he took the Franciscan habit at Forano in December 1670. Ordained in 1678, he taught philosophy to younger friars and then preached missions in the surrounding country.

When infirmity ended his mission work, he turned to contemplation, worked miracles, and knew ecstasies. Even as a constant sufferer he served as guardian at Maria delle Grazie in San Severino in 1692 and 1693. He died there on 24 September 1721, was beatified in 1786, and was canonised in 1839. His feast falls on 24 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-zeno:
Zeno, bishop of Verona, is entered in the Martyrology on 12 April as a martyr under Gallienus, though he was probably a confessor. He likely governed Verona's Church from 362 to 380. A basilica, San Zenone, honours him at Verona, and some thirty churches and chapels bear his name.

His statue in episcopal insignia stands prominent in the basilica's choir, and coins bearing his likeness once circulated. His body's translation on 21 May and his consecration on 6 December were formerly commemorated. Jerome and Gennadius omit him, but Ambrose calls him a bishop of holy memory, and Gregory tells a miracle at his Verona church. A poem from Ratherius's writings lists him eighth among Verona's bishops. The entry sifts a thin record with care.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stefano-mader:
Stefano Maderno, a sculptor of the Roman school just before Bernini, is remembered for one statue above all. Born in 1576 and dead in 1636, probably of Lombard origin near Como, he may have been related to Carlo Maderna, architect and sculptor of Bissone. His works appear often in churches where Carlo laboured. He began by copying the antique and made highly esteemed bronze models.

His fame rests on the statue of Cecilia over her tomb in St Cecilia in Trastevere, Rome, executed in his twenty-third year and never surpassed or equalled. The martyr's body, found by Paschal I in Callistus's catacomb and viewed anew unchanged in 1599, was reproduced by Clement VIII's command. Maderno carved a delicate, small body lying face down, knees together, arms crossed at the wrists, head veiled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-terracina-sez:
Terracina, Sezze, and Piperno form a diocese in Rome's province. Terracina city stands near the Amaseno estuary, on a promontory for the old town and beside the Via Appia for Pius VI's new town. Its harbour, among the safest, serves coasters exporting grain, wine, oil, and vegetables from marshes and hills. Hunting and fishing also profit it. The cathedral of St Caesareus holds pillars of the temple of Rome and Augustus and a mosaic ambo.

On a promontory stand ruins of the temple of Venus, with fortifications and Theodoric's palace. Terracina, Roman Tarracina and ancient Auxur, was a Latin city under the kings.
