Volscians captured it, ceding it to Rome in 406, and Hannibal failed to take it after Capua. Antoninus Pius enlarged its harbour. Pepin gave it to the Holy See, Byzantines seized it about 780, and Charlemagne expelled them. Saracens landed in the ninth century, and the Frangipani held it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-of-cel:
Thomas of Celano, Franciscan friar, poet and writer of saints' lives, was born at Celano about 1200 and died about 1255. One of the first disciples of St. Francis, he joined the order probably in 1215. In 1221 he went with Caesar of Speyer on the mission to Germany, and the next year he became custodian of the houses at Mainz, Worms, Speyer and Cologne.

Back in Italy by September 1223, he lived close to Francis himself. After Francis was canonized in July 1228, Thomas wrote the First Life at Gregory IX's order, then a Second Life between 1244 and 1247, and later a treatise on Francis's miracles. He also wrote two sequences in honour of Francis, and most likely the Dies Irae and the Life of St. Clare.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urbino:
Urbino is a city of the province of Pesaro and Urbino in Italy, set on a hill between the Metaurus and Foglia valleys in mountainous but well-tilled country. Its cathedral, near the ducal palace, was designed by Count Federico da Montefeltro but wholly transformed in the nineteenth century, after its sixteenth-century cupola and much of the building fell in 1789. Valuable pictures survive there, including a Last Supper and a St Sebastian by Barocci.

Other churches include St Francis, finished in 1350, partly Romanesque and partly Gothic, with sculptures by Constantino Trappola and paintings by Barocci and Procaccini, and St Dominic. The entry moves from churches and art to the diocese, its bishops, and the ducal court that made Urbino famed. It offers a compact guide to a hill city of art and church history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vigevano:
Vigevano is a Lombard diocese in the province of Pavia, its city a great agricultural centre where gold was still washed from the Ticino into the mid-nineteenth century. Its cathedral, built in 1100 and rebuilt in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries by the architect-bishop Caramuel Lobkowitz. Stands beside the Dominican church of St Peter Martyr, built by Filippo Maria Visconti in 1445, and Bramante's castle of 1492, now a royal palace.

Earliest notices date from the tenth century, when King Arduin favoured it for hunting. A Ghibelline commune, it was besieged and taken by Milan in 1201 and 1275, surrendered to Azzone Visconti in 1328, shared Milan's fortunes, endured a siege by its native son Francesco Sforza. Passed to Sardinia by the Treaty of Worms in 1743. Until 1530 it belonged to Novara, and Sforza procured its erection as a diocese.
doe-osti-2997305-radiation-effects-on-ne:
What radiation does to networks-on-chip is studied by Matthew Cannon, Paul Thelen, Amiya Kumar, and co-authors, in Sandia report SAND2025-12148 dated September 2025. A network-on-chip links the many cores inside a modern processor package, including AI accelerator engines. In space and defense settings, radiation can flip bits and hang the fabric that every core shares.

The project built firmware and test scripts for a chip image containing a Versal AI Core, checking logic through on-chip debug tools. Two radiation test campaigns ran at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and Texas A&M University, with firmware upgrades between them, including fuller use of the AI engine. Results show which functions survive exposure and which need hardening, guiding chip choices for high-radiation missions.
doe-osti-3004847-musikal-multiphysics-si:
Clint Dawson of the University of Texas at Austin leads a four-institution team in the final report for DOE award DE-SC0022316. The project, MuSIKAL, built a coastal digital twin: a living simulation of the Gulf Coast that blends models and data to predict flooding. Storm surge and heavy rainfall events, like Hurricane Harvey's Houston flooding, are the driving cases.

Partners at Notre Dame, Louisiana State University, and Pacific Northwest brought storm surge modeling, high-performance computing, and earth science. Machine learning accelerators speed the multiphysics simulations so forecasts can run at useful scales. The twin framework also folds in land use and demographics, since flood harm depends on who and what sits in the water's path. The report's long publication and talk list shows the platform being carried to the coastal modeling community.
doe-osti-3005014-demonstration-of-electr:
Mark Williamson, Krista L. Hawthorne, Bethany Dean-Kersten, and colleagues at Argonne summarize a demonstration in final CRADA report ANL/CFC-C2024-24534. Under a GAIN voucher, the lab worked with Global Nuclear Fuel, Americas to convert uranium oxide powder to uranium metal by electroreduction. Metallic fuel for advanced reactors starts from such metal, and GNF's oxide comes straight off its production line.

Five electroreduction tests were run on batches up to 0.33 kilograms of oxide, at currents up to 16 amperes. Reduction was thorough and the metal product stayed clean. The oxide powder, fresh from converting uranium hexafluoride, is unusually fine, and fine powder had not been reduced this way before. Particle size proved no obstacle. The result gives GNF a scalable route from its existing product to metallic fuel feedstock.
doe-osti-3009668-extended-gutzwiller-app:
An extended form of the Gutzwiller approximation is set out by Nikhil Seshadri and Yu Zhang of Los Alamos in LA-UR-25-32176, issued December 19, 2025 under the SULI program. The Gutzwiller method is a wave function shortcut for strongly correlated electrons; this extension adds nonlocal correlations.

The target systems are cavity quantum materials, where light trapped in a cavity mixes with matter and can steer its state. The extended framework folds in electron-electron and electron-photon interactions that act between sites, not just on one site. Tests across coupling regimes show the added correlations helping to stabilize exotic phases. This is part one, the theory, of a planned series.
doe-osti-3377914-commercialization-of-re:
Commercialization of the Reflected Target Non-Intrusive Assessment tool, or ReTNA, is the subject of a Technology Commercialization Fund final report, TCF-23-20118, issued as NLR/TP-5700-99466 in July 2026. Devon Kesseli and Grant Zheng of the National Laboratory of the Rockies worked with Kyle Kattke and Patrick Marcotte of Solar Dynamics LLC. ReTNA analyzes the optics of heliostats, the mirrors that aim sunlight in concentrating solar plants, indoors and without touching them.

Heliostat fields live or die on aim: a mirror slightly off sends its reflected spot off the receiver. An indoor, non-intrusive measurement tool lets makers and operators check mirror shape and focus before a field is built or during maintenance. The report closes out the fund's base technology work on bringing that tool toward the market.
doe-osti-3936611-core-model-proposal-411:
Seven Pacific Northwest National Laboratory staff propose a major upgrade to the GCAM energy and climate model in Core Model Proposal 411, report PNNL-39503, dated September 2026. Xin Zhao, Pralit L. Patel, and James A. Edmonds head the author list. The new part is a macro-economic module called KLEAM, paired with updates to the farm sector.

GCAM tracks how energy, land, and trade shift over decades across world regions. KLEAM adds fuller links between farm wages, worker movement, and growth. One change sets how fast farm worker output can rise in each region, scaled by how far that region has moved out of farm work. The authors argue the caps keep the model from showing farm wage gaps that real economies do not keep. Model users get the full case for the change.
don-orsino:
F. Marion Crawford continues his Saracinesca family saga in Don Orsino, first issued by Macmillan in 1891 and reprinted many times since. Young Don Orsino lives in the newer Rome with his father and mother in the vast old palace that has housed his line for centuries. The narrator warns that he writes as a historian, pinning facts like moths with dates for pins.

The opening chapters place Orsino among the last of the old Roman princes' world, where most of his father's peers are dead and a new Italy is forming. Palace rooms, family pride, and quiet talks carry the early action; one scene lingers on a pale lady in dim light and a love that dares not speak plainly. Crawford builds the tale on manners and blood, showing an old order's heir caught between duty to his house and his own heart.
father-damien-an-open-letter-to-the-reve:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Father Damien as an open letter in 1890, and it became one of the great defenses in English prose. Father Damien, a Belgian priest, had given his life to the leper settlement on Molokai in Hawaii, and died of the disease himself. A Honolulu clergyman, the Reverend Dr. Hyde, then wrote a letter calling Damien coarse, dirty, and impure. It reached print, and Stevenson answered.

Stevenson had visited Molokai and seen the settlement's work. He answers Hyde charge by charge, in anger held to a fine edge, and closes by asking what Hyde had risked beside his desk. The letter was published for charity in Damien's honor, and it still reads as a model of righteous rebuttal.
giordano-bruno:
Walter Pater's essay Giordano Bruno, Paris: 1586, reconstructs an afternoon at the Sorbonne. On Whit-Sunday curious Parisians crowd to hear a Dominican friar who skipped the university mass. Bruno speaks at length about the Spirit, stressing how freely and independently it works. Pater sets the scene in the last Valois kings' Paris. Into it steps the Nolan philosopher with his doctrine of an infinite universe, alive in every part.

Pater treats Bruno as a temperament before a heretic: a mind drunk on the unity and liberty of spirit. The essay follows his teaching toward the stake at Rome in 1600, without letting the fire swallow the man. Readers get one of Pater's finest imaginary portraits in essay form. It is also a lost chapter of his Gaston de Latour, the Renaissance studied through its boldest friar.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SzebedinskyGeno: Columnist Jack Anderson used his October 1971 Washington Post column to attack praise coming from the White House. President Nixon and Vice President Agnew had lauded an editor whose views Anderson identifies as anti-Jewish, Geno Szebedinsky. Anderson, famous for exposing official misconduct, treated the praise as a scandal worth naming in print. The article shows his muckraking style at work on the Nixon administration.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WatergateIndict: nsia-WatergateIndictment3-7-74EllsbergNotes Watergate Indictment 3-7-74 Ellsberg Notes: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
i-say-no:
Wilkie Collins opens I Say No at a girls' school, where Emily Brown and her friends hold a smuggled supper in a bedroom black and still under Miss Ladd's strict rules. Emily, an orphan whose father's death in Australia hides a mystery, leaves school to become a governess and companion. Her friend Cecilia Wyvil and the steadfast Alban Morris enter her story.

A crumpled letter signed by Emily's schoolmistress, found by Dr Allday, tightens the web around the secret of her father's disgrace and the identity of Miss Jethro. Collins builds the novel on his title's refusal: Emily will not accept the charity or the explanations offered her. Late Collins, this tale mixes sensation plotting with an unusually stubborn heroine's moral independence.
kimono:
Kimono is John Paris's novel of an Anglo-Japanese marriage, published in 1922. Fourteen chapter headings map the story. The early chapters cover the marriage itself and the honeymoon eastwards. A chapter named Nagasaki and one called Across Japan carry the couple into the country.

An embassy chapter and one on a half-caste girl widen the view. Ito San, the Yoshiwara women, and a geisha dinner follow in the list. The family altar, dwarf trees, the great Buddha of Kamakura, and Nikko close the contents. Paris uses the marriage plot to show two cultures meeting and misunderstanding each other. The novel reads as both love story and a period tour of Japan for English readers.
love-at-arms-being-a-narrative-excerpted:
Rafael Sabatini's Love-at-Arms, dated 1907, retells a tale from the chronicles of Urbino. That small Italian court was ruled by Guidobaldo da Montefeltro. The book begins with the voice of the people, then a mountain path. A young swordsman is soon deep in love and danger.

Chapters bring Monna Valentina, the insidious Gonzaga, and an amorous duke. A fool asks questions that no courtier dares to ask. Vows, plots, and duels carry the story to its close. Sabatini loved old Italy, and his research shows in every scene. Readers get romance, treachery, and swordplay in rich measure.
meno:
Plato's Meno opens with a blunt question: can virtue be taught? Socrates answers that he does not even know what virtue is. Benjamin Jowett's translation and introduction frame the dialogue for English readers. The conversation becomes a lesson in how to define anything at all.

Meno offers lists of virtues for each age and station, but Socrates wants one shared meaning. Attempts to define virtue as power, or as delight in honorable things, also fail. Along the way Socrates uses shape and color to show how definitions work. The dialogue remains a starting point for debates about teaching and knowledge.
modern-prose-and-poetry-for-secondary-sc:
Margaret Ashmun edited this school anthology for Houghton Mifflin in 1914. Ashmun had taught English at the University of Wisconsin. The title promises modern prose and poetry for secondary schools, with notes, study helps, and reading lists. Every selection appears by special permission of its copyright owner.

The Riverside Press printed the book at Cambridge, Massachusetts. A transcriber's note explains the symbols replacing pronunciation marks. Such apparatus helped teachers guide students through unfamiliar words and authors. Anthologies like this one shaped what American high-school students read as modern literature, pairing classroom selections with guidance for further reading.
sylvie-and-bruno:
Lewis Carroll's Sylvie and Bruno opens with verses asking whether all our life is but a dream seen faintly in a golden gleam athwart time's dark stream. The book is Carroll's last long work of fiction, a fairy tale woven through a story of grown-up life in England.

The contents promise the mixture at once: Less Bread! More Taxes! gives the first chapter its cry, then come a birthday party, a cunning conspiracy, a beggar's palace, and a magic locket. Sylvie and Bruno, the fairy children, ride on a lion, meet a jester and a bear, visit Dogland, and encounter the other professor. Carroll's nonsense songs and wordplay run beside a serious story of love and duty in the waking world.
the-brochure-series-of-architectural-ill: The Brochure Series of Architectural Illustration, Volume I, came out in Boston from Bates and Guild in 1895. The pages shown are the volume's index and list of plates, with no editor or author named. The first plates show Venetian palaces: the southwest angle of the Ducal Palace, Palazzo Contarini Fasan, and Palazzo Cavalli. Then come Byzantine-Romanesque doorways in Apulia, at the cathedrals of Trani and Conversano and the basilica at Altamura. The cloister at Monreale in Sicily gives four plates of its double capitals. Vitale, close the list shown.
the-first-soprano:
Mary Hitchcock wrote The First Soprano as a tale of church life, printed at Cleveland in 1912. The contents move from a church service and a choir rehearsal to a church social and a missionary meeting.

The tale opens on a Sunday in a church at New Laodicea, with the organ sounding and the choir in the rear loft. Well-dressed crowds fill the pews in a soft stir of silk. Pride, fine music, and true faith clash in such a house. Heads like Is God Demonstrable and Sell That Ye Have show a soprano pressed to weigh her gift, her wealth, and her soul.
the-golden-volcano: Jules Verne wrote The Golden Volcano. Edward Baxter translated and edited this version. Olivier Dumas wrote a preface to the French edition. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list in two parts. Part I runs from An Uncle's Legacy and The Two Cousins. It runs through Montreal to Vancouver, Skagway, and the Chilkoot Pass. It reaches Dawson City and a claim in the Klondike. Part II opens with A Winter in the Klondike.
the-indolence-of-the-filipino:
José Rizal wrote this essay in Spanish for a Madrid review. La Solidaridad printed it in five parts. They ran from July 15 to September 15, 1890. Charles Derbyshire translated it into English here. He also Englished Rizal's two great novels. James A. Robertson added the notes. The editor praises Derbyshire's faithful rendering. Robertson's notes show the breadth of Rizal's learning.

The editor also tells the frontispiece's story. Rizal sketched his own face in Berlin in 1887. Professor Blumentritt knew him only by letter. The sketch would let Blumentritt spot him at a station. Rizal's essay takes up a standing charge against Filipinos. Their supposed laziness is its subject. He answers the charge from history. The essay belongs to his campaign of blunt truths.
the-inferno:
Henri Barbusse wrote this novel. Under Fire had made his name. An English edition appeared in 1918. It was translated from the hundredth French edition. Edward J. O'Brien supplied an introduction. Chapter I settles the narrator in a boarding-house room. Madame Lemercier has praised the house's advantages. She leaves him alone at last. He stands before the glass and looks around. The room is grey and smells of dust.

Everything in the room feels worn by strangers. Two chairs and smeary armchairs furnish it. A table holds a piece of green felt. The carpet is frayed from door to window. A path of feet has worn it down. The mantelpiece has lost its sharp edges. Paint is smudged where hands touch most. Barbusse turns a cheap lodging into a meditation. Human contact wears the world down slowly. The narrator calls himself a man like every other man.
the-memories-of-fifty-years-containing-b: W. H. Sparks published The Memories of Fifty Years at Philadelphia and Macon, Georgia, in 1870. Only the title page, dedication, and the first sentence of the preface are present here, so the memoirs themselves do not appear. The title promises brief biographical notices of distinguished Americans and anecdotes of remarkable men, drawn from a long life of observation spent chiefly in the Southwest. Sparks dedicated the volume to his brother Ovid Garten Sparks and his nephew Colonel Thomas Hardeman of Macon.
the-story-of-geographical-discovery-how-: Joseph Jacobs tells how the world became known in twelve chapters, with twenty-four maps. Chapters begin with the world of the ancients. Medieval travels and routes to the Indies follow. The partition of America comes next. Tasman and Cook explore the South Seas. African and polar exploration follow. Annals of discovery close the book. Only the opening pages and lists appear here. A note explains Sebastian del Cano's arms. His ship first circled the globe. A note on a Babylonian map follows. Jacobs's narrative itself does not appear.
the-voyage-of-verrazzano:
Henry C. Murphy argues that the claim of discovery in America by Verrazzano has no real basis. His pages form part of a larger work on the first European voyages to the coast that became the United States. A new map said to be by Hieronimo de Verrazano had just been produced, with a learned memoir by J. Carson Brevoort in its support. That prompted Murphy to print his chapter on its own.

He adds papers on Verrazzano that Buckingham Smith brought from archives in Spain and Portugal before his death. George H. Moore placed them at his disposal. The letter said to be Verrazzano's had come down in a fragmentary, distorted form through Ramusio's collection. Murphy prints it complete in Dr. Cogswell's English version, so readers can judge the passages he examines.
tieck-the-old-man-of-the-mountain-the-lo:
Three Romantic tales by Ludwig Tieck travel together in this English volume. The Old Man of the Mountain opens the set, followed by The Lovecharm and Pietro of Abano. The last tells of the medieval scholar Pietro, rumored in legend to command magic and spirits.

Folklore, history, and the supernatural blend in all three stories, each in a different key. A love charm works too well; a mountain elder keeps his secret; a scholar's learning brushes the demonic. Tieck moves among the modes with effortless control. The tales capture German Romanticism's fascination with the borderland between the natural and the marvelous. Short-story readers will find the set rich and strange.
